detail.abstract: This case-based exercise places students inside the project manager's office on a USD 200 million retail megaproject in Pakistan and asks them to do what every project manager dreads: deliver early, without raising risk. Set in Lahore in June 2013, the case unfolds against the global statistical reality that nine out of ten megaprojects run over schedule and over budget (Flyvbjerg, 2014). Students convert a fixed Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) into a workable schedule on a project management software, allocate contractors and service providers as resources, identify the critical path, and then compress the schedule by tweaking dependencies, working overtime, and adding resources, without inflating cost-related risks already identified in the project's risk register.

title: Integration Without Cohesion: Fragmentation as Institutional Equilibrium in Africa and Beyond

detail.abstract:
Why does regional integration remain limited despite the expansion of formal frameworks? In Africa, decades of political commitment to continental unity, culminating in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and early implementation initiatives such as the Guided Trade Initiative, have not produced corresponding levels of functional integration in trade, mobility, or policy coordination. Existing explanations emphasize institutional weakness, sovereignty constraints, or external dependency, although these dimensions are often examined separately.

Drawing on theories of regional integration and comparative political economy, this article investigates the enduring gap between formal integration and functional cohesion. It argues that fragmentation should be understood not merely as a consequence of institutional weakness or adverse external conditions, but as a self-reinforcing institutional equilibrium shaped by the interaction of identity regimes, economic structures, and political authority. To account for these dynamics, the article develops a three-walls framework organized around the emotional wall, the economic wall, and the social wall. These dimensions explain how exclusionary citizenship regimes, economic insecurity and market fragmentation, and political incentives reinforce patterns of separation across multiple levels.

The analysis identifies the conditions under which integration becomes politically and economically viable while recognizing the trade-offs associated with sovereignty, distribution, and authority. Fragmentation emerges as a durable equilibrium sustained through feedback effects across social, economic, and political spheres. By situating African integration within the wider dynamics of the global political economy, the article contributes to debates on regionalism, comparative political economy, and postcolonial governance and offers analytical leverage for understanding persistent fragmentation across the Global South.

title: Formalising the Skill Supply Chain: Human Capital Bottlenecks and Sustainable Manufacturing in Pakistan's Furniture Sector

detail.title: Formalising the Skill Supply Chain: Human Capital Bottlenecks and Sustainable Manufacturing in Pakistan's Furniture Sector
detail.abstract: Sustainable supply-chain management theory has now expanded enough to encompass the social dimensions of production, yet the social arm of the triple bottom line has received less architectural attention than the environmental. In skill-based product industries-where product quality depends on the tacit, embodied capability of artisans rather than on machinery or process specification-this asymmetry leaves a critical upstream resource ungoverned. This chapter argues that in such industries, the skilled artisan is not merely a labour input but an upstream capability supplier whose reliability, renewal and credibility are conditions of sustainable production. In the craft-production traditions of South Asia, this figure is the Karigar. Drawing on Pakistan's furniture sector as an empirical case, and on the Karigar Initiative-an emerging skill-formation intervention anchored in a large formal furniture manufacturer in Pakistan-the chapter develops the Credible Skill Supply Chain Framework: a seven-stage architecture through which tacit craft knowledge is signalled, recognised, translated, formed, certified, absorbed and governed for renewal. The framework extends Seuring and Müller's (2008) TBL-SSCM social dimension from a compliance register into an architectural one, and generates four mutually reinforcing sustainability outcomes: economic, social, environmental and institutional. The chapter argues that formalisation should not erase informal mastery but make it visible, teachable, certifiable and renewable. In skill-intensive product industries, the sustainability of the supply chain depends on the sustainability of the skill-formation system that feeds it.

title: The Fire and the Train: Discourse, Power, and Decision in the Lahore Orange Line Metro Project

detail.title: The Fire and the Train: Discourse, Power, and Decision in the Lahore Orange Line Metro Project
detail.abstract: On the morning of 13 January 2017, Uzair Shah, General Manager (Operations) at the Punjab Mass Transit Authority (PMA) and Project Manager of Lahore's Orange Line Metro Train (OLMT), is summoned to the Chief Minister's Secretariat. The summons follows the death of seven workers two nights earlier in a fire at a makeshift residence operated by a subcontractor of Habib Construction Services (HCS), the civil works contractor for Package 1 of Pakistan's first rail-based mass transit project. The fire is the latest event in an eighteen-month cascade that has already produced a Lahore High Court (LHC) stay-order on construction near eleven heritage sites, the termination of the Package 2 contractor (Maqbool-Colson JV) and its successful counter-litigation, the displacement of more than 200 families along the route, a pending Supreme Court appeal, ongoing protests from the Lahore Bachao Tehreek (LBT) and its civil society coalition, and growing financial penalties under the China Exim Bank loan agreement. Shah's decision what to recommend at the 9 a.m. meeting-is no longer only technical. By January 2017, the OLMT has become a contested narrative space, with at least five distinct discourses authored by different stakeholders, each making a different claim about what the project is and for whom. This case is built to take students through that narrative-led reality of Pakistan's first transport megaproject in real time, and to give them analytical tools to act.

title: Unequal Adoption of AI Writing in Scientific Publishing

detail.title: Unequal Adoption of AI Writing in Scientific Publishing
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether the diffusion of AI-assisted writing could become a new source of inequality in scientific publishing after the release of ChatGPT. I construct an article-level dataset of 130,879 research articles from 91 Elsevier journals, linking detector-based AI-writing scores from article introductions to author-background measures and publication-timeline data. Detected AI-writing signals rose sharply after ChatGPT but diffused unevenly, with larger increases among papers associated with male, non-OECD, and non-English-predominant author backgrounds. In the short run, however, this uneven diffusion did not translate into clear changes in published-author representation by gender, OECD status, or English-language background. Publication-timeline results are stage-specific: higher detected AI-use scores are associated with longer pre-acceptance review, especially from receipt to revision, while descriptive patterns suggest shorter post-acceptance stages. Journal-level difference-in-differences estimates, however, do not indicate systematic timeline effects. If current adoption patterns persist, AI-assisted writing may reduce language- and geography-based barriers while amplifying gender inequality.

title: The Invisible Green Building: Exploring the Gap Between Environmental Certification and User Recognition

detail.title: The Invisible Green Building: Exploring the Gap Between Environmental Certification and User Recognition

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support for this study was provided by the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) Faculty Initiative Fund (FIF) for the project 'Pro-Environmental Behaviour in Closed University Communities'.

detail.abstract: While environmental certification frameworks like LEED have become dominant global benchmarks for sustainable construction, a persistent gap remains regarding internal occupant engagement. This paper investigates this misalignment by analyzing a pioneering green-certified industrial facility in Pakistan's export-driven textile sector. The study uncovers a distinct empirical paradox: despite demonstrating exceptionally high pro-environmental worldviews, the building's everyday occupants possessed negligible awareness of its formal eco-certified status. Utilizing a mixed-methods research design, the study evaluates quantitative data from occupant surveys using the New Ecological Paradigm (NEP) scale alongside deep qualitative interview insights. The findings indicate that because the organization prioritized securing strategic outward legitimacy with international supply chain buyers, the technical standard failed to socially embed itself within the lived practices of workplace users. By moving institutional decoupling theory down to the micro-level, the paper conceptualizes this phenomenon as "certification without connection" and constructs the Certification-User Recognition (CUR) Framework. This two-by-two matrix maps out four unique variations of user-level decoupling, extending macro-organizational debates on institutional legitimacy while providing built-environment practitioners with a practical diagnostic tool to align technical design benchmarks with meaningful human experience.

title: Extending the "Principle of Effective Demand"-Did Keynes Produce an Ad Hoc Tautology?
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Extending the "Principle of Effective Demand"-Did Keynes Produce an Ad Hoc Tautology?
detail.abstract: Keynes extended his Principle of Effective Demand (PED), which explains how effective demand determines employment, to cover changes in effective demand and, inter alia, their price and output effects. However, owing to Keynes's poor presentation and Friedman's critique, the latter extension failed to gain traction, thwarting a fuller realization of the PED's potential as a fundamental macroeconomic principle. According to Friedman, Keynes's equation is a tautology, and ad hoc in its application. The paper demonstrates that Keynes obtained his equation in the form he did not because he was manipulating identities, but because his theory drew on the PED which requires that employment and output be substantively determined as functions of effective demand in wage units. His equation is therefore neither tautology nor ad hoc. It represents a genuine extension of the applicability of Keynes's Principle of Effective Demand, and opens a potentially useful line of enquiry in macroeconomics.

title: From Herding Machines to Autonomous Agents: A Taxonomy of AI-Driven Flash Crash Mechanisms and the Regulatory Void

detail.title: From Herding Machines to Autonomous Agents: A Taxonomy of AI-Driven Flash Crash Mechanisms and the Regulatory Void

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping financial markets-accelerating execution, automating allocation, and concentrating analytical capacity within a shrinking set of foundational models. Prior work has documented AI's contribution to instability through algorithmic herding and highfrequency volatility, but the literature lacks a systematic classification of the mechanisms through which AI triggers catastrophic, self-reinforcing market dislocations, or "flash crashes." This prospective review proposes a three-category taxonomy: (1) endogenous algorithmic herding crashes, driven by correlated model behaviour; (2) exogenous model error cascade crashes, in which AI system failures propagate across interconnected venues; and (3) adversarial generative-AI disinformation crashes, in which fabricated narratives trigger automated trading responses. The taxonomy is grounded in the structural parallel between contemporary AI model homogeneity and the homogenization of Value-at-Risk (VaR) models before the 2008 crisis-a link recently formalized by Meng and Chen (2026). The analysis is extended to the emerging frontier of agentic AI-autonomous systems capable of multi-step planning and inter-agent interaction-which introduces qualitatively new systemic risks that existing regulatory frameworks are unprepared to 1 AI-Driven Flash Crash Mechanisms and the Regulatory Void address. The October 2025 cryptocurrency liquidation cascade, which liquidated over $19 billion within 24 hours, serves as the primary empirical case study. The article concludes with policy recommendations on model-diversity mandates, real-time AI trading surveillance, and adaptive circuit-breaker design.

title: Supply and Demand for Money in Pre-Industrial Societies

detail.title: Supply and Demand for Money in Pre-Industrial Societies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: The author gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Sven Svensson Foundation for Numismatics, the Gunnar Ekstrand Foundation, and the Sven and Dagmar Salén Foundation.

detail.abstract:
In pre-industrial societies, the supply and demand for money were closely tied to the availability of commodity money, typically silver coins. This chapter develops a theoretical framework for monetary systems without central banks. On the supply side, coin output depended on the availability of precious metals and the institutional organization of minting. Under free minting, private agents could bring bullion to the mint and receive coins, which they distributed through market transactions. Because bullion could also be melted from coins, this system created a self-regulating mechanism adjusting the money supply through minting and melting. By contrast, under government-controlled minting the state monopolized coin production and introduced coins into circulation mainly through public expenditures, especially military wages and administrative salaries. This system allowed greater fiscal control but also carried a risk of over- or under-issuance.

On the demand side, labour specialization, comparative advantage, and expanding trade increased the need for money as a medium of exchange, while precautionary and speculative motives reflected risk and wealth storage in economies with weak insurance and financial systems. Monetary taxation and wage payments required a minimum level of labour division and functioning local markets, since households needed to obtain coins through exchange before they could pay taxes in coin. Once this threshold was reached, monetary taxation and wage payments reinforced monetization by increasing coin circulation and market integration. The chapter concludes by introducing the equation of exchange as a framework linking money supply, velocity, output, and prices in pre-industrial economies.

title: The Gravity of OECD-Bound Migration, 1960-2020: Uncovering Contemporary and Deep-Rooted Determinants
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Gravity of OECD-Bound Migration, 1960-2020: Uncovering Contemporary and Deep-Rooted Determinants
detail.abstract: This study examines the determinants of migration from non-OECD origins to OECD destinations from 1960 to 2020 using a structural gravity framework. We first argue for a more comprehensive approach to migration dynamics than typically found in the literature. Utilizing Shapley dominance decomposition across a wide range of contemporary and historical drivers, we find that migration networks, historical ties, development, natural disasters, and conflict make comparable contributions and must be considered jointly. Second, we document shifting effects among origin-specific drivers. Natural disaster exposure is negatively associated with migration in 1960-1990-reflecting immobility under binding constraints-but becomes positively associated in 1990-2020. Conflict intensity remains a consistent positive driver. Economic development follows the "migration-hump" pattern in the earlier period, though this relationship weakens and shifts over time. Third, we demonstrate the significant role of dyadic determinants, introducing a novel ancestry-based connectedness measure derived from the World Migration Matrix. This indicator captures the persistent effects of deep-rooted demographic and cultural ties and exhibits robust explanatory power even after controlling for geographic distance, cultural proximity, and traditional historical linkages.

title: Auto-Deleveraging and the Solvency-Fragility Tradeoff in Perpetual Futures Markets

detail.title: Auto-Deleveraging and the Solvency-Fragility Tradeoff in Perpetual Futures Markets
detail.abstract: Perpetual-futures exchanges guarantee solvency via auto-deleveraging (ADL), confiscating winners' gains once the fund is exhausted. We show this last-resort backstop is itself a source of fragility. Because it taxes the winning side rather than pre-committed capital, the arbitrageurs who absorb a liquidation cascade are also its loss-mutualization buffer, and they rationally flee it. A global game yields a unique threshold equilibrium, a position run by the would-be insurers. Solvency is thus bought with fragility: the run can deplete the confiscatable buffer and break the solvency it promises, while added arbitrage capacity raises run risk even as deeper markets lower it.

title: Climate Stress and International Migration from MENA
affiliations: ,  and Migration Policy Group

detail.title: Climate Stress and International Migration from MENA
detail.abstract:
Existing research on the drivers of international migration is constrained by incomplete
measurement of volumes, directions and country coverage. Most studies focus on recent
decades, a narrow set of OECD destinations or a single flow type, even though categories
are blurred, new destinations have emerged and many developing countries now host large
migrant populations. Recent work suggests that migration drivers are best understood within
a broader migration system rather than in isolation. However, even in this newer literature,
long-run historical ties, such as deep ancestry links or very old migrant stocks, are still
rarely analyzed jointly with contemporary drivers and environmental pressures in a unified
empirical framework.
In this paper, we focus on MENA countries and use bilateral flow estimates from Abel
(2018) in a gravity framework to analyse how environmental stress interacts with the broader
social, political, and historical structures that organise migration. We distinguish fast-onset
shocks, measured by the number of people affected by floods and storms, from slow-onset
anomalies, captured by 12-month SPEI indicators for unusually dry and unusually wet conditions.
These origin-year shocks have been analyzed in a rich context of civil conflict,
development, urbanization, and agrarian exposure, and we further augmented the study
with historical migrant stocks around 1960 and a new ancestry stock measure we developed,
reflects historical ties built up in the Colonial Era. This study is one of the first to
incorporate deep ancestry-based ties into an empirical analysis of migration from MENA.
Our results show that fast-onset disasters affect emigration from MENA in a non-linear
way: small and moderate events are largely absorbed locally, while very severe shocks lead to
sharp increases in cross-border outflows. Deviations from normal moisture in either direction,
whether drought or excess rainfall, are also associated with higher emigration. In addition,
migrant stocks and ancestry links are strong and robust predictors of where migrants move,
even after we control for other conditions.

title: Downward Reclassification and University Enrollment: Evidence from the University of Idaho

detail.title: Downward Reclassification and University Enrollment: Evidence from the University of Idaho
detail.abstract: We examine the enrollment consequences of the University of Idaho's 2018 voluntary reclassification from the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) to the Football Championship Subdivision (FCS). The Vandals became the first school to make the drop since the NCAA split the top division in 1978. Using a synthetic control method with a donor pool of non-Power Five FBS institutions, we find no statistically significant negative effect on total enrollment. Idaho's enrollment trajectory closely tracked its synthetic counterfactual through 2021 and outperformed it in 2022-2024. These results suggest that the enrollment costs of downward reclassification may be overstated, complementing recent evidence that the enrollment benefits of upward reclassification are similarly uncertain.

title: The Local Fiscal and Economic Effects of Population Aging
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Robert F. Wagner Graduate School of Public Service

detail.title: The Local Fiscal and Economic Effects of Population Aging
detail.abstract: Advanced economies, including the United States, are undergoing a sustained demographic transition toward older populations, driven by declining fertility and increasing longevity. While existing research examines the macroeconomic implications of population aging and the fiscal impacts for higher level governments, less is known about how population aging affects local fiscal and economic outcomes. Using a demographic shift-share design that exploits pre-existing variation in age structures, this paper analyzes the causal impact of changes in the elderly population share on county-level economic and fiscal outcomes between 2010-2022, a period that spans the retirement of the Baby Boom generation. Consistent with increased consumption demand from retirees, the results show that the aging of the Baby Boomers had little effect on local economic output or the size of government, but led to higher house prices and population growth, suggesting that local demand-side effects offset reductions in labor supply. These effects were heterogeneous, with an increased elderly share generating measurable economic gains in urban areas.

title: Commercial Financing Disclosure Laws and Nonbank Lending: Who Benefits and Who Suffers?
affiliations: University of Basel - Faculty of Business and Economics and University of Zurich - Department Finance

detail.title: Commercial Financing Disclosure Laws and Nonbank Lending: Who Benefits and Who Suffers?
detail.abstract: Commercial Financing Disclosure Laws (CFDL) are state-level regulations that require nonbank lenders to provide transparent disclosures to small businesses when granting them credit. This study documents that nonbank lenders decrease interest rates and increase loan amounts for borrowers following the enactment of CFDL. The effects are more pronounced for marginal borrowers, such as startups and franchise entrepreneurs. Yet small business loans exempt from CFDL mandates experience a higher cost of credit and a reduction in lending volume. Those loans are also more likely to default. Overall, this study suggests that, while CFDL helps curb potential predatory practices by forcing transparency in small business lending, nonbank lenders pass on compliance costs on to less-regulated entities.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Submitted for editorial peer-review to Revista Facultad de Ciencias Económicas de la Universidad de Guayaquil.

detail.abstract: This study presents an updated empirical estimate of the private return on education in Ecuador, based on data from the 2025 National Survey on Employment, Unemployment and Underemployment (ENEMDU). Adopting the theoretical framework of human capital developed by Mincer (1974), an ordinary least squares (OLS) econometric model was used to analyze the impact of education and work experience on individual incomes. The research is based on a random representative sample of 999 observations, with a logarithmic transformation applied to monthly labor income to correct heteroscedasticity and ensure model stability. Empirical results reveal a robust and statistically significant correlation between education level and income level (p < 0.01). Our results indicate that the marginal return of an additional year of schooling is approximately 6.5%, all other things being equal. Furthermore, the inclusion of a quadratic experience term produces a negative coefficient (β =-0.00038), confirming the existence of a concave age-income profile in the Ecuadorian labor market. These data suggest that experiences' marginal utility decreases over the life cycle despite this increasing productivity. The model explains 14.9% of the variance in wages (= 0.1487), thus providing an essential benchmark for assessing the effectiveness of 𝑅² human capital investments in the current socioeconomic context of Ecuador.

title: Stress Testing Tail Risk in India: A Comparative Evaluation of EVT-Copula and Gaussian Models

detail.title: Stress Testing Tail Risk in India: A Comparative Evaluation of EVT-Copula and Gaussian Models
detail.abstract: Standard Gaussian Value-at-Risk (VaR) frameworks systematically underestimate tail risk in financial markets characterised by fat tails and leptokurtosis. This paper develops and validates a GARCH(1,1)-Extreme Value Theory (EVT)-Student-t Copula framework for three Indian asset classes, Nifty 50 (equities), Gold (INR), and USD/INR (currency),using 18 years of daily data spanning September 2007 to December 2025. Marginal tail distributions are modelled via Peaks-Over-Threshold Generalised Pareto Distribution (POF-GPD) fitted to GARCH-filtered residuals, while cross-asset dependence is captured using a Student-t copula estimated by maximum likelihood. The resulting EVT-Copula VaR and Expected Shortfall (ES) estimates are benchmarked against their Gaussian counterparts across three portfolio allocations, and the models are backtested against realised 2026 returns. Across all asset classes, the EVT-Copula framework produces VaR estimates that are 5-20% higher than Gaussian VaR, and Expected Shortfall exceeding Normal VaR by about 60% across all portfolios. Backtesting against the realised breach events in January-April 2026 confirms that EVT-Copula ES bounds actual losses more tightly than Normal VaR on every occasion. These findings provide direct empirical evidence that Gaussian models materially understate downside risk in the Indian multi-asset context, and that EVT-based ES is a more reliable regulatory and portfolio risk metric.

title: The Optimal Timing of Product Introduction and Safety Investments for Automated Vehicles

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: The emergence of autonomous vehicles (AVs) raises important questions regarding the interaction between liability regulation, technological development, and market adoption. While AVs have the potential to substantially improve road safety in the long run, their early deployment is likely to involve elevated accident risks and uncertainty regarding legal responsibility. This paper examines how alternative liability regimes affect a monopolistic producer’s incentives to invest in AV safety and its decision regarding market entry. Building on the dynamic model of Dawid et al. (2022), we develop an analytical framework that links liability allocation to intertemporal safety investments and market diffusion. We first analyze the benchmark case of certain producer liability and show that stricter producer liability may reduce safety investments when market demand is low, but can strengthen long-run investment incentives once demand reaches a sufficiently high level. Furthermore, delayed market entry is shown to reduce cumulative safety investments, increase accident probabilities, and lower producer profits. We then extend the model by introducing uncertainty about future liability regulation and demonstrate that the qualitative results remain robust under both open-loop and Markov investment strategies. From a welfare perspective, neither full producer nor full consumer liability is optimal. Instead, an intermediate liability regime that balances producer responsibility with the internalization of accident externalities generates the highest social welfare. The findings suggest that accelerating the deployment of autonomous vehicles, supported by appropriately designed liability rules, can improve both safety outcomes and technological progress, while regulatory uncertainty does not fundamentally alter these conclusions.

title: YouTube Influencers as Information Intermediaries
affiliations: , Brigham Young University - Marriott School, Brigham Young University and Texas A&M University - Department of Accounting

detail.title: YouTube Influencers as Information Intermediaries
detail.abstract: We examine the role of influencers who provide long-form video content on YouTube as information intermediaries in capital markets. Many investors increasingly rely on influencers to inform their trading decisions, but regulators have expressed concerns about the potential harmful effects of influencer content. We find that the videos of YouTube influencers are associated with increased market activity, particularly from retail investors, and that negative video content relates to net retail investor selling pressure around earnings announcements. Influencer coverage is also associated with increased efficiency in the pricing of earnings news. Finally, we provide evidence that a number of influencer and video attributes moderate their market effects. Overall, our findings offer a nuanced understanding of the important and growing role that YouTube influencers play in capital markets.

detail.abstract: This review essay seeks to invite a wider consideration of Tuuli Wohlström's doctoral thesis 'Europe Beyond the Courts: Constitutionalism, Pluralism and Integration in the Nordic Countries'. Prompted by the observation that the Nordic countries have been overlooked in the EU legal pluralism discourses due to court-centric perspectives, Wohlström documents manifold conflicts with, and limits to, EU law, and argues that to understand these, it is necessary to expand the frame of reference to the broader constitutional cultures. Wohlström shows that in the Nordic countries, limits to EU law have predominantly been set by parliaments and through ex ante constitutional review mechanisms. However, she argues that EU law has brought about 'major shifts' in the institutional configurations, with a reluctant and vexed process of strengthening the power of courts. This culminated with the Ajos case of the Danish Supreme Court where, for the first time, a Nordic court said 'No' to the CJEU. The present reviewer adds broader comments from the point of view of comparative European constitutional law, and suggests that many Nordic constitutional values – especially the social welfare state – ought to be regarded as a model, rather than be replaced by neoliberalism and neofunctionalism through EU governance. The review also calls for a formal acknowledgement of structural problems in EU research, and puts forward a policy proposal to support the international publication of doctoral theses on national and comparative European constitutional law.

title: Measured, not Priced: Structural Identification of Discount-rate Sentiment

detail.title: Measured, not Priced: Structural Identification of Discount-rate Sentiment

detail.abstract: Can a small, structurally restricted state-space system measure a sentiment state with a recognizable economic signature? We impose a behaviorally augmented dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) state-space model on a monthly panel of macroeconomic, valuation, sentiment, and anomaly observables, and identify a persistent discount-rate sentiment state through sign and exclusion restrictions disciplined by over-identification tests and by shrinkage-path and perturbation audits. The state tracks the Baker-Wurgler index (correlation 0.88) with the familiar sentiment chronology, and raises the cross-sectional R 2 of the Fama-French 25 portfolios from 0.10 to 0.31. Its price of risk is Shanken-significant but not robust to misspecification-aware inference; the stochastic discount factor is rejected; there is no tradable alpha; and a pre-registered duration prediction returns a null. The state is measured, not priced: the measurement discipline-which itself detected and removed a spurious duration result-is the contribution.

title: Toward Human-Centered Sustainability. Emotional, Relational, and Cultural Utility in Economic Behavior: Insights from Thailand

detail.title: Toward Human-Centered Sustainability. Emotional, Relational, and Cultural Utility in Economic Behavior: Insights from Thailand
detail.abstract: Contemporary sustainability debates increasingly recognize that ecological crises cannot be understood solely through assumptions of rational utility maximization and growthcentered development. Drawing on insights from behavioral economics, well-being research, and sustainability studies, the paper develops a broader conception of utility that incorporates emotional, relational, and cultural dimensions of human welfare. It makes three contributions. First, it proposes emotional utility, relational utility, and cultural utility as complementary dimensions of human welfare that help explain why well-being depends upon psychological stability, social relationships, and culturally meaningful forms of life. Second, it introduces the concept of behavioral sustainability, defined as the long-term reproduction of sustainable patterns of behavior through supportive social, emotional, cultural, and institutional conditions. Third, it illustrates the relevance of this framework through the case of Thailand, where concepts such as sabai-sabai, kreng jai, nam jai, and the Sufficiency Economy Philosophy reflect culturally grounded understandings of well-being that go beyond material accumulation. The analysis suggests that sustainability should be evaluated not only according to ecological outcomes and economic performance but also according to its capacity to support trust, belonging, resilience, and enduring quality of life. Sustainable development therefore requires conceptions of welfare that account for what people need to live well, not only what they consume.

title: The Epistemic Filter Theory of Survey Inference

detail.title: The Epistemic Filter Theory of Survey Inference
detail.abstract: This paper develops the Epistemic Filter Theory of Survey Inference, a social-theoretical and methodological framework that connects projected stochasticity, random sampling, measurement design, and research validity. The paper introduces and begins from the non-play-dice paradigm, defined here as the claim that apparent stochasticity can arise when an observer, researcher, or model has access only to a projected subset of a more complex system. In statistical physics, the Mori-Zwanzig projection operator formalism expresses this logic by deriving reduced stochasticlooking dynamics from exact Liouvillian evolution. In social research, the analogous problem is methodological rather than ontological: researchers cannot observe the full social field and must instead rely on sampling frames, measurement instruments, analytic models, and validity diagnostics. The framework therefore treats random sampling, questionnaire measurement, weighting, factor analysis, and structural modeling as epistemic filters that determine what becomes visible, what remains outside the dataset, and how uncertainty enters inference. The paper formulates mathematical survey operators, defines a five-construct measurement model, proposes validity and reliability criteria, specifies factor and structural models, develops platform-based implementation scenarios, and provides full reproducible R scripts for simulation, validation, and Bayesian updating. Applications are developed for public opinion research, journalism studies, media literacy, digital trace research, influencer economies, misinformation research, platform governance, and hidden-population analysis.

title: “Disentangling the Influence of CSR Initiatives on the Performance of Banking Institutions”
affiliations: State University of Bangladesh, North South University and

detail.title: “Disentangling the Influence of CSR Initiatives on the Performance of Banking Institutions”
detail.abstract: This study aims to investigate the effects of different corporate social responsibilities (CSR) on the organizational performance of the banking sector. The target population of this study was bank employees working at various bank branches in Bangladesh. In this investigation, the data gathering procedure was conducted utilizing a Google Form distributed via email, accompanied by a cover letter, to facilitate participation among bank employees. The study collected data from the current bank employees of several banking institutions in Bangladesh. They were sent a survey invitation to participate, and after their approval, their responses were gathered. A five-point Likert scale was used to determine the item-wise questionnaire, with '1' indicating 'Strongly Disagree' and '5' indicating 'Strongly Agree'. The final sample size was 263. Moreover, to evaluate the hypothesis, a 5% significance level and SPSS software were used to analyze the data for research purposes. The outcome of this study shows that internal and external CSR activities have a positive and significant impact on the organizational performance development of Bangladesh's banking sector. These factors can account for 52.70% of the variability observed in forecasting the performance of bank organizations. External CSR initiatives (β = 0.318; t = 5.937) have the highest effect on a bank's performance. Additionally, a substantial correlation coefficient (r = 0.436) is present between internal CSR and bank performance. This study might provide significant clues to the management committees of the banking sector that can severely influence a bank's performance development.

title: OmegaMacro Composite Late‑Cycle Indicator (CLCI): Methodology
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: OmegaMacro Composite Late‑Cycle Indicator (CLCI): Methodology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of OmegaMacro Research, a macro research publication. No external financial or personal relationships influenced this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
The OmegaMacro Composite Late-Cycle Indicator (CLCI) is a weekly, systematic macro-financial indicator that measures accumulated late-cycle pressure on a 0–100 scale. It is built from seven distinct blocks — Yield Curve, Credit, Labour, Liquidity, Earnings Revisions, Valuation, and Breadth — each aggregating public data from US and European official sources. The composite is read as a percentile against its own history and mapped to five descriptive bands (subdued, normal, elevated, high, and very high) with a direction note. The published signal is probabilistic and descriptive, not categorical: it states where current conditions sit relative to history, not that a recession will occur.

The indicator was developed on the 2001 and 2008 recessions and validated out‑of‑sample on the 2020 episode, which it discriminated at an AUC of 0.95 against the full non‑recession contrast set. An economic‑relevance demonstration over 2016–2023 shows that a simple, pre‑specified allocation conditioned on the published band improved on both a passive 60/40 portfolio and the Faber 10‑month trend‑following rule on a risk‑adjusted basis, with a deflated Sharpe ratio of 0.80 against the development search. We report these results with honest caveats: the 2020 episode is a single, externally‑driven shock; the signal is conservative on mild recessions following overheated expansions; and the economic‑relevance test is illustrative, not a trading recommendation.

The paper describes the full architecture, the evaluation protocol, and the named limitations. The exact production weights, the preprocessing parameters, and the composite‑to‑regime transformation method are proprietary and are not disclosed. The indicator's historical output series are openly deposited in a public replication pack with a cryptographic parameter‑file hash as proof of pre‑commitment.

This paper is educational research of general circulation and does not constitute investment advice.

title: The Life-cycle Inconsistencies in U.S. Savings Policy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Life-cycle Inconsistencies in U.S. Savings Policy
detail.abstract: Traditionally, the choice between pre-tax and post-tax savings during working years was based on a simple comparison of observed marginal tax rates in the present to expected marginal tax rates in retirement. However, the advent of AGI-linked systems-such as the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) for student loans and Premium Tax Credits (PTC) for stateexchange health insurance-has fundamentally changed this calculation. The new financial landscape means the pre-tax versus post tax saving decision no longer hinges solely on federal income tax rates. Younger workers whose student loan payments or insurance premiums are directly tied to their Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) have a strong incentive to maximize pre-tax savings options to increase immediate liquidity. This decision will lead to significantly higher costs and loss of financial flexibility in retirement.

title: Poverty as a Systemic Equilibrium: An Integrated Household Systems Framework (IHSF) for Development Dynamics
affiliations: and

detail.title: Poverty as a Systemic Equilibrium: An Integrated Household Systems Framework (IHSF) for Development Dynamics
detail.abstract:
This study develops an Integrated Household Systems Framework (IHSF) that reconceptualizes poverty as a nonlinear, dynamic system arising from interactions among cognitive, social, economic, and institutional processes. Households are modeled as coupled decision systems in which psychological capacity, social capital, economic strategy, and institutional access co-evolve. The framework formalizes these dynamics as a discrete-time system with endogenous feedback, bounded variables, and complementarities. 

The model shows that poverty can emerge as a locally stable equilibrium sustained by reinforcing constraints, while development is a path-dependent, non-equilibrium trajectory driven by cumulative feedback effects. A critical capital threshold separates these regimes: below it, the system converges to a low-income equilibrium; above it, reinforcing interactions generate sustained growth.

An illustrative simulation confirms these dynamics. By endogenizing multiple dimensions within a unified system, the framework explains the limited impact of isolated interventions and highlights the importance of coordinated, multidimensional development strategies.

title: Belief Distortions and Endogenous Risk Aversion
affiliations: Purdue University - Daniels School of Business and Purdue University - Daniels School of Business

detail.title: Belief Distortions and Endogenous Risk Aversion
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic equilibrium model in which belief distortions interact with habit formation to generate heterogeneous and time-varying risk attitudes. Two types of investors have identical preference parameters ex ante but differ in beliefs: biased investors extrapolate from recent aggregate growth, while rational investors hold correct beliefs. Through equilibrium wealth transfers, belief distortions affect the consumption, habits, and risk aversion of rational investors as well. This spillover mechanism generates opposing movements in individual risk aversion and non-monotonic aggregate risk aversion over the business cycle. Consequently, market risk premia and volatility rise not only in contractions but also in strong expansions, patterns for which we provide empirical evidence. The model also reconciles positive cross-sectional and negative time-series relations between wealth and portfolios.

title: One Small Step for Man, One Giant Leap for the IRS: Source of Income Without Sovereignty in Space Mining and Space Transportation
affiliations: University of Florida Fredric G. Levin College of Law

detail.title: One Small Step for Man, One Giant Leap for the IRS: Source of Income Without Sovereignty in Space Mining and Space Transportation
detail.abstract: Imagine a U.S. person earning income from a copper mine in Chile. Now imagine the same person earning income from mining an asteroid. Imagine an entity earning income from transporting passengers from the United States to Italy. Now imagine the same entity earning income from transporting passengers from the United States to the International Space Station, or from the International Space Station to an outpost on the Moon. The first question addressed in this article is whether the existing federal income tax framework treat these taxpayers the same way. This Article shows that it does not. Section 863(d) of the Internal Revenue Code sources income from space and ocean activities to the United States if derived by a U.S. person, subject to carve-outs. This Article examines the carve-out for transportation income under subsection (d)(2)(B)(i), and the carve-out for mining and natural-deposit activity under subsection (d)(2)(B)(iii). It argues that, under existing law, neither carve-out applies to its space-based counterpart. The consequence is that income from extraterrestrial mining and space transportation derived by a U.S. person remains U.S.-source, while the same income derived by a non-U.S. person is foreign-source under the same provision. The second question addressed in this article is what consequeces this bidirectional asymmetry produces, and whether the fisc or taxpayers are left worse off. Finally, the Article considers the allocation that a registration-based source rule, drawing on Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, would produce.

title: On Hilbert's 8th Problem: II
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: On Hilbert's 8th Problem: II
detail.abstract: The Riemann Hypothesis is reformulated probabilistically and reduced to a single positivity requirement. Using the Hadamard factorisation of the Riemann ξ-function, RH is shown equivalent to Thorin's condition: that ξ(1 2)/ξ(1 2 + √ s) be the Laplace transform of a generalised gamma convolution (GGC). A GGC random variable realising this transform is constructed explicitly and unconditionally in the zero-free region Re > 1, from Lévy representations of the Gamma function and the Euler product for the zeta function; its Thorin density is the boundary value of ξ ′ /ξ on a vertical line, carried to the critical line by a half-power subordination acting as a Poisson extension. The Mellin transform onto the critical strip is then computed directly from the moment sequence, no positivity enters, leaving a single residual requirement, nonnegativity of the resulting Thorin measure, whose atoms are the zeros: nonnegativity holds if and only if every non-trivial zero lies on the critical line.

title: Endogeneity in ESG and Climate Finance Research: A Literature Review of Challenges and Solutions

detail.title: Endogeneity in ESG and Climate Finance Research: A Literature Review of Challenges and Solutions
detail.abstract: Endogeneity, the correlation between explanatory variables and the error term in a regression, is arguably the most persistent challenge in empirical corporate finance. When a researcher estimates the effect of ESG engagement on firm performance, or the impact of carbon emissions on stock returns, the fundamental question is whether the relationship reflects genuine causation or is an artifact of omitted variables, simultaneity, or measurement error (Roberts & Whited, 2013). The answer determines whether findings can credibly inform investment decisions and public policy. I confront this challenge directly in my own dissertation research on university endowment behavior under economic policy uncertainty. The Baker-Bloom-Davis EPU index is a national-level variable, which substantially reduces concern about reverse causality because no single institution's portfolio decision can influence the national policy uncertainty index. But omitted variable bias remains a concern in any observational design. For that reason, my dissertation relies on a layered robustness strategy rather than on coefficient significance alone. Oster-style coefficient stability analysis shows that the EPU coefficient moves only 1.2% when the full set of controls is added, producing a delta of 50.9 under the conventional Rmax assumption. Additional diagnostics include year-level clustering, two-way clustering, placebo tests using lead uncertainty, functional-form checks across logit, probit, and linear probability models, and entropy balancing across the endowment size distribution. That experience motivates this review. Understanding why standard OLS inference breaks down and what credible alternatives look like is not an abstract exercise. It is the difference between a defensible finding and a suggestive correlation. This paper reviews eight papers that collectively map the endogeneity problem and its solutions as they apply to ESG and climate finance. The review follows a two-part structure. The first part examines why standard inference fails, through the foundational work of Leamer (1983), Roberts and Whited (2013), and Oster (2019). The second part examines the solutions through five landmark papers that successfully implement credible identification strategies: Angrist (1990) introduces instrumental variables, Bennedsen, Nielsen, Perez-Gonzalez, and Wolfenzon (2007) apply instrumental variables to corporate finance, Dell (2010) introduces regression discontinuity design, Flammer (2015) applies regression discontinuity to an ESG question, and Ahern and Dittmar (2012) demonstrate natural experiments with difference-in-differences. The overarching argument is that ESG research must move beyond adding controls and hoping for coefficient stability toward the identification strategies these papers demonstrate.

title: Collusion Under Algorithmic Pricing: How Robust is It?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Collusion Under Algorithmic Pricing: How Robust is It?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
The increasing use of artificial intelligence in strategic market environments has raised concerns about the emergence of algorithmic collusion. Recent studies have shown that reinforcement learning (RL) agents can learn to sustain supra-competitive prices in repeated pricing games without explicit communication or coordination, posing significant challenges for competition policy and antitrust regulation. This paper investigates the mechanisms underlying collusive behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning environments and proposes algorithmic modifications designed to promote convergence toward competitive Nash equilibria.

We begin by analyzing a repeated duopoly pricing game formulated as a potential game. Despite the favorable equilibrium properties of this class of games, we demonstrate that standard tabular Q-learning agents frequently converge to collusive outcomes rather than competitive equilibria. To address this problem, we introduce Smooth Q-Learning, a novel extension of Q-learning inspired by the Smooth UCT Search framework. The algorithm incorporates stochasticity by partially conditioning action selection on observed competitor behavior, thereby improving exploration and reducing the tendency toward collusive strategies. We further enhance this approach by integrating a planning component, resulting in the Smooth Dyna-Q algorithm, which combines model-based simulation with reinforcement learning to accelerate convergence.

Simulation results show that both algorithms reliably identify Nash equilibria and substantially reduce the incidence of collusive behavior. Smooth Dyna-Q achieves particularly strong performance, exhibiting faster convergence and greater stability than standard Q-learning. To evaluate robustness beyond potential games, we test the algorithms in the repeated Bertrand pricing environment of Calvano et al. (2020), where conventional Q-learning is known to converge to tacit collusion. The proposed algorithms continue to perform effectively, although stronger smoothing parameters are required to ensure equilibrium convergence in more complex environments.

The findings suggest that algorithmic collusion is not an unavoidable consequence of reinforcement learning and that carefully designed learning mechanisms can promote competitive market outcomes while preserving adaptive decision-making capabilities.

title: Taxing the Transfer of Compensatory Partnership Interests
affiliations: University of Florida Levin College of Law

detail.title: Taxing the Transfer of Compensatory Partnership Interests
detail.abstract:
The proper rules for taxing the exchange of partnership interests for services have never been settled. This paper argues that background policy considerations support a regime that treats the receipt of most profits interests as nontaxable and the receipt of capital interests as taxable, treats the historic partners as not recognizing gain or loss on the issuance of the interest, and limits cost recovery for the partnership to its historic basis in the assets deemed transferred to the recipient service partner (generally in the case of a capital interest). Central to the analysis is the claim that different considerations support deferral or taxation on the partnership side of the exchange from those that support deferral or taxation on the partner side.

Efficiency considerations suggest modifications to current or proposed rules in the area consistent with the regime just described. First, the same treatment should apply to transfers of capital interests in transactions involving already-existing partnerships as to those in transactions that create partnerships. Second, Congress should amend section 83(h) to conform cost recovery in the subchapter S setting to the rule advocated here for cost recovery under subchapter K. Third, and more ambitiously, Congress should extend the same treatment to the C corporation context.

title: Automating The Safety Net
affiliations: University of Miami - School of Law, University of Southern California Gould School of Law and Indiana University Maurer School of Law

detail.title: Automating The Safety Net

declarations.ethicsApproval: The research in this article was approved by Institutional Review Boards at all three authors' institutions.

detail.abstract:
Each year, millions of eligible Americans fail to access tax credits, health insurance, or food assistance to which they are legally entitled. This failure occurs in part because most public benefit programs in the United States operate on an opt-in model: to enroll, individuals must first learn that a program exists, determine whether they qualify, gather required documentation, complete an application, and navigate whatever verification processes the agency requires. One solution that has attracted significant attention from policymakers, administrators, and advocates is “automatic enrollment.” Automatic enrollment refers to when the government identifies eligible individuals through administrative data and enrolls them without requiring an affirmative application on the individual’s part. Yet despite its promise, surprisingly little work has examined the on-the-ground realities of implementing automatic enrollment across the varied landscape of public benefit programs.

This Article sheds light on recent efforts to automate enrollment in public benefits in the United States. Drawing on nearly thirty semi-structured interviews with federal and state officials, policy experts, technologists, and advocates who have experience advocating for automatic enrollment, implementing automatic enrollment, or otherwise reducing administrative burdens, the Article maps the landscape of automatic enrollment initiatives across a range of benefit programs, including the advance Child Tax Credit, Medicaid, and the Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) program.

The interviews reveal both progress and persistent obstacles. Renewal rates in Medicaid have dramatically increased in recent years, and new programs like Summer EBT demonstrate that benefits can be designed with automatic enrollment from the start. Innovations have popped up at all levels of government and across policy domains. Yet our interviewees identified significant challenges, such as administrative decentralization, legal and technical barriers to data sharing, limited state capacity, and political opposition rooted in concerns about fraud, privacy, and immigration enforcement. The Article outlines reforms that address these barriers, including harmonizing eligibility definitions, improving data infrastructure, increasing state capacity, and building political trust. Automatic enrollment in public benefits has moved from theory to practice. Understanding what enabled recent successes and what obstacles persist is essential to closing the gap between eligibility and enrollment.

title: Is Money Overrated? Misperceived Satisfaction from Income
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Is Money Overrated? Misperceived Satisfaction from Income
detail.abstract:
People often make important choices in pursuit of higher income, but do they place too much weight on income when deciding what path to take? We propose a simple model of misspecified learning in which individuals overestimate the marginal satisfaction from income—the expected effect of an income increase on overall life satisfaction—and therefore give income too much importance in their decisions. Guided by this model, we designed a pre-registered experiment that elicits beliefs about the marginal satisfaction from income and randomly assigns scientific evidence about it. Respondents substantially overestimate the marginal satisfaction from income both for themselves and for others, but especially for themselves. These biases shrink when respondents are exposed to scientific evidence, and the effects persist one month later. To study whether these beliefs matter for behavior, we measure income-versus-non-income trade-offs using job-choice scenarios tailored to each respondent and a real-world decision the respondent is facing. To elicit the latter, we make a methodological contribution: an AI-led interview method that moves beyond static, predefined survey instruments by combining the flexibility of qualitative interviewing with the discipline of closed-ended survey measurement. We find that biased beliefs are consequential: after learning that income matters less for life satisfaction than they initially thought, respondents place less weight on income in their decisions.

title: The Use and Misuse of Average and Marginal Energy Prices: Implications for Climate Policy
affiliations: Econic Partners and University of British Columbia (UBC)

detail.title: The Use and Misuse of Average and Marginal Energy Prices: Implications for Climate Policy
detail.abstract:
Many governments and institutions use marginal price signals, such as fuel and carbon taxes, to meet emission reduction targets. However, the responses of firms and individuals to these price signals are often calculated using average prices commonly reported in economic data, rather than marginal prices. This paper first documents that the marginal price of electricity paid by U.S. manufacturing plants is 50% lower than the average price. To do so, we construct a novel dataset of both average and marginal electricity prices, and the wedge between these, using plant-level microdata from the U.S. Census and utility-level electricity rate schedules for over two hundred utilities. Second, we provide guidance on when average prices are an appropriate proxy for marginal prices in price elasticities by identifying economic and geographic characteristics that predict variation in this wedge. Overall, the magnitude of this wedge suggests that the standard use of average energy prices to calculate responses to carbon taxes may underestimate the energy price increases needed to meet emissions targets by 50%.

title: Reassessing the Role of Standardized Tests in University Admissions
affiliations: Harvard University - Department of Statistics, Harvard University, Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) and Harvard University

detail.title: Reassessing the Role of Standardized Tests in University Admissions
detail.abstract:
There is a long-running debate over using standardized test scores to inform college and graduate admissions decisions, with some arguing that test scores are an important signal of academic strength and others arguing that they are biased and exclusionary. Here we revisit this issue by analyzing a novel dataset of more than 13,000 applications over roughly a decade to a large public policy master’s program in the United States. Consistent with past work, we find that GRE scores substantially improve predictions of first-year grades relative to predictions based on GPA alone. However, when these predictions are used to inform admissions decisions, we find that test scores only modestly improve the expected academic quality of admitted students. The gap shrinks further when we augment the test-aware and test-blind predictive models with more fine-grained information available in student transcripts and other application materials. Specifically, we estimate that incorporating standardized test scores in our setting would result in admitting students who perform, on average, only 0.03 grade points better. We show—both empirically and theoretically—that this pattern stems from a subtle distinction between predictions and decisions. Even with improved predictions, the downstream admissions decisions are often the same; and where there are differences, they often involve selecting between similarly qualified applicants. Our results indicate that standardized test scores may be less important for university admissions than previously suggested.

title: Granular Instrumental Variables: Estimation and Inference
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Granular Instrumental Variables: Estimation and Inference
detail.abstract: We develop an estimation and inference framework for granular instrumental variables (GIVs) in models with latent aggregate shocks. Our key insight is that valid GIVs are characterized by the orthogonal complement of the factor-loading space. This characterization yields a feasible procedure for constructing GIVs when factor loadings are unknown and does not require a large cross-sectional dimension. We provide practical procedures for inference and specification testing, and apply the framework to estimate the aggregate equity market multiplier. Our empirical results reveal substantial heterogeneity in equity demand elasticities across investor sectors and may provide nuanced support for the inelastic-markets hypothesis.

title: Competition and Misconduct in Certification Markets with Externalities

detail.title: Competition and Misconduct in Certification Markets with Externalities
detail.abstract:
Vehicle inspections—commonly known as smog and safety checks—are often delegated to private agents, much like other quality certification markets. When these agents compete, they face incentives to misreport quality—especially when consumers do not internalize the external costs of misreporting. Theory and evidence from Chile’s concentrated vehicle-inspection markets suggest that these incentives are significant: misreporting emerges as soon as competition is introduced. We find that delegating each market to a single agent proves effective in reducing approval rates, without compromising service quality or the ex-ante competition for the market, while delivering substantial and permanent reductions in vehicle emissions.

title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk and Moral Hazard

detail.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk and Moral Hazard
detail.abstract:
Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 52%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

title: Experiential and Social Learning

detail.title: Experiential and Social Learning
detail.abstract:
How does a person’s own learning experience affect their ability to learn from others? We conduct a field experiment on chlorination in Pakistan, where randomized “learning-arm” households use a tool to track their children’s diarrhea before and after chlorine distribution. Learning-arm households with learning-arm neighbors chlorinate significantly more one year after the withdrawal of the tool, with children’s health improving by 0.08 SD relative to all other households receiving chlorine. Neither learning households without learning-arm neighbors, nor non-learning households with learning-arm neighbors, exhibit sustained behavior change, results which have significant implications for intervention and evaluation design.

title: Digital Safe Havens: The Economics of Tokenized Treasuries

detail.title: Digital Safe Havens: The Economics of Tokenized Treasuries
detail.abstract:
We study the emerging market for tokenized US Treasuries and yield-bearing dollar instruments on public blockchains. Using a comprehensive dataset that combines on-chain transactions, protocol-level total value locked, pool yields, and monetary policy and stress events, we document three core findings. First, yields can be decomposed into distinct components reflecting issuer fees, lending premia, leverage, basis-trade carry, and collateral pledgability, with the latter generating economically large implicit convenience yields. Second, monetary policy transmission into on-chain dollar markets is highly heterogeneous across product designs, with administratively set rates adjusting slowly and basis-trade-backed instruments displaying economically amplified responses to policy shocks. Third, tokenized Treasuries serve as digital safe havens during episodes of cross-asset stress, attracting large inflows during risk-off events while simultaneously exposing new fragilities arising from the interaction between on-chain composability and off-chain reserve structures, particularly through stablecoin balance sheets. Overall, we provide insights into the distinctive dynamics of pricing, transmission, and fragility of digital Treasuries as decentralized and traditional financial infrastructures increasingly integrate.

title: Forecasting with Uncertain Persistence

detail.title: Forecasting with Uncertain Persistence
detail.abstract:
With uncertainty about persistence, we show that forecasts necessarily become more persistent and over-react at long horizons. For these reasons, correctly specified and Bayesian forecasts may under-react at short horizons and over-react at long horizons. These results provide a unified explanation for several asset pricing and forecasting puzzles, including: (i) the excess responsiveness of long-horizon rates to short rates, (ii) the dominance of apparent term premia for long-term rates, (iii) the ex post predictability of bond yields, (iv) the excess volatility of long-horizon forward prices, (v) the excess persistence of long-horizon forecasts, and (vi) the over-reaction of long-horizon forecasts.

title: Is Growth Additive?
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), Banco de España and New York University (NYU) - Department of Finance

detail.title: Is Growth Additive?
detail.abstract:
Growth theory is based on the assumption of exponential total factor productivity (TFP) growth, or that the conditional expectation of the next TFP increment is proportional to the current level of TFP. In the U.S., we find strong evidence that TFP growth is conditionally additive, not exponential. Even starting from low priors, Bayesian estimation selects the additive model over the exponential one. In addition, professional forecasts and international TFP series are consistent with the additive model but not with the exponential one.

detail.title: Racial Disparities in Education During and Following the Pandemic: Evidence in Connecticut through 2025
detail.abstract:
We examine pandemic related racial and ethnic disparities in test scores, absenteeism, and disciplinary incidents for K-12 students in the State of Connecticut through the 2024-25 school year. Notably, most existing pandemic studies only cover absenteeism through 2022-23, and minimal quantitative evidence exists on the post-pandemic incidence of student discipline related behaviors. Consistent with prior studies, we find persistent negative effects of the pandemic on test scores, as well as substantial disparities in test scores along racial and ethnic lines. For middle school, we also find persistent post-pandemic increases in both severe disciplinary incidents overall and racial and ethnic disparities in severe discipline incidents. However, we document substantial recovery in racial and ethnic disparities in attendance rates and chronic absenteeism by 2024-25. For all outcomes, most of the increases in disparities are associated with Black and Latinx students attending schools that had worse pre-pandemic outcomes and higher pre-pandemic shares of students who are either economically disadvantaged or face learning barriers.

title: Congestion Pricing and Emergency Medical Service Response: Evidence from New York City
affiliations: , Pace University - Department of Economics, Bentley University - Department of Economics, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) - NY Office, West Virginia University - Department of Economics, SUNY Purchase College and Bentley University

detail.title: Congestion Pricing and Emergency Medical Service Response: Evidence from New York City
detail.abstract:
Large cities worldwide have adopted congestion pricing to reduce urban traffic, with well-documented benefits for travel speeds, accident rates, and air quality. This paper identifies a novel external benefit: faster emergency medical service (EMS) response times. We provide the first evidence on how the congestion pricing program in New York City – the first comprehensive cordon-based congestion pricing system in the U.S. that was implemented on January 5th, 2025 – affects EMS performance. Exploiting the sharp geographic boundary of New York City’s congestion relief zone at 60th Street and a difference-in-discontinuities design, we first document substantial changes in traffic and mobility near the boundary: vehicular traffic declines by roughly 18 to 21 percent, accompanied by increases in pedestrian and bicycle activity. Consistent with these first-stage mechanisms, we find that congestion pricing improves EMS performance, reducing total travel times by 63–70 seconds (approximately 5–6 percent). Effects emerged quickly and show little evidence of displacement to adjacent areas. A concurrent FDNY directive requiring transport to the nearest hospital confounds standard difference-in-differences estimates but not our boundary-based design. These findings suggest that cost-benefit analyses of congestion pricing systematically understate net social benefits by omitting emergency response improvements.

title: Losses from a Disability: Temporal Variety and Earnings in the Long Run
affiliations: Columbia University - Barnard College

detail.title: Losses from a Disability: Temporal Variety and Earnings in the Long Run
detail.abstract:
Using diaries covering 25-61-year-olds in the American Time Use Survey 2009-24, this study demonstrates that temporal variety—doing more different things in a day—is income superior. Linking these data to underlying Current Population Surveys, propensity-score models show that people stating that they have a mobility/physical disability in each of two consecutive annual surveys undertake almost 4 percent fewer activities per day than other, demographically identical individuals. They also earn about 50 percent less. Combining the estimated impact of income on temporal variety with the implied reductions in variety incurred by those with the disability yields a monetary equivalent of lost variety exceeding that of lost earnings. Measuring disability status only once yields much smaller estimated shortfalls in temporal variety and earnings. That suggests that one-time self-reports of disabilities, which underlie the bulk of studies on the impacts of disabilities on earnings, also underestimate long-term effects.

title: International Trade in an Uncertain World

detail.title: International Trade in an Uncertain World
detail.abstract:
We develop a tractable quantitative model of international trade in which agents make bilateral investments in resilience under general equilibrium uncertainty. Under both complete and incomplete financial markets, we show that these bilateral investments solve a portfolio problem of choosing trade partners. Countries' risk profiles become determinants of trade flows, income and welfare, whose first moments are affected by the second moments of productivity and trade costs. Changes in global economic uncertainty have heterogeneous effects across countries, depending on how they affect real hedging opportunities. The opening of trade can raise or reduce income volatility, but is revealed-preferred to autarky.

title: Causal Inference for Asset Pricing
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Stanford University, Stockholm School of Economics, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE), Central European University (CEU) and University of Minnesota, Finance

detail.title: Causal Inference for Asset Pricing
detail.abstract:
Portfolio choice involves substituting across many assets at once, complicating inference about asset demand. An elementary condition often captures this behavior in theory and practice: homogeneous substitution conditional on observables (e.g., factor loadings, maturity, credit ratings). We characterize natural experiments identifying demand elasticity and price impact under this condition. Cross-sectional IV and difference-in-differences identify relative elasticity, own- minus cross-price elasticity for assets sharing observables. But a missing-coefficient problem leaves substitution unidentified: the coefficients on observables mechanically absorb it. Identifying substitution requires time-series regressions on portfolios sorted on observables. We apply the framework to corporate bonds, comparing alternative Fed asset-purchase programs.

title: Neighborhood Effects and Missing Markets for Opportunity
affiliations: Harvard University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Neighborhood Effects and Missing Markets for Opportunity
detail.abstract:
Experimental and quasi-experimental studies show that childhood neighborhoods have substantial causal impacts on children’s adult earnings and other long-term socioeconomic outcomes. Several market failures are likely to lead to excessive residential segregation by parental income and to an under-supply of mixed-income neighborhoods. Missing markets for opportunity originate in capital market imperfections for borrowing on children’s future earnings, neighbor spillovers, behavioral biases, and housing search frictions. Customized housing mobility services combined with subsidized housing vouchers can help low-income families move to higher-opportunity areas. Place-based policies that create mixed-income neighborhoods appear to increase long-term outcomes for less-advantaged children.

title: Quantitative Easing and Government Debt Sustainability
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and University of Bristol

detail.title: Quantitative Easing and Government Debt Sustainability
detail.abstract:
We show that quantitative easing (QE) worsens government debt sustainability. In our model, the government has a negative primary balance and downward-sloping debt demand that makes interest rates endogenous. The central bank has long-term capital and remits profits to the fiscal authority. QE depletes this capital stock, reducing future remittances and crisis-fighting reserves. Contrary to Sargent and Wallace (1981), where greater monetary accommodation lowers the steady-state debt level, we show that QE increases the steady-state level of debt and shifts the default boundary inward, thus heightening fragility and reducing debt sustainability. Moreover, while QE can keep interest rates low for extended periods, sustaining a QE-backed rate peg requires a growing central-bank footprint and accelerating capital depletion, until financing costs rise sharply. Under certain parameters, large-scale QE makes previously sustainable debt levels unsustainable, leading ultimately to sovereign default.

title: Analyzing Occupational Licensing Across Nations
