detail.title: Analyzing Occupational Licensing Across Nations
detail.abstract:
Relatively little is known about occupational licensing across nations. We assemble harmonized estimates of licensing prevalence for 44 countries using nationally representative surveys, including new surveys for previously unstudied countries. Licensing ranges from roughly 14 percent of workers in Denmark to more than 40 percent in India and South Africa. Licensed workers earn 6 to 19 percent higher wages than comparable unlicensed workers across specifications. Licensing prevalence is negatively associated with GDP per capita and governance quality, and positively associated with informal employment, suggesting occupational licensing is intertwined with labor market efficiency, formalization, and long-run economic development.

title: The Rise of Female Autonomy and the Decline of Fertility: The Role of Mismatch

detail.title: The Rise of Female Autonomy and the Decline of Fertility: The Role of Mismatch
detail.abstract:
The fertility decline is everywhere in the world today and goes back decades for rich countries. Birthrates have been below replacement in the U.S. and Europe since the mid-1970s. Completed cohort fertility in the U.S. was lower for those born in 1955 than for 1975. The reasons for the initial declines involve greater female autonomy and a mismatch between the desires of men and women. Men generally benefit more from maintaining traditions; women often benefit more from eschewing them. When the probability is low that men will abandon traditions, some career women will not have children and others will delay.

title: Mapping Monetary Transmission: Housing, CPI Measurement and the Two Faces of Inflation

detail.title: Mapping Monetary Transmission: Housing, CPI Measurement and the Two Faces of Inflation
detail.abstract: Why did the sustained monetary expansions after the global financial crisis produce weak consumer-price inflation for a decade, while the post-pandemic expansion was followed by a broad inflation surge? The question is still a matter of debate. In this paper I review three literatures which speak to it but which have developed largely in isolation from one another: monetary transmission, money-inflation regime dependence, and CPI shelter measurement. I read the three against a shared coordinate system, in which five transmission channels (asset-price, user-cost, cash-flow, tenure-flow, and measurement-lag) are crossed with two inflation regimes (low-inflation anchored and high-inflation unanchored). The contribution of the paper is the mapping itself and not a new empirical estimate. The mapping, however, generates a prediction which, as far as I can see, none of the three literatures yields on its own. Overall, the reading assigns the central role to the measurement-lag channel. Under CPI architectures built on rental equivalence or smoothed stratified rent, this channel dominates symmetrically across inflation regimes. The smoothing that mutes a housingfinance pulse on its way into headline CPI is the same smoothing that delays a shelter disinflation on its way out of it, and the lag structure is comparable in both directions. For the 2022-24 U.S. disinflation the pass-through mechanics were established by Ball and Koh (2025), Adams et al. (2024), Loewenstein et al. (2024), and Cotton (2024). In the taxonomy this mechanism becomes the fifth transmission channel, and I argue that it can organise both the 2010s and the 2021-23 episodes. With other words, one transmission structure, operating under two different regimes, can generate the missing inflation of the post-GFC decade as well as the inflation surge of 2021-23. However, transmission differs across countries. This variation can be traced back to four observable institutional parameters: CPI shelter construction, mortgage-contract structure, housing supply elasticity, and outright homeownership. An illustrative scoring of twenty advanced and upper-middle-income economies sorts the sample into four transmission regimes: muted, smoothing-dominated, cash-flow-dominated, and a hot zone in which channels compound. Economies with similar shelter weights occupy different quadrants of this map. Hence, basket weight alone cannot explain the pattern. The taxonomy is meant as a coordinate system in which the post-GFC and the post-pandemic episodes can be tested jointly.

title: Tax Incentives and Venture Capital Risk-Taking: Evidence from the QSBS Program
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and

detail.title: Tax Incentives and Venture Capital Risk-Taking: Evidence from the QSBS Program
detail.abstract:
Do tax subsidies prompt investors to take on risk? We address this question by looking at investors' responses to changes to the Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) program, which reduces capital gains taxes on startup investing. We do so under a framework in which some startup investors — venture capitalists (VCs) — combine outside funding with incentive-based compensation, while others invest their own funds. Using bunching, triple-differences, and matching designs that exploit industry eligibility, investment vintage, and holding-period requirements, we analyze data from 158 thousand investor–firm pairings over two decades. We identify strategic investment timing, with subsidies prompting bunching at tax-eligible holding-period thresholds. Most notably, when and where tax subsidies apply, VCs shift their project selection toward riskier ventures: they invest more in pre-commercial stage startups, become more likely to provide startups with their initial capital, and invest more in startups with pre-existing debt, while becoming less likely to co-syndicate their investments. Tax-subsidized VC-backed ventures show higher failure rates, but on the flip side, attain higher valuations at exit and are more likely to reach "unicorn status." None of these patterns are observed for comparable non-VC investors in startups exposed to the same tax subsidies. Our tests further show that tax incentives lead to reallocation toward more innovative industries, yielding more impactful patents. Our study is the first to show that tax policy can shift entrepreneurial financing toward riskier, more innovative, and valuable startups.

title: Did Drug Decriminalization Increase Overdoses

detail.title: Did Drug Decriminalization Increase Overdoses
detail.abstract:
We study the effect of drug decriminalization on overdose mortality using Oregon's Measure 110 and Washington's Blake decision. Synthetic-control estimates show that both decriminalization regimes sharply reduced drug arrests and were followed by sustained increases in overdose mortality relative to matched counterfactuals. The estimates imply approximately 1,186 excess deaths in Oregon and 1,895 in Washington from 2021 through 2023. We also revisit the role of fentanyl supply shocks. A fentanyl-share control may partly capture enforcement-driven declines in non-fentanyl NFLIS reports, while alternative fentanyl measures leave positive overdose effects.

title: Past v. Present: Perception of  Theories of Justice in India
affiliations: and SVKM's Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies (NMIMS) - Kirit P Mehta School Of Law

detail.title: Past v. Present: Perception of  Theories of Justice in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The said empirical research has been conducted in light of the Master's in Law curriculum in Kirit P. Mehta School of Law.

detail.abstract:
Background:
Theories of justice have traditionally been studied as a part of jurisprudence, but they also influence judicial reasoning and the development of law. This empirical study examines whether the perception of justice among law students aligns with the approach adopted by the Supreme Court of India in recent constitutional and criminal law decisions. The research analyses landmark judgments delivered between 2015 and 2025 concerning Article 21 and the death penalty, identifying the theories of justice reflected in these decisions

Methodology:
A questionnaire based on anonymised case scenarios was administered to 102 law students and recent graduates across India. Each response was mapped to a corresponding theory of justice and compared with the reasoning adopted by the Supreme Court.

Findings: 
The findings indicate that while respondents often agreed with the Court in matters involving dignity, equality and personal liberty, they differed in cases concerning statutory interpretation, public health and competing constitutional interests. These variations suggest that perceptions of justice are shaped not only by legal doctrine but also by broader social and moral considerations. The study highlights the continued relevance of jurisprudential theories in constitutional adjudication and emphasises the need to bridge the gap between theoretical legal education and practical legal reasoning.

title: Quality, Selection, and Congestion: Equilibrium Hospital Outcomes During Covid-19

detail.title: Quality, Selection, and Congestion: Equilibrium Hospital Outcomes During Covid-19
detail.abstract:
We examine the importance of hospital quality, patient selection, and congestion in affecting equilibrium health outcomes, using Covid-19 pandemic data. Our main outcome is mortality, controlling for unobserved selection with distance instruments. Intensive care unit strain increased hospital mortality: without congestion, deaths would fall 9.6%. Patients value hospitals with high baseline quality, but their choices did not reflect capacity strain information. Equilibrium counterfactuals show that if patients were informed about capacity strain and believed quality signals were more precise, deaths would drop 3.8%. However, using more precise information but not accounting for congestion would cause Covid-19 deaths to rise 3.8%.

detail.title: Information-Theoretic Duality Between Regression Topology and Statistical Mechanics——A Data-Driven Equivalence of the Ehrenfest Classification Validated on the 2D Ising Model as the Physics Cornerstone for the Factor Hierarchy Law
detail.abstract:
This paper establishes an exact information-theoretic duality between econometric regression topology and statistical mechanics. We demonstrate that an autonomous, data-driven Quadruple Test, grounded in the Factor Hierarchy Law, can blindly detect, precisely quantify, and correctly classify thermodynamic phase boundaries in perfect mathematical equivalence with the Ehrenfest paradigm, without any prior knowledge of Free Energy functions.

The validation platform is the two-dimensional Ising model. Verification proceeds in two stages: pristine algebraic validation on the Onsager-Yang exact solution, and stochastic robustness testing on finite-lattice Monte Carlo simulations. We openly declare that because data derives from the known Onsager-Yang formula, this contribution is the rigorous proof of an exact informational duality between two independent frameworks—a mandatory metrological calibration, not an independent empirical discovery.

Positive controls: Exhaustive search blindly locks onto Tc = 2.260 (deviation 0.009 at step 0.01). A grid-refinement study demonstrates monotonic convergence to ~10⁻⁸ under Golden Section Search—the limit of 64-bit machine precision. An analytical proof confirms the Chow F-statistic achieves a unique global maximum exactly at T₀ = Tc; in the analytical limit, localization error is strictly zero. Chow F = 118,074 against a null control of 3.12 (266-fold difference, permutation p = 0.000). Interaction effect: p = 0.000, ΔR² = 0.991. A symmetry-breaking switch at h = 0 yields Chow F = 989.41 (p = 0.000). Interaction R² peaks at Tc (deviation 0.03). Multi-response-function and anisotropic validations all lock onto theoretical Tc values (deviations < 0.007).

Negative controls: A 3,000-point scan over 4 variables finds no false positive of comparable magnitude (maximum SNR 164,000:1). Monte Carlo simulations (L=16-128, 8 observables) detect Tc in all sizes; all cross-size candidate peaks are excluded by F-value decay criterion.

Core discoveries: (1) Two distinct regime-switching topologies—"Rule-Reset" (interaction-dominated) and "Direction-Reversal" (intercept-jump-dominated)—map in exact informational duality onto Ehrenfest's second-order and first-order transitions. (2) Chow F(h=0) is an informational proxy for the order parameter, decaying from 691 million to 55 across 7 orders of magnitude and precisely mirroring latent heat vanishing. The F-statistic's ~38-fold amplification originates from its quadratic M² structure (theoretical lower bound β_F/β_M ≥ 2 confirmed). (3) Interaction R² is a precise proxy for second-order transition intensity (peaks at 0.9992, deviation 0.03).

Methodological contribution: A Severe Test (sensu Mayo) is completed—22 independent verification checkpoints spanning five dimensions, all passed. Cross-disciplinary integration with the Tang Break (Tang, 2026h-j) and financial regime switches (Tang, 2026g) establishes the physics cornerstone for the Factor Hierarchy Law, proving it is an informational dual of thermodynamic symmetry-breaking structures.

detail.title: The Weight of Services: Sectoral Productivity and the Sign of Aggregate TFP Growth in Brazil

detail.abstract: In a services-dominated middle-income economy, sectoral weighting can determine the sign of aggregate total factor productivity (TFP) growth. We document this for Brazil. Constructing sectoral TFP indices from value-added Solow residuals with KLEMS-calibrated factor shares (2007–2024), we find that services TFP—the largest sector by value added (70%)—declines by roughly 8.5 index points, while agricultural TFP rose and industrial TFP was broadly flat. Weighting by economic size yields a composite index that falls to 94.7 (2007=100) by 2024, reversing the flat-to-rising reading of industry-tilted averages; the sign flip survives the pandemic window, the plausible range of factor shares, and Domar–Hulten weighting. Embedding the empirical moments in a three-sector New Keynesian DSGE model, we trace a monetary double dividend: innovation raises sectoral TFP, compresses marginal cost and inflation, and induces an endogenous interest-rate cut under the estimated Taylor rule, amplifying the output gain. The R&D elasticity on industrial TFP is positive but imprecise (ηˆI = 0.264, p = 0.18, T = 18); the services public-investment channel is calibrated from the literature (ηg,S = 0.219). The fiscally neutral Lei do Bem raises GDP by +0.27% at peak (CEV +0.12%); a full package yields +0.73% (CEV +0.26%), an upper bound on the calibrated channel. Brazil’s elevated neutral real rate is what makes the dividend operative.

title: Benefit-Based Taxation can Include Substantial Redistribution

detail.title: Benefit-Based Taxation can Include Substantial Redistribution
detail.abstract:
Contrary to a long-standing concern, we present evidence that classical benefit-based labor income taxation in the tradition of Smith (1776) is consistent with income redistribution through transfers and negative average tax rates both theoretically and---in plausibly-specified simulations---quantitatively at levels which reflect U.S. policy over the past several decades. As redistribution is widespread in practice, our results remove an obstacle to the benefit principle’s plausibility as a prevailing normative foundation of tax policy.

detail.title: Iranian Journal of Economic Studies
detail.abstract: According to recent developments and research in causal inference applications, understanding applied modeling in causal effects is particularly important in econometrics. We also provide an outline of econometrics' use of causal Inference. While most economists recognize randomized controlled experiments as the preferred method for concluding, a considerable portion of empirical research in econometrics relies on observational data, which presents challenges such as confounding and potential loss of exogeneity. In this context, we examine two contemporary research types: randomized experiments and observational studies. When linear estimators are biased towards dynamic causal effects due to carryover facts or serial correlation in the imputation mechanism, applying a nonparametric framework is suggested. Because the nonparametric framework does not rely on functional assumptions about the underlying data-generating processes, such as linearity or limited. Our review of the dynamic causality study approach, the linear method, which includes LP and VAR, and nonlinear statistical modeling, which provides for BART and their use in econometrics, are all reviewed in this paper. Dynamic systems modeled using linear parametric models often encounter limitations impacting forecasting accuracy and policy implications. BART specifications can produce more precise tail forecasts than the VAR structure on the nonparametric framework. Finally, BART has the lowest RMSE in linear and nonlinear data generation processes, and the performance of BART essential variables in a macroeconomic data set is optimal compared to other regression estimators.

title: Mechanism Without Edge: The Options Crash-Insurance Premium Across Five Asset Classes

detail.title: Mechanism Without Edge: The Options Crash-Insurance Premium Across Five Asset Classes
detail.abstract: A popular retail literature claims that dealer options positioning yields tradeable directional edges. We show the opposite-and, in doing so, identify what options positioning actually prices. Across five asset classes (S&P 500 single names, SPX/NDX/RUT index options, ES/NQ index futures, COMEX gold, Deribit BTC/ETH) and multiple regimes (2010-2026, spanning the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 bear), options data price a common crash-insurance premium: the variance, correlation, and downside-variance premia share a common crash factor (collapsing together in stress), and a Barndorff-Nielsen-Shephard decomposition traces it to the jump (tail) component of variance-a persistent 5-7% of variance that makes every premium collapse in stress (the eight worst short-volatility entries in sixteen years all fall in February 2020, at-67 volatility points). A principal-components analysis confirms a shared crash factor (Kelly & Jiang, 2014); the jump "fears" of Bollerslev & Todorov (2011) are its source. This premium is risk compensation, not alpha. By contrast, every directional claim-gamma-exposure magnets, net premium flow, order-flow footprints, 0DTE pinning-is an artifact: under the Harvey et al. (2016) data-mining bar all seven second-moment signals clear |t| > 3 while zero of nine directional signals clear even |t| > 2, and the GEX-conditional strategy does not beat a coin flip (p = 0.41). The lone directional-sounding mechanism, gamma pinning, predicts volatility, not direction, and is economically redundant with implied volatility (∆R 2 = 0.000). We supply a seven-test protocol for separating mechanism from edge and transparently report a look-ahead artifact it caught in our own analysis.

title: Emergency Cash Transfers and Student Test Scores: Evidence from Brazil's Auxílio Emergencial
affiliations: Department of Economics FEA/USP and

detail.title: Emergency Cash Transfers and Student Test Scores: Evidence from Brazil's Auxílio Emergencial
detail.abstract: This paper studies the effects of Brazil's Auxílio Emergencial, an unconditional emergency cash transfer implemented during the Covid-19 pandemic, on 9th grade and 3rd year high school students test scores observed in Spaece, the state-level exam from Ceará. We link administrative social-assistance to standardized test scores records and exploit an age-based eligibility cutoff in a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, which caused a group of families to receive five monthly instalments of BRL 1,200 and other BRL 1,800. The results show negative effects on March 2022 Spaece exam, shortly after the return to in-person schooling, in Portuguese, Mathematics, and the combined score for the 9th grade. The same is observed for 3rd year Portuguese and combined score for 3rd year high school students. Results for the end-of-year exam suggest continued lower performance for the more exposed group. Placebo estimates using the 2019 Spaece assessment reveal no outcome discontinuity at the eligibility cutoff. These findings suggest that emergency transfers, even when effective as social protection, may not be sufficient to protect learning when schooling inputs are severely disrupted.

title: What Useful Alphas?
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and Federal Reserve Board of Governors

detail.title: What Useful Alphas?
detail.abstract: This paper examines about 200 published long-short anomaly equity portfolios (Chen and Zimmermann (2022)). Over the period through 2005 (December 2005 and earlier) and across all stocks, their median zero-investment return was an impressive 48 bp per month. Using only post-2005 years (January 2006 onward) reduces this to 19 bp. Using only "non-micro" top-3,000 stocks in the top 90% of market capitalization reduces this to 26 bp. Using only post-2005 and non-micro stocks reduces this to 7 bp. Even modest allowances for luck or transaction costs would have eliminated even these 7 bp. The evidence strongly suggests that published academic anomalies have been useless to non-micro-cap portfolio managers in the 21st century. Public stock markets were very efficient.

title: Pin Risk, Jumps, and Option Trading
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Pin Risk, Jumps, and Option Trading
detail.abstract: Single-name option trading is shaped by three forces Black-Scholes omits: the risk concentrated near expiry, stochastic and rough volatility, and discrete jumps-unscheduled and scheduled. We develop the mathematics of all three, beginning where the risk is most acute (pin risk and the breakdown of delta-gamma hedging), then building the Heston and rough Bergomi pricing engine, the Eraker-Johannes-Polson SVCJ jump-diffusion framework, the Dubinsky-Johannes treatment of scheduled earnings jumps, and the covered call with its dynamic management. A Heston Monte Carlo of 120,000 paths quantifies the result: a 25-delta monthly covered-call overlay on a high-volatility name raises the Sharpe ratio from 0.11 to 0.17 and the median one-year return from-2.4% to +5.0%, while a defined-risk iron condor barely earns its risk on an underlying this volatile. We close with the long-convexity mirror image-the deep out-ofthe-money long-dated call popularized in the GameStop episode-and show why its long vega is structurally unhedgeable in a thin single-name market. The claim is practical: disciplined strike selection, expiry management, and event-aware rolling capture the variance and jump risk premia while controlling the tail exposures buywrite programs routinely underestimate.

title: When Alternative Data Help: Sector-Matched Nowcasting of GDP in a Data-Scarce Economy
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria and Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: When Alternative Data Help: Sector-Matched Nowcasting of GDP in a Data-Scarce Economy
detail.abstract: We evaluate whether mixed-frequency macro-financial indicators and sector-targeted alternative data improve nowcasts of Nigerian sectoral GDP growth, and use reconstructed first-release GDP vintages to assess whether latest-vintage forecast evaluation is misleading. Using quarterly real value added for Total GDP, Agriculture, Industry and Services over 2010Q1-2025Q4, we estimate a ridge-regularised factoraugmented MIDAS model under a ragged-edge vintage design and compare it with AR(1), order-selected AR(p), random-walk and macro-only factor benchmarks, as well as a suite of machine-learning estimators. Four findings emerge. First, mixed-frequency information is most valuable early in the quarter, when official GDP data are unavailable. Second, alternative data improve accuracy only when matched to the sector's production process, while indiscriminate pooling can erase the gain. The clean case is Agriculture: night-time lights significantly reduce nowcast errors relative to AR(1), AR(p) and random-walk benchmarks, under both RMSE and MAE loss and excluding pandemic quarters. Gains for Total GDP, Industry and Services are correctly signed against weaker benchmarks but are not robust to tougher comparisons. Third, when machine-learning estimators are given the same sector-augmented information as the factor model, their point-forecast differences from ridge FA-MIDAS are small and almost always statistically insignificant, indicating that information design matters more than estimator complexity. Fourth, reconstructed first-release GDP vintages from thirty-two statistical releases show that routine within-base revisions are small over the reconstructed window; the main real-time discrepancy is the 2019 rebasing, concentrated in oil-dominated Industry. The practical lesson is that alternative data improve sectoral nowcasts only when they are sector-matched and tested against demanding benchmarks.

title: Cross-Asset Transmission Dynamics: Labor Market Elasticity, the 10-Year Treasury Yield (TNX), and Nasdaq Index Convexity

detail.abstract: This paper explores the structural and empirical relationships between macro labor indicators (nonfarm payrolls, unemployment rate), the 10-Year U.S. Treasury Yield (TNX), and the performance of the high-duration, technologyheavy Nasdaq Composite Index. Spanning the volatile six-year macro-regime from 2020 to 2026, we examine the shifting correlations that define the modern cross-asset landscape. We analyze how the post-pandemic stimulus peak, the aggressive 2022-2023 Federal Reserve tightening cycle, and the subsequent "higher-for-longer" 2024-2026 environment altered the equity risk premium (ERP). By evaluating the structural transmission vectors of the TNX into growth equity valuations, we model the mechanical sensitivity of mega-cap technology and artificial intelligence infrastructure firms to shifts in the risk-free rate. Finally, we contextualize this framework using empirical data from the Q2 2026 labor slowdown to demonstrate how modern market microstructure and sectorspecific profit-taking disconnect localized index moves from broader macroeconomic relief rallies.

title: Distortion-Based Risk Comparisons in the Presence of Background Risk
affiliations: University of Cádiz

detail.title: Distortion-Based Risk Comparisons in the Presence of Background Risk
detail.abstract: This paper characterizes comparisons between distortion-based risk contributions in the presence of a background risk, as introduced in Tsanakas and Barnett (2003). We provide representations in terms of tail conditional expectations and establish a connection with concomitants of order statistics that yields an explicit form, where concomitants capture the dependence between the background risk and the primary risk. In particular, we extend several characterizations of the increasing convex order in the framework of univariate concave distortion functions to a bivariate framework with background risk. Finally, we obtain explicit characterizations within the class of elliptical distributions, where the ordering reduces to conditions on location and dependence parameters. The results provide a unified perspective on distortion-based risk allocation and stochastic orders.  [This version: June 11, 2026]

title: The Prometeia Italian Quarterly Model: Past, Present and Future
affiliations: Prometeia, Prometeia Associazione, Prometeia SpA, Prometeia Association, Prometeia SpA and Prometeia SpA

detail.title: The Prometeia Italian Quarterly Model: Past, Present and Future
detail.abstract: For more than 40 years, Prometeia has built and used large-scale econometric models. This paper presents the latest vintage in this long tradition and highlights how changing economic conditions, regulatory requirements and model uses have shaped its features. The role of financial markets and the mechanisms for the transmission of economic policies are treated with care. The paper presents the models general theoretical and econometric characteristics, describes the main features of the estimations, assesses the models dynamic properties through a set of simulations, and summarizes its estimation and forecasting properties and performance.

title: Mortgage Securitization and Information Frictions in General Equilibrium

detail.title: Mortgage Securitization and Information Frictions in General Equilibrium

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We develop a quantitative general equilibrium model of the U.S. mortgage market where securitization, as a technology, links the credit and asset-backed security markets. Heterogeneous lenders trade in a securitization market subject to adverse selection: originators are privately informed about loan quality, while buyers anticipate a higher share of low-quality loans when household defaults rise. This friction generates an information-friction multiplier: a feedback loop where surges in household defaults drive down security prices, reduce lender liquidity, and contract mortgage credit supply. Applied to the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), the model reproduces two-thirds of the observed contraction in mortgage credit and the collapse of mortgagebacked security issuance, with information frictions amplifying the credit contraction by a factor of roughly 1.2. We use the framework to evaluate post-GFC credit guarantee policies. Post-GFC pricing stabilizes credit but generates a fiscal deficit. Pricing guarantees to reflect the amplification effects of information frictions eliminates the deficit and delivers welfare gains for both borrowers and lenders.

title: On the Monotonicity and Concavity of Effective Risk Aversion
affiliations: Shihezi University

detail.title: On the Monotonicity and Concavity of Effective Risk Aversion
detail.abstract: Apparent risk aversion has been extensively studied in the savings problem, but the corresponding portfolio choice object-effective risk aversion, which is the direct determinant of the risky portfolio share-has never been characterized for heterogeneous investors. For HARA utility functions with k > 1, apparent prudence is greater than k times apparent risk aversion if and only if the consumption function is concave. Under this condition, this paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for effective risk aversion to be increasing and concave in wealth. In the Merton model, where apparent prudence equals k times apparent risk aversion, these properties hold whenever income exceeds the subsistence consumption. The results resolve the tension: under a decreasing MPC, apparent risk aversion falls in wealth whereas effective risk aversion rises, the resolution lying in the distinction between the optimal level of investment in risky assets and the share.

title: Automated Identification of Emerging Financial Risks Through Natural Language Processing of Regulatory and Corporate Disclosures

detail.title: Automated Identification of Emerging Financial Risks Through Natural Language Processing of Regulatory and Corporate Disclosures
detail.abstract:
The increasing complexity of global financial markets has amplified the challenge of identifying emerging risks before they materialize into systemic disruptions. Traditional risk management frameworks rely heavily on quantitative indicators derived from market prices, balance sheets, and macroeconomic variables. While these approaches remain valuable, they often fail to capture early qualitative signals embedded in textual disclosures produced by corporations and regulatory institutions. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) have created new opportunities for extracting risk-relevant information from large volumes of unstructured text, enabling more proactive approaches to financial surveillance. 
This study proposes and evaluates an NLP-based framework for the automated identification of emerging financial risks through the analysis of regulatory publications and corporate disclosures. Drawing upon developments in machine learning, transformer architectures, and financial text analytics, the framework integrates topic modeling, sentiment analysis, semantic embeddings, and risk signal detection mechanisms to identify evolving patterns of concern across multiple disclosure sources. A realistic empirical design utilizing annual reports, earnings call transcripts, regulatory enforcement releases, and supervisory communications is presented to demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. 
The findings suggest that NLP systems can detect emerging risk themes significantly earlier than conventional financial indicators. In particular, changes in linguistic patterns, disclosure tone, uncertainty expressions, and thematic concentration provide valuable leading indicators of financial vulnerability. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI-enabled financial risk monitoring while offering practical insights for regulators, investors, auditors, and corporate governance professionals seeking to strengthen anticipatory risk management capabilities.

title: Commentary Incentives and Asset Bubbles: Evidence from Learningto-Forecast Experiments
affiliations: , Shanghai International Studies University, Utrecht University and University of Jinan

detail.title: Commentary Incentives and Asset Bubbles: Evidence from Learningto-Forecast Experiments

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of the Business School, University of Jinan in China (Approval Number: 2024001). Our experiments were preregistered via AsPredicted, which can be accessed via https://aspredicted.org/d9fp43.pdf.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how alternative incentive structures for public online commentary affect asset-price dynamics in a learning-to-forecast environment. We compare four settings: a baseline without commentary, non-incentivized commentary, commentary with peer endorsement, and commentary with financial incentives. We find that allowing commentary is associated with lower mispricing than the baseline. Adding a like mechanism reverses much of that improvement, leading to larger bubbles and slower convergence. When a financial incentive is added to the like-based system, mispricing and volatility are significantly lower than in the like-only treatment. Contextual analysis (employing 100 coders and an LLM) offers suggestive evidence that financial rewards encourage high-quality comments that stabilize subsequent market expectations, especially those offering fundamental insights. However, in a like-only environment, the desire for social recognition often associates with negative emotional venting, resulting in a failure to break speculative price momentum.

title: Money and Coinage: Origins, Functions, and Institutions

detail.title: Money and Coinage: Origins, Functions, and Institutions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: The author gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Sven Svensson Foundation for Numismatics, the Gunnar Ekstrand Foundation, and the Sven and Dagmar Salén Foundation.

detail.abstract:
This chapter investigates the origins and evolution of money from its prehistoric beginnings
to the introduction of coinage and credit. Drawing on archaeological, anthropological, and
economic-historical evidence, it explores how early humans used commodities such as cattle,
grain, and tool materials (e.g., flint and obsidian) as media of exchange and stores of value
as early as 9000 BC. These items fulfilled the core monetary functions: serving as a medium
of exchange, unit of account, and store of value, though the standard of deferred payment
was slower to develop due to its reliance on formalized credit and trust. The standard of
deferred payment developed more gradually, since impersonal credit required trust,
information, repeated interaction, or institutions capable of reducing adverse selection and
moral hazard.
The chapter contrasts the commodity theory—which views money as emerging
spontaneously from barter—with the state theory, which sees money as a legal construction
backed by the fiscal authority of the state. The archaeological record demonstrates that
money in its basic form emerged prior to states and taxation systems, challenging strong
versions of the state theory of money. However, the standardization of money—especially
in the form of coinage—required an issuing authority capable of specifying weight and
fineness, enforcing legal tender laws, and protecting the monetary system against fraud.
Money is therefore best understood as a hybrid institution: it could originate in decentralized
exchange, but it became increasingly standardized, regulated, and institutionally
supported as economies grew more complex. Coinage and later credit systems facilitated
the expansion of long-distance trade, market complexity, and economic coordination
across time and space.

title: Consumption Data and the Geography of Hidden Populations
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business, Federal Reserve Board of Governors and

detail.title: Consumption Data and the Geography of Hidden Populations
detail.abstract: Accurate demographic measurement is fundamental to economic research, yet many populations are systematically undercounted in official data. We develop a new approach that uses market-generated consumption data to measure the geography of hard-to-count populations. We apply the approach to construct a proxy for Hispanic immigrant presence across U.S. counties from 2006 to 2022 using local expenditures on Hispanic-distinctive food products. The measure closely tracks Census and school-enrollment benchmarks and responds to immigration-enforcement shocks. For Venezuelan immigrants, it expands geographic coverage from 21 ACS-reported counties to over 600. The framework can be applied to other undercounted populations and can facilitate research when official local demographic data are incomplete.

title: Generating Risk Scenarios Adverse to Cooperative Vehicle Infrastructure Perception: An Optimization-Based Framework
affiliations: Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, Central South University, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei University of Technology and Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: Generating Risk Scenarios Adverse to Cooperative Vehicle Infrastructure Perception: An Optimization-Based Framework
detail.abstract: Existing approaches for concrete scenario generation and assessment primarily focus on trajectory-level interactions while neglecting physical perception constraints, such as sensor field-of-view limitations and occlusions from surrounding objects, leading to unrealistic risk representations. To fill this gap, this study proposes a framework that integrates vehicle dynamics, environmental constraints, and perception limitations into a unified generation process. Specifically, vehicle trajectories are parameterized using a kinematic bicycle model and perturbed through controlled variations in longitudinal acceleration and steering angle. A voxel-based surrogate perception metric is introduced to efficiently evaluate cooperative perception (CoP) by modeling line-of-sight occlusions, which achieves a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy. By modeling perception limitations, the framework generates not only risky but also CoP-adverse scenarios. A multi-constraint optimization framework driven by the genetic algorithm is proposed, which ensures that generated scenarios satisfy physical feasibility, road compliance, collision avoidance, and degraded perception conditions, while increasing interaction risk between agents. Experimental results based on real-world trajectory datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach can effectively generate diverse and high-risk scenarios with reduced CoP performance and satisfactory computational efficiency. This framework may not only help generate CoP-adverse scenarios for the assessment and evaluation of vehicle-infrastructure CoP systems, but also offer a tool for the construction of scenario library to support end-to-end learning-based methods.

title:
When Leveling Performance Doesn't Level Pay 
AI, Openness, and Rank-Based Amplication
affiliations: Competitio Consulting

detail.title:
When Leveling Performance Doesn't Level Pay 
AI, Openness, and Rank-Based Amplication
detail.abstract: AI compresses within-task performance dierences, yet it need not compress pay. I model tasks by openness σ τ , the share of output remaining on the human judgment margin once execution becomes shared technology, and show that as the execution stack rises, within-task performance variance falls toward the judgment oora lower bound on dispersion, not on paythat grows with openness. Under a xedshare wage bargain, AI compresses pay dispersion on every xed task; but labor migrates toward open tasks, where this variance oor is high, so aggregate dispersion can rise through composition. A rank-based pay extension strengthens the eect: when execution is commoditised, rank is determined by judgment alone, so the judgment dierences that set the variance oor also determine each worker's share of surplus, and pay variance rises precisely where human work remains most relevant.

title: Over-Issuance as a Non-Cooperative Equilib rium: A Game-Theoretic Critique of Competitive Note Issue

detail.title: Over-Issuance as a Non-Cooperative Equilib rium: A Game-Theoretic Critique of Competitive Note Issue
detail.abstract: The free banking school maintains that competitive note issue under laissez faire self-regulates through the adverse clearing mechanism: overissuing banks suffer disproportionate reserve drains through the interbank note exchange and are compelled to contract. This paper identifies conditions under which that mechanism fails. Three layers of analysis are deployed. First, a dynamic game of note-dueling exhibits a first-mover disadvantage: the would-be disciplinarian is economically marginalized before its attack can be completed. Second, once universal over-issuance obtains, any disciplinary attack triggers market scrutiny that exposes the attacker's own over-issuance-no bank will sacrifice its income to punish a rival. Third, note-dueling between symmetric overissuers is mutually assured destruction; the attacker cannot prevent the target from deploying the same weapon in return. Each layer independently suffices to break the self-correction mechanism. The free banking school's premises-brand discrimination, adverse clearing, long-term bank rationality-do not guarantee the conclusion drawn from them.

title: Cultural or Institutional? Decomposing the Persistent East-West Childcare Frontier in Post-Reunification Berlin
affiliations: Universitat Internacional de Catalunya and Universitat Internacional de Catalunya

detail.title: Cultural or Institutional? Decomposing the Persistent East-West Childcare Frontier in Post-Reunification Berlin
detail.abstract: Why does formal childcare use among young children continue to diverge along the former inner-German border, three decades after reunification? Germany illustrates a broader social investment policy paradox: expanding childcare provision does not automatically translate into take-up, since take-up reflects both cultural legacies and institutional environments that are normally inseparable. Berlin offers a rare opportunity to disentangle these channels. As the only German city divided between two sovereign states and subsequently reunified, Berlin has seen substantial post-1990 residential mobility that generates mothers whose cultural origin and current institutional environment are mismatched. Using a 2 × 2 origin-by-residence design with SOEP data for Berlin mothers of children aged 0-35 months (2003-2021, N = 255), we find that the institutional environment of current residence, not the cultural background of origin, is the primary driver of the persistent East-West childcare gap. These findings point to supply-side reform as the more promising lever for closing the gap.

reference: San Diego Legal Studies Paper No. 26-020; Behavioural Public Policy (forthcoming 2027, Special Issue)
title: Personalization in Regulatory Trust: Behavioral Challenges of Using Past Behavior to Predict Future Compliance
affiliations: Bar-Ilan University - Faculty of Law, Bar-Ilan University - Faculty of Law and University of San Diego School of Law

detail.title: Personalization in Regulatory Trust: Behavioral Challenges of Using Past Behavior to Predict Future Compliance

publicationDetails.detailsText: San Diego Legal Studies Paper No. 26-020
publicationDetails.journalName: University of San Diego Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article examines the behavioral foundations, promises, and limits of personalized regulation that uses past behavior to predict future compliance. As regulators increasingly differentiate enforcement burdens according to compliance histories, pressing questions arise about the accuracy, fairness, and behavioral consequences of doing so. Drawing on behavioral public policy research, including work on honesty pledges, voluntary compliance, motivational crowding, and domain-specific cooperation, the article develops a behaviorally grounded framework for when and how past behavior can legitimately inform regulatory trust. Its argument is twofold. First, the predictive value of past behavior is real but limited: it varies across regulatory domains, is moderated by situational and developmental factors, and is sometimes inverted, as when prior compliance licenses later violation. Second, personalized trust is not only predictive but constitutive: by signaling (dis)trust and reallocating monitoring and administrative burdens, it reshapes the very motivation and behavior it purports to forecast, through mechanisms that include intrinsic motivation, self-concept maintenance, procedural justice, psychological reactance, moral licensing, algorithm aversion, and social norms. Two distinctions organize the analysis: a spectrum of relatedness, running from same-domain through adjacent to unrelated past conduct, and a distinction in the direction of inference, between predicting that conduct will recur and predicting that one kind of conduct forecasts another. These dynamics bear most heavily on individuals; for organizations, path dependence and compliance culture tend to make past conduct a steadier signal. The article identifies when personalized trust improves compliance, when it risks crowding out intrinsic motivation or entrenching inequality, and the design principles that can help regulators navigate these tensions.

title: Integrity First: Warren Buffett's Decision Architecture, the Principal-Agent Tradition, and the Limits of Compensatory Modeling

detail.title: Integrity First: Warren Buffett's Decision Architecture, the Principal-Agent Tradition, and the Limits of Compensatory Modeling
detail.abstract: Warren Buffett evaluates people by three criteria-integrity, intelligence, and energyin that strict order, with integrity as a threshold condition rather than a weighted factor. No surplus of intelligence or energy compensates for an integrity deficit. The evaluation terminates at the first criterion if it fails. This paper argues that Buffett's framework is not merely practical wisdom but a precise instantiation of lexicographic preferences: a preference structure formally non-representable by any real-valued utility function, a direct consequence of Debreu's 1954 representation theorem. The principal-agent tradition-the lineage of economists whose work on incentive design and optimal contracting has shaped corporate governance advice for fifty years-encountered this impossibility result, found it intractable, and proceeded without it. The advice that followed-align incentives, improve monitoring, elaborate governance structurespresupposes that the principal-agent relationship is cooperative, without offering tools to determine whether it is. That prior question-whether the relationship is cooperative at all, and what determines its cooperative character-is what Buffett's framework answers first. His sixty-year track record at Berkshire Hathaway, and the organizational architecture he built around threshold-first screening, constitute the most sustained natural experiment in applied decision theory of the past century. This paper, situated at the intersection of corporate governance, law and economics, and decision theory, traces the formal structure of what Buffett does, the modeling choice that closed the principal-agent tradition's vision, and the practical and epistemic consequences for the boards, regulators, and institutions that have been receiving advice the underlying models were not equipped to give.

title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and Carbon Emissions in Emerging Markets
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business, Asian Development Bank and Academy of Finance - International Finance Department

detail.title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and Carbon Emissions in Emerging Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 854

detail.abstract: This paper empirically examines the impact of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) on carbon emissions in 13 emerging market economies (EMEs), using panel local projections over the period 1990 to 2023. The results indicate that rising EPU significantly increases carbon emissions. However, the impact varies across economic and institutional characteristics. Specifically, EMEs with lower initial carbon emissions, higher energy intensity, carbon pricing mechanisms, greater financial development, higher trade openness, stronger political stability, greater renewable energy reliance, and higher research and development intensity exhibit a weaker response to EPU. Moreover, high-income EMEs experience a muted response in emissions, whereas lowerincome EMEs face a more pronounced impact. Additionally, EMEs with low climate vulnerability see a stronger positive response in emissions compared to their high-vulnerability counterparts. These findings highlight the critical role of institutional and structural factors in shaping the emissions response to EPU, offering important policy insights for mitigating environmental risks in uncertain economic conditions.

title: Does Retail Attention Predict Returns? Evidence from Robinhood "Popularity" Data, 2018-2020

detail.title: Does Retail Attention Predict Returns? Evidence from Robinhood "Popularity" Data, 2018-2020
detail.abstract: A large body of behavioral finance research, beginning with Barber and Odean (2000), finds that individual investors who trade frequently tend to underperform the market, partly due to their tendency to chase recently attention-grabbing stocks rather than making decisions based on new information. Commission-free, "gamified" trading apps such as Robinhood have been argued to amplify this tendency by directing user attention toward stocks with extremely recent price moves. Using historical data on Robinhood user holdings ("popularity"), along with daily stock prices for 57 stocks from May 2018 to August 2020, this paper examines whether increases in retail popularity predict subsequent returns. The results indicate that a stock's popularity change relative to its own history does not significantly predict its return over the following week. However, when attention is measured relative to other stocks on the same day, identifying stocks likely to appear on a "Top Movers"-style list, stocks in the top 5% of daily popularity change underperform the rest of the sample by about 0.95 percentage points over the following week (p = 0.007). These results suggest that attention-driven underperformance depends on relative attention rather than absolute popularity changes and that specification choices substantially affect whether this effect is detectable.

title: Cultural Sentiment and Housing Market Predictability: Evidence from Cantopop Lyrics in Hong Kong

detail.title: Cultural Sentiment and Housing Market Predictability: Evidence from Cantopop Lyrics in Hong Kong
detail.abstract: Cultural sentiment provides forward-looking information about housing market dynamics that standard macroeconomic indicators do not fully capture. I use a BERT-based natural language processing pipeline to construct two sentiment indices with distinct properties: a chart-weighted index derived from chart data, and a release-based love-song index constructed from love songs in the award-based artist corpus. I find that the chart-weighted index predicts aggregate housing transaction volume out-of-sample, reducing forecast errors by 33.8%. The release-based index predicts cross-sectional price heterogeneity. A one-standard-deviation increase in the sentiment index is associated with an 11.6 percentage points larger price increase in the most supply-constrained districts compared to districts with no Village Zone exposure.

title: LINGO: The Deterministic Linguistic Gate Engine Why AI Accuracy Is Decided at the Input, Not the Output, and Why Almost No One Builds There

detail.title: LINGO: The Deterministic Linguistic Gate Engine Why AI Accuracy Is Decided at the Input, Not the Output, and Why Almost No One Builds There

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of SnapStak.ai and the sole developer of the CON10X platform, including ConteX Law, LINGO, CLARA, and AXIOM, which are the subject of this paper

detail.abstract: Almost every existing approach to AI reliability intervenes after generation: it checks a completion once produced, trains a verifier to catch what slipped through, or votes across samples to detect disagreement. Each of these operates on an output that already exists. This paper argues that the decisive lever sits earlier, at the input, and that almost nothing in the field is built there. ConteX Law states the principle: where four governing pillars are satisfied to completeness against a source of truth, a generative model's capacity to confabulate collapses and its output becomes reproducible. A principle stated is not a principle enforced, and a law of this kind is only as good as the mechanism that decides whether its condition has been met before the model is ever asked to write. This paper sets out the theory behind LINGO, the deterministic linguistic gated engine that computes the ConteX Law completeness gate and turns the law from a stated relationship into a running, checkable measurement, applied to the input rather than the output. It argues that an engine of this kind must be linguistic in what it asks of a model, deterministic in how it turns an answer into a verdict, and gated in that it decides before generation rather than validates after it. This is not one design choice among several. It is the architecture required to secure the three properties a law of this kind demands: reproducibility, falsifiability, and modelindependence. The paper states the general contract any such engine must satisfy, works a small example by hand, situates LINGO within the wider CON10X stack alongside CLARA and AXIOM, all three of which act before generation rather than after it, and states plainly what LINGO does not claim. No implementation detail, taxonomy, or scoring internals are disclosed; the concern here is the theory an engine of this kind must embody, not the engine itself.

detail.abstract: US firms hiring foreign workers in low-skill nonfarm jobs face a binding quota on the H-2B visa, allocated in part through a randomized lottery. We evaluate the quota's marginal impact using the lottery, a novel firm survey, and a preanalysis plan. Firms exogenously employing more H-2B workers in low-skill jobs increase production (elasticity 0.20-0.22), investment (1.5-2.1), and profits (0.15). The elasticity of substitution between H-2B and US workers is very low (0.8-2.0). Thus the effect on US employment is zero or positive overall, and positive in rural areas. Forensic analysis suggests similarly low substitutability of black-market labor.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we match grid-level climate data to bilateral migration data from three waves of the Indian Census to investigate the effect of climate variability on interstate migration in India. Using relevant meteorological indicators of climate variability to measure the frequency, magnitude and duration of drought and excess precipitation, based on the Standard Precipitation Index, we find that increases in drought frequency and magnitude in the origin state increases bilateral migration rates between origindestination state pairs, controlling for several time-varying and time-invariant factors. To avoid simultaneity of migration flows with the climate variations, we look at climate conditions in the 5 years preceding migration as push factors to increase bilateral migration. We also use the PPML estimator in our regressions to account for the empirical specification which is based off a random utility model traditionally used in the trade gravity model literature.

detail.abstract: India is witnessing a rapid expansion of its artificial intelligence startup ecosystem, with valuations driven primarily by the quality and scale of training data, proprietary models, and the ability to generate commercially viable AI outputs. Yet, the legal frameworks governing the disclosure of intellectual property risks connected to such training data remain largely underdeveloped. This paper examines the structural gap between the valuation methodology of Indian AI startups and the disclosure requirements embedded in Indian company law. Drawing upon Sections 134 and 166 of the Companies Act, 2013, the provisions of the Copyright Act, 1957, the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the paper argues that Indian AI companies may be raising investment capital based on assets whose copyright status has not been independently verified, audited, or disclosed to investors. The paper uses the emergence of India's first AI unicorn, Krutrim, and the landmark litigation in ANI Media Pvt. Ltd. v. OpenAI Inc. & Anr. as contextual anchors. It further draws on the December 2025 working paper of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) on Generative AI and copyright. The paper concludes by proposing a model legislative and governance framework, including mandatory training, a data rights register, a copyright clearance obligation before major fundraising, and a board-level AI risk disclosure mechanism.

title: A Review Of The Nigerian Startup Act, 2022

detail.title: A Review Of The Nigerian Startup Act, 2022
detail.abstract: The Nigerian business ecosystem has in recent years witnessed rapid growth, particularly in the technology- driven startup sector, which plays a crucial role in innovation, job creation, and economic diversification. However, despite its potential, the startup ecosystem has been bedeviled by numerous challenges, including fragmented regulatory regime, bureaucratic bottlenecks, unfriendly tax policies, and limited access to funding. These factors have contributed to high startup failure rates and discouraged both local and foreign investments. The enactment of the Nigerian Startup Act (NSA) 2022 marked a revolutionary step towards addressing these issues by introducing a harmonized legal and institutional framework that is targeted at fostering Innovation and entrepreneurship. The aim of this study Is to critically review the Nigerian startup Act, evaluating the Act’s provisions, regulatory frameworks and its impact on the Nigerian business ecosystem. The research adopts a doctrinal methodology, relying on primary sources such as statutes, government reports, and international startup laws, alongside secondary sources such as scholarly articles, online publications, and policy analysis. Through content analysis, the study investigates the role of the Act in resolving regulatory uncertainties, promoting access to capital, safeguarding intellectual property rights, and enhancing Nigeria’s position within the global digital economy. Findings reveal that while the Act introduces innovative mechanisms such as the Startup Label, Investment Seed Fund, and a National Council for Digital Innovation and Entrepreneurship, challenges remain in its centralized governance structure, restrictive eligibility requirements, and slow adoption at state level. Nevertheless, the Act represents a remarkable milestone in Nigeria’s quest to become Africa’s leading startup destination. In conclusion, the study critiques the transformative potential of the NSA, and equally highlights the urgent need for strategic reforms, inclusivity, and sustained political will to ensure its effective implementation and long-term impact on Nigeria’s economy.

title: Spatial Sound Field Modeling of Ship Pass-By Noise with Hydrophone Offset Correction
affiliations: Naval University of Engineering, Naval University of Engineering, Naval University of Engineering  and Naval University of Engineering

detail.title: Spatial Sound Field Modeling of Ship Pass-By Noise with Hydrophone Offset Correction
detail.abstract: To improve the modeling accuracy of ship pass-by noise fields under distance-location uncertainty, a spatial sound field modeling method with hydrophone offset correction is proposed. First, hydrophone signals measured during a lake experiment are used to extract the acoustic features of ship pass-by noise based on root-mean-square energy, sound pressure level, and time-frequency analysis. Second, under the assumption that the source level remains relatively stable under the same operating condition, an error function is constructed to estimate the vertical offset of the hydrophone relative to the ship track, and the corresponding correction is applied to the closest point of approach distance. Furthermore, based on the corrected geometry, the distance–sound pressure level (D-SPL) curve is reconstructed and fitted using a neural network to establish the spatial distribution of sound pressure levels over the water-surface reference plane. Meanwhile, propagation models for different frequency bands are built based on one-third-octave bands, and the overall sound pressure level is reconstructed through energy summation. Finally, the proposed method is validated by comparison with lake-trial validation-track data. The results show that, under the experimental conditions considered in this study, the proposed model can effectively describe the basic spatial variation law of ship pass-by noise. The relative error of the validation data is controlled within 6.5%, with an average relative error of 1.89%. These results indicate that the proposed method can provide a useful reference for ship pass-by noise assessment and spatial sound field prediction under lake-trial conditions.

title: Land, Power and Population Density in the Global Population Shifts of 1500 – 1960
affiliations: ,  and Brown University

detail.title: Land, Power and Population Density in the Global Population Shifts of 1500 – 1960
detail.abstract: The regional distribution of world population underwent profound changes during the age of exploration and colonization, in which a handful of European powers colonized the better part of the remaining continents. One consequence is that countries in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand, after sharp contractions of indigenous populations following exposure to Old World diseases, today have populations in which European or African descendants form majorities and speak predominantly European languages. Migration and in some cases colonization also altered population compositions in countries including South Africa, Cape Verde, Fiji and Singapore. And descendants of émigrés came to outnumber those of "stayers" in some non-colonizing countries, including Ireland and Lebanon. We identify major determinants of who settled where, during this era of colonialism and migration, demonstrating that both "natural" factors like availability and fertility of agricultural land and climate and disease prevalence, on the one hand, and power inequalities and cultural variables, on the other, explain the broad patterns of migration.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Road User Behavior: A Scoping Review of Current Paradigms and Future Frontiers
affiliations: University of Michigan at Dearborn, University of Michigan at Dearborn, University of Michigan at Dearborn, University of Michigan at Dearborn, Toyota Motor Engineering & Manufacturing, Toyota Motor Engineering & Manufacturing, Toyota Motor Engineering & Manufacturing, University of Michigan at Dearborn, Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology and University of Michigan at Dearborn

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence for Road User Behavior: A Scoping Review of Current Paradigms and Future Frontiers
detail.abstract: Road user behavior remains the primary precipitating factor in global traffic crashes, yet the methodologies used to analyze these complex human dynamics are undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift. Traditional statistical inference, once the cornerstone of safety research, is increasingly being superseded by high-dimensional Artificial Intelligence (AI) modeling capable of capturing non-linear relationships. This scoping review synthesizes 140 peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2026 to systematically map the state-of-the-art AI-driven behavioral analysis within crash-related contexts. To structure this evolving landscape, we introduce an original six-layer analytical taxonomy. This framework traces the intricate pathways connecting behavioral categories (such as impairment, distraction, and tactical maneuvers) to computational domains (including Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Natural Language Processing), functional objectives, and evaluation indicators. Through Sankey-based operationalization, we analyze the research trajectories for both drivers (128 studies) and vulnerable road users (52 studies). Our synthesis reveals a field currently dominated by ”predictive fidelity”, optimizing model accuracy, often at the significant expense of ”operational viability” and real-time safety metrics required for field deployment. Notably, the recent surge in Large Language Models (LLMs) across 31 studies marks a pivotal transition toward semantic reasoning, allowing researchers to move beyond numerical data toward narrative-based information extraction and automated scenario generation. By highlighting critical structural gaps in explainability, temporal relevance, and real-world implementation, this review provides a strategic roadmap for the next generation of AI-integrated traffic safety research, advocating for a transition from black-box prediction to deployable, human-centric safety intelligence.

title: Local Newspapers and Local Events: Ownership, Market Structure, and Responsiveness
affiliations: and Wake Forest University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Local Newspapers and Local Events: Ownership, Market Structure, and Responsiveness
detail.abstract: How do ownership and market structure affect the production of local public information? Local newspapers supply information that citizens can use to monitor local conditions, but observed coverage combines editorial choices with the arrival of newsworthy events. We measure responsiveness using Powerball and Mega Millions jackpot wins. All newspapers observe the same national lottery event, while newspapers in the winning state face an exogenous increase in local relevance. Controlling for jackpot size and lagged lottery sales separates local relevance from national salience and consumer demand. Newspapers nearly double lottery coverage after in-state wins. Responsiveness increases after transitions to non-investment owners, but transitions into investment ownership do not generate this increase. Newspapers in concentrated markets publish fewer articles overall, yet respond more strongly to highly salient local events. Complementary COVID-19 evidence shows that newspapers also respond to substantive local public health information. The results indicate that ownership and market structure shape how local public information is produced and made available to citizens. This matters for public economics because heterogeneity in information production can affect citizen monitoring, local accountability, and the information environment in which public policy is evaluated.

title: Is Old Trafford Still a Fortress? Manchester United's Home Advantage and the Bruno Fernandes Era
affiliations: Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM)

detail.title: Is Old Trafford Still a Fortress? Manchester United's Home Advantage and the Bruno Fernandes Era
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether Old Trafford remains a distinctive source of competitive advantage for Manchester United in the Premier League era. Using match-level Premier League data from 1993/94 through 2025/26, I construct a symmetric team-match panel of 25,408 observations from 12,704 fixtures and estimate home-advantage models for points, goal difference, and win probability. The final empirical specification is intentionally conservative: it uses team-season fixed effects, so identification comes from within-club, within-season differences between home and away matches rather than from cross-club differences in quality. The model then compares Manchester United's home premium with the league-wide home premium and allows the difference to vary across eras: the Ferguson era, the post-Ferguson pre-Bruno period, the Bruno/COVID transition, and the modern Bruno Fernandes era. The results are nuanced. Premier League home advantage is large and statistically significant throughout the sample. Manchester United's full-sample additional home-points premium is not statistically significant, partly because Ferguson-era United were also elite away from home. In the post-Ferguson period, the relative Old Trafford premium weakens, especially in goaldifference terms. In the modern Bruno era, however, United's additional home premium becomes positive again relative to the Premier League benchmark. I then add an exploratory player layer focused on Bruno Fernandes. Season-level key-pass data indicate that Bruno's creative output is positively associated with Manchester United's shot volume, although not reliably with goals or points in a seven-season sample. The paper concludes that the Old Trafford story is not one of simple disappearance. Manchester United's advantage appears to have changed in form: from broad institutional dominance in the Ferguson period, through post-Ferguson erosion, toward a modern version in which renewed home performance and player-centered creative dependence coexist.

title: Seemingly Anchored Inflation Expectations
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Seemingly Anchored Inflation Expectations
detail.abstract:
Empirical evidence commonly cited as indicating that inflation expectations have become better anchored includes the declining sensitivity of expectations to inflation surprises over time, particularly around the adoption of inflation targeting. These patterns are typically attributed to the influence of explicit or implicit inflation targets on inflation expectations. We show that this evidence is consistent with a model of experience-based learning in which individuals learn solely from their life-time history of realized inflation, without anchoring their expectations to an announced inflation target. In this model, the prolonged experience of low short-run inflation persistence in the pre-COVID decades renders long-run expectations insensitive to inflation surprises, matching the patterns observed in empirical anchoring tests. A unique prediction of the experience-based learning model is also borne out in the data: the decline in surprise sensitivity since the 1980s is strongest among younger individuals. The memory of low inflation persistence experiences further explains why long-run inflation expectations remained stable in the face of the post-COVID inflation surge. At the same time, simulations indicate that the sensitivity of long-run expectations to inflation surprises would rise sharply if individuals were to experience another sustained episode of highly persistent inflation. Overall, long-run inflation expectations may be less firmly anchored than commonly believed.

title: Early Warning of Systemic Shock Caused by the US-Israel Tension with Iran: A Lotka-Volterra Approach
affiliations: University of Dar es Salaam and Catholic University of Mbeya

detail.title: Early Warning of Systemic Shock Caused by the US-Israel Tension with Iran: A Lotka-Volterra Approach
detail.abstract: Following the geopolitical conflict between the US-Israel and Iran, the world has experienced a surge in fuel price. This becomes a threat to both micro and macroeconomic growth if the war could be prolonged. Using the industrial network data from 1995-2018 and crude oil price volatility from the beginning of the war (February 27, 2026) to April 2, 2026, this study developed the mathematical model adopted from the Lotka-Volterra theory to examine how the disruption of crude oil triggers the systemic shock. The results reveal that crude oil price volatility occurred during the conflict was below the tipping point of [[EQUATION]], indicating the system remained resilient during the period. Additionally, the shock impact was so small that can be absorbed. However, the interaction strength of the system exceeds the critical transition of [[EQUATION]], implying that the industrial network is highly connected and therefore, vulnerable to systemic shocks if the parameters exceed the tipping points. This study concludes that, if the war could be prolonged beyond the threshold, the global economy could be endangered to collapse completely. The study offers an early warning of systemic shocks, thereby, economists and policy makers can suggest the optimal strategies for shock mitigations during the geopolitical conflicts.

title: The Pass-through of Tariffs and Exchange Rates
affiliations: École Nationale de la Statistique et de l'Analyse de l'Information (ENSAI), University of British Columbia (UBC) - Department of Economics and University of Lausanne

detail.title: The Pass-through of Tariffs and Exchange Rates
detail.abstract:
This paper shows that the currency in which traded goods are invoiced has a first-order implication for the short-run impact of tariffs on the economy. If prices are set in terms of producer’s currency (PCP), a unilateral tariff is contractionary on impact, reducing GDP, and causing a deterioration in the trade balance. By contrast, with prices pre-set in buyers currency (LCP), the same tariff shock is expansionary, and improves the trade balance. The key difference between the two regimes lies in the differential exchange rate pass- through under PCP relative to LCP. In welfare terms however, the situation is reversed. A tariff under LCP leads to a fall in short-run welfare, as consumption and investment fall sharply, while the same tariff may be welfare enhancing under PCP. Under dollar currency pricing (DCP), we find results intermediate between the two invoicing regimes. With retaliation, the stark difference in pricing regimes is attenuated.

title: The Art Critics Won't Save You from the Robots: Confronting A.I. as Misappropriation

detail.title: The Art Critics Won't Save You from the Robots: Confronting A.I. as Misappropriation

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (A.I.) systems require a wealth of training data, which is often harvested from creators without their consent, and then used to train systems whose intent is to replace those same creators. This has sparked a wave of judicial opinions, law review articles, and popular press think pieces that perform textual and information-based analyses of whether A.I. systems are a transformative use of copyrighted works. This article argues that a better approach lies in a separate thread of copyright theory, which is a far more direct approach toward addressing harms: direct copying is an unfair business practice which, if left unchecked, makes it impossible for creators to reap what they had sown at great expense. There is precedent to this preferred thread in U.S. law, most closely in the "hot news doctrine," which can be minimally modified to provide guidance on how unfair practices in this new realm of A.I. can be identified and possibly regulated.
