title: Making the Immaterial Material: How Plaintiffs Plead Social-Media Harms in the Shadow of Section 230
affiliations: Stanford University, Law School and

detail.title: Making the Immaterial Material: How Plaintiffs Plead Social-Media Harms in the Shadow of Section 230

publicationDetails.detailsText: Stanford Public Law Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Stanford Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: When families allege that social media platforms cause addiction, depression, and self-harm among young users, they confront a recurring legal obstacle: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which courts have interpreted to immunize platforms from liability for harms linked to speech. This article examines how plaintiffs in a landmark multidistrict litigation constructed a products liability theory capable of surviving that obstacle. Through a thematic content analysis (TCA) of 70 individual complaints from In re Social Media Adolescent Addiction/Personal Injury Products Liability Litigation, we make three contributions. First, we show that complaints converged on the same arguments and evidence, including a nearly universal disclaimer separating design from speech. Second, we identify a gendered theory of product defect, in which social media products were framed as unreasonably dangerous specifically for adolescent girls. Third, we uncover a shared sequential architecture-moving from adolescent vulnerability to corporate targeting to exploitative design to profit motive-that represents an evolution from earlier cases in which plaintiffs failed to distinguish product design from content. After revealing these patterns using TCA, we illustrate them using specific excerpts from complaints. Ultimately, this article demonstrates how plaintiffs can translate intangible software features into concrete, legally cognizable injuries.

title: Structural Macroeconomics with AI Agents
affiliations: and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Structural Macroeconomics with AI Agents
detail.abstract: We propose a method for simulating structural macroeconomic models in which the rational expectations decision rule is replaced by the forward pass of a large language model. Holding the economic environment fixed—the same states, information, budget constraints, and feasibility conditions—we substitute the optimizing policy of a rational household with that of a frozen, pre-trained language model, which we call an AI agent, inside a canonical incomplete markets, life-cycle model of consumption and saving. Benchmarked against the model's own rational-expectations solution, frontier language models jointly reproduce a range of empirical consumption puzzles that the rational benchmark misses: a marginal propensity to consume that is large and declines with the size of the income shock, excess sensitivity of consumption to anticipated income changes, a discrete drop in spending at the exhaustion of unemployment benefits, and a failure to smooth consumption across the retirement income drop. Each of these regularities has separately motivated a tuned departure from the rational benchmark; AI agents match them simultaneously in a single calibrated economy, with no parameter fit to any of them. Because the two benchmarks face an identical environment and differ only in the decision rule, the gap between them captures the behavioral content of replacing optimization with a language model. Decomposing this gap, we find that it does not reflect distorted beliefs but rather a failure to act on them: a cognitive wedge between beliefs and actions.

title:
Does AI Create a "Permanent Underclass"?
 From Market Structure to Complementary Assets, Industry Resilience, and the Choice of Metric
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title:
Does AI Create a "Permanent Underclass"?
 From Market Structure to Complementary Assets, Industry Resilience, and the Choice of Metric

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Vox Technologies, Inc., which works on robotics and AI infrastructure (the Robot Foundation Layer standards project). The author has no financial relationship with any frontier AI laboratory analyzed in this paper. Generative AI was used to verify the paper's empirical claims against primary sources (a multi-vote fact-checking harness, described in the Methodology Note); the text was written by the author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding; it was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
In April 2026, the New York Times warned that Silicon Valley is "bracing for a permanent underclass." This working paper tests that claim against standard economics in two stages: first building the logic with established frameworks (the economics of tort law, industrial organization, complementary-assets theory, effective demand), then verifying the facts that logic presupposes against primary sources (Epoch AI, METR, the World Economic Forum, the EU AI Act, Stanford's Digital Economy Lab, the ILO, the NBER).

  Five findings organize the analysis. (1) What gates AI substitution is not capability but the insurability of residual error: deployable automation = min(capability, insurability). (2) The frontier labs can hold market share while earning little durable rent: open-weight models trail the frontier by roughly three months and enterprise spending is violently contested. Share is not rent; profit migrates instead to the adjacent complementary assets. (3) Followed to its end, the underconsumption logic does reach "a permanent underclass is a stable equilibrium," but measured reliability gaps (the best generalist robot policy completes 17.7% of real-hardware tasks; agent autonomy remains capped) pull the near-term shape back to a ratcheting Minsky cycle: partial substitution punctuated by financial crises. (4) The reprieve is a clock, not a wall: the agentic task horizon doubles roughly every seven months. (5) Whether the picture is pessimistic or  optimistic is a question of metric: measured in rent, wealth concentrates; measured in consumer surplus, AI is strongly equalizing. The future splits: access to capability more equal than ever, and the wealth that access converts into more concentrated than ever.

detail.abstract: Bibliometric analysis and science mapping underpin literature reviews, research-policy studies and field-mapping papers, yet the common workflow stitches together several desktop applications and statistical packages, each with its own installation, file formats and learning curve - and institutional data-governance rules increasingly prohibit uploading licensed database exports to third-party servers. Biblio Infinity is a free, MIT-licensed, browser-based application that runs the complete bibliometric pipeline in one place, entirely client-side. It imports Scopus CSV, Web of Science, PubMed, BibTeX, RIS and OpenAlex corpora; merges and de-duplicates multi-database collections with reviewable, criteria-based PRISMA-style screening; computes statistics dashboards (h- and g-index, author impact, Bradford and Lotka laws), keyword co-occurrence, co-authorship, country, direct-citation, reference co-citation and bibliographic-coupling networks with association-strength normalization, Louvain clustering with modularity and silhouette diagnostics, Brandes betweenness pivotal points, Kleinberg burst detection, reference publication year spectroscopy, thematic strategic maps, three-fields plots, historiographs and world collaboration maps; and exports publication-ready SVG/PNG figures and standalone reports. Optional AI features (cluster naming, map interpretation, research-gap suggestions) receive only aggregated cluster terms and counts - never the underlying records - and every AI output carries a verify-before-citing notice. Version 1.0 ships with an 82-check validation audit in which the served functions, extracted verbatim and hash-locked by a sync guard, must reproduce values computed independently in Python (networkx, python-louvain, textbook formulas). We describe the architecture, the validation strategy and the tool's intended role in research and teaching.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Demand for Redistribution: Panel Evidence
affiliations: Keio University and University of Zurich - Department of Finance

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Demand for Redistribution: Panel Evidence
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence advances, does the coalition for redistribution widen or narrow? In a 14-wave Japanese panel, we find it widens, through two channels. Within person, those who warm to AI also warm to redistribution, the opposite of what self-interest predicts, though the link weakens where success is read as earned, not lucky. Across occupations, the most AI-exposed turn toward redistribution after ChatGPT though their own AI views do not. The shift concentrates among educated, higher-income workers. Overall, AI’s advance is met with compensation, not backlash, even from those self-interest says should resist it.

title: Sociobioeconomy as a Decolonial Analytical Framework: Rethinking Bioeconomy from Amazonian Territories
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sociobioeconomy as a Decolonial Analytical Framework: Rethinking Bioeconomy from Amazonian Territories
detail.abstract: Bioeconomy has become a dominant framework for sustainability transitions, particularly in biodiverse regions such as the Amazon. However, its conceptual openness has enabled the convergence of divergent agendas, often reproducing extractive dynamics through new institutional and discursive arrangements. This article examines bioeconomy as a field structured by political, economic, and epistemic tensions, in which different configurations produce distinct socioecological outcomes. Drawing on a qualitative and transdisciplinary approach, the study combines documentary analysis of 26 institutional reports with fieldwork conducted across six Amazonian territories involving Indigenous, quilombola, and riverine communities. The findings show that dominant bioeconomy approaches, centered on technological innovation and global market integration, tend to reconfigure rather than overcome historical patterns of resource appropriation, inequality, and epistemic marginalization. In contrast, territorially embedded practices reveal alternative forms of economic organization grounded in ecological regeneration, collective governance, and epistemic plurality. Building on this distinction, the article proposes Sociobioeconomy as an empirically grounded analytical framework structured around three dimensions: socioecological organization, territorial governance, and epistemic plurality. By bringing ecological economics, political ecology, and decolonial thought into dialogue, the study offers a tool for distinguishing between bioeconomic trajectories that reproduce existing socioecological dynamics and those with transformative potential.

title: A Research Framework for Ecological Macroeconomics
affiliations: Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI)

detail.title: A Research Framework for Ecological Macroeconomics
detail.abstract: Ecological macroeconomics has been expanding as a sub-field within ecological economics in the last decade. Applying almost exclusively non-neoclassical, or `heterodox', macroeconomic theory, ecological macroeconomic models incorporate biophysical stocks and flows. Yet, they are not well-suited to exploring the more transformative agendas proposed within ecological economics writ large. The challenges of doing so are prodigious, but that points to the need for research. With the ultimate goal of informing policy-oriented models, including scenario models, this paper proposes a framework for research along a `research-to-application pipeline'. It argues the need for a common framework and suggests combining two well-established practices: from macroeconomics, the practice of characterising models by their accounting relationships, behavioural rules, and closures; and, from system dynamics modelling, the adoption of `confidence-building procedures'. The proposed research-to-application pipeline creates a division of labour over the the task of confidence building, with the accounts-behaviour-closure (or `ABC') approach provides a common language. The paper refers to existing work and explicitly addresses the critical realist critique of model closure.

title: Demand System of Functional Dairy Foods and its Projection: Implications for Dairy Processing in Tamil Nadu
affiliations: ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi, INDIA, National Dairy Research Institute, ICAR- National Dairy Research Institute and National Dairy Research Institute - Department of Dairy Economics, Statistics & Management

detail.title: Demand System of Functional Dairy Foods and its Projection: Implications for Dairy Processing in Tamil Nadu
detail.abstract: The study examines the demand structure and future prospects of functional dairy foods (FDF) in Tamil Nadu using primary data collected from 220 respondents (160 consumers and 60 sales points). A double-log demand model was employed to estimate income and price elasticities, while a growth rate approach was used to project demand up to 2036. The results indicate that functional dairy foods currently account for a small but emerging segment of the dairy sector, constituting about 1.26 per cent of total milk production and 3.78 per cent of processed milk in milk-equivalent terms. The demand analysis reveals heterogeneous consumption behaviour across products, with significant expenditure elasticities observed for fortified milk, probiotic drinks, and malted milk foods. Own-price elasticities were significant and inelastic for most products, indicating relatively stable demand in response to price changes. Crossprice relationships suggest limited and product-specific substitution and complementarity effects among functional dairy foods. Demand projections under pessimistic (2.12%), business-as-usual (5.44%), and optimistic (8.18%) growth scenarios indicate steady expansion, with total demand reaching 157.44, 181.29, and 203.40 ML/year by 2036, respectively, corresponding to compound annual growth rates of 1.51, 2.61, and 3.53 per cent. The findings suggest that while the functional dairy segment is still in a nascent stage, it holds potential for gradual expansion driven by income growth and changing dietary preferences. From a policy perspective, strengthening supply chains, improving product accessibility, and enhancing consumer awareness will be important to support sustained growth in the functional dairy food sector.

title: The Effects of Global Trade Uncertainty and Bilateral Trade Dependence on Korea's Exports and Imports
affiliations: Yeungnam University

detail.title: The Effects of Global Trade Uncertainty and Bilateral Trade Dependence on Korea's Exports and Imports
detail.abstract: This paper examines how global uncertainty is transmitted through bilateral exports and imports in a highly open and GVC-intensive economy and whether these effects vary according to bilateral trade dependence. Using bilateral trade data for 2000-2024, we estimate a gravity-type model with the Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) estimator. The results provide several important findings. First, global trade uncertainty significantly reduces Korea's trade flows, with stronger effects on imports than on exports. In particular, the World Trade Uncertainty Index (WTUI) is more robustly associated with trade contractions than the broader World Uncertainty Index (WUI), indicating that Korea's trade is particularly sensitive to trade-related uncertainty. Second, the effects of uncertainty are also asymmetric across major trading partners. U.S. uncertainty primarily reduces Korea's exports, consistent with the role of the U.S. as a major finaldemand market, whereas China-related uncertainty has stronger negative effects on imports, reflecting China's central position in Korea's regional supply-chain networks. Third, greater bilateral trade dependence does not necessarily amplify the adverse effects of uncertainty shocks. While Korea's exports are broadly vulnerable to global uncertainty regardless of dependence levels, import vulnerability differs across dependence groups. These findings highlight the importance of tradespecific uncertainty and bilateral trade structure in shaping how global shocks are transmitted in highly open economies.

detail.abstract: The rapid evolution of urban environments necessitates the implementation of sophisticated paradigms such as the 'Smart City' to mitigate the adverse effects of hyper-urbanization. This paper evaluates the synergy between Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) and the Internet of Things (IoT) as a cornerstone for sustainable mobility and enhanced urban quality of life. Unlike conventional traffic management, our approach focuses on the deployment of decentralized intelligent architectures and Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) to facilitate real-time data processing. Through the application of reinforcement learning techniques, specifically Q-learning algorithms, the study demonstrates a significant optimization of traffic flows, leading to a measurable reduction in CO2 emissions and energy consumption. The findings validate the 'green kilometers in motion' framework, illustrating how 'Agents of Things' can transform urban infrastructure into a self-adaptive ecosystem. The results provide a robust empirical basis for integrating advanced IoT-driven solutions into modern urban planning strategies to achieve environmental and economic resilience.

title: Expectation Formation and Keynes's Theory of Effective Demand
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Expectation Formation and Keynes's Theory of Effective Demand

contentType.other: Pre-print of a paper accepted for publication

detail.abstract: Victoria Chick highlighted a critical gap in Keynes's General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money: the absence of a formal theory of expectations formation, despite its central role in the Principle of Effective Demand (PED). This paper addresses that omission by reconstructing a mechanism of short-run expectation formation. It develops a layered approach in which entrepreneurs' expectations of prices and sales proceeds are conditioned by industry-level price formation and by macro-level spending and income expectations. Within the PED, this framework shows how higher-level structures-including Keynes's consumption function and multiplier-inform the expectations guiding firms' production decisions. The analysis also clarifies the relationship between micro-based and macro-based versions of the PED. These represent alternative closures, with distinct causal properties, of a common value relation that characterizes the PED. The micro version generalizes firms' profit maximization behaviour to the macro level and is reductionist; the macro version imposes aggregate spending and income constraints on micro behaviour, and is emergent. The paper shows how these can be unified within Keynes's open-system methodology to provide a coherent account of expectation formation.

title: Four Paths to Hilbert's Eighth Problem
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Four Paths to Hilbert's Eighth Problem
detail.abstract: We place the generalized gamma convolution (GGC) reformulation of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) within the wider landscape of "real-zeros" programs-Pólya-de Bruijn-Newman, Lee-Yang/Cardon, Jensen polynomials, and van Dantzig-Wald-and, in light of recent work (Rodgers-Tao 2020; Konstantopoulos-Patie-Sarkar 2024), identify the most promising path. Three theses organise the paper. First, RH is a single positivity statement in four equivalent costumes: a Pick (Nevanlinna) condition, a complete-monotonicity (Thorin) condition, the de Bruijn-Newman value Λ dBN = 0, and van Dantzig membership of ξ in the Laguerre-Pólya class. Second, the algebraic operations native to the GGC and Wald frameworks-subordination, Esscher tilting, and Fourier/Möbius resummation-are provably incapable of supplying that positivity: they preserve or relabel it, never generate it. Third, the generative front is the Lee-Yang/Cardon construction, anchored by the unconditional von Mangoldt positivity that distinguishes ξ from Pólya's counterexample. We keep two tiers strictly separate throughout-an unconditional (subordinator) tier and an RH-equivalent (GGC) tier-and we make no claim to prove RH; the contribution is a map of the terrain and a program with explicit partial targets.

title: How Does Monetary and Fiscal Policy Affect the Economy in the Face of Large Shocks?
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics and University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: How Does Monetary and Fiscal Policy Affect the Economy in the Face of Large Shocks?
detail.abstract:
We build a model that combines (i) heterogeneous households with incomplete markets, and (ii) state-dependent pricing with strategic complementarities by firms, to analyze the effects of large macroeconomic shocks and policy interventions. Both features significantly influence the transmission of fiscal stimulus and monetary policy—heterogeneous households because of failures of Ricardian equivalence, and state-dependent pricing because of its nonlinear effects on inflation. We use our model to quantify how monetary and fiscal policy shaped macroeconomic dynamics in response to the large shocks of 2020, and how alternative policy choices could have led to different aggregate and distributional outcomes. We find large departures from Ricardian equivalence and strong stepping-on-a-rake effects of interest rate changes. The large unfunded fiscal transfer program helped prevent deflation in 2020 and significantly raised output throughout 2021 and 2022, but led to permanently higher prices. The monetary easing through 2020 and 2021 also contributed to preventing deflation, but had a minimal impact on GDP. The monetary tightening from 2022 lowered the maximum inflation rate, but contributed to persistently above-trend inflation. These policies led to net welfare gains for low-wealth households and net welfare losses for high-wealth households, but those welfare effects are due to incomplete markets for idiosyncratic risk not aggregate stabilization. Alternative commitments to funding fiscal stimulus could have achieved similar short-term effects on inflation and output with a much smaller long-term increase in the price level.

title: Baby Busts and Growth Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics,  and London Business School - Department of Economics

detail.title: Baby Busts and Growth Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy
detail.abstract:
The secular decline in birth rates across the globe over the past seven decades has slowed population growth, raised average ages, and reshaped labor markets and the macroeconomy. Contrary to the widespread expectation that these trends hamper economic growth, we find lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings. These patterns are not explained by educational upgrading, rising female labor force participation, the declining importance of agriculture, or neoclassical-Solow mechanisms. We argue that they reflect the endogenous, labor-saving response of technology to the scarcity of younger workers. Consistent with this interpretation, countries and regions with lower birth rates exhibit more labor-saving patents and growing high-tech activity. There is also higher TFP growth across countries and industries. Exploiting cross-country variation in WWII military and civilian deaths, we find that declines in younger population, rather than population size per se, drive our results.

detail.abstract: Maternal and Child Health (MCH) programs promote safe motherhood by linking financial incentives for institutional delivery with health-worker outreach and family-planning education. I study how MCH programs influence reproductive behavior through pre-conception margin, by affecting contraceptive use and fertility, and post-conception margin by affecting whether unintended pregnancies continue to birth. Using a difference-indifferences design exploiting India's national MCH program, I find that it increased the probability of modern contraceptive use by 7 percentage points and reduced fertility among older women. In contrast, the program increased unintended pregnancies ending in births among younger women by 4 percentage points. Evidence from a later-phase reform of the program that expanded health-worker incentives shows that greater contact with community health workers contributed to this rise. These findings reveal an unintended consequence of maternal health interventions: by simultaneously promoting planned and protected pregnancy, they can inadvertently constrain women's reproductive autonomy.

title: Understanding Cross-State Variations in Medicaid Enrollment During and After the COVID-19 Pandemic
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - University of California, San Diego, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: Understanding Cross-State Variations in Medicaid Enrollment During and After the COVID-19 Pandemic
detail.abstract:
The implementation and unwinding of the FFCRA's continuous coverage requirement generated historically large changes in Medicaid enrollment during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a combination of descriptive and causal analyses, we examine the substantial cross-state differences in these changes, which remain little understood. We find that policies designed to ease unwinding frictions, as well as federal fiscal assistance to states, have little predictive power, suggesting limited roles for administrative design or liquidity constraints. Political preferences have modest predictive power during the unwinding period. Pandemic-era Medicaid expansions and more generous baseline eligibility thresholds are strongly associated with larger net enrollment gains.

title: Literature Review and Evidence Aggregation: a Toolkit for Applied Micro
affiliations: University of Chicago,  and University of Oxford

detail.title: Literature Review and Evidence Aggregation: a Toolkit for Applied Micro
detail.abstract:
Consider an analyst interested in predicting the size of an effect. She has identified a set of prior published studies of similar effects. We provide a toolkit for (i) summarizing the prior literature, (ii) making predictions of effects in new contexts, and (iii) correcting for the bias from selectivity in the prior literature. We illustrate these methods with empirical examples from labor, public, behavioral, environmental, and development economics. Some of the tools are relevant even when only three prior studies are available. We show how it is possible to use covariates to transparently make predictions for a new context by reweighting prior estimates. The mean effect—after correcting for selectivity—is between 12% and 21% of the simple mean in our empirical examples. We conclude with a cookbook for practitioners producing meta-analyses.

title: Importing Aggregate Demand
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Economics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Importing Aggregate Demand
detail.abstract:
How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

title: The Labor Market Value of Community College Bachelor’s Degrees: Initial Evidence from a Resume Audit Study in Early Childhood Education
affiliations: Bowdoin College, University of Texas at Dallas, Northwestern University, University of South Carolina - Moore School of Business - Department of Economics and Texas A&M University - George Bush School of Government and Public Service

detail.title: The Labor Market Value of Community College Bachelor’s Degrees: Initial Evidence from a Resume Audit Study in Early Childhood Education
detail.abstract:
Community colleges are more financially, academically, and geographically accessible than four-year institutions. Yet despite most community college students intending to earn a bachelor’s degree, few successfully transfer and complete one. Community College Baccalaureate (CCB) programs have emerged as an alternative pathway, allowing community colleges to confer bachelor’s degrees directly. However, little is known about how employers value these credentials in the labor market. To address this question, we conduct the first resume audit study of CCB degrees, submitting fictitious applications to real job vacancies while experimentally varying applicants’ educational credentials, degree-granting institutions, and demographic signals. In this pilot study, we focus on the early childhood education (ECE) labor market, a rapidly growing CCB field characterized by labor shortages and increasing educational requirements. We find that employers view CCB degrees similarly to both traditional bachelor’s and associate degrees, with statistically indistinguishable interview-request rates across degree types. A text analysis of employer callback messages reveals little evidence that employers communicate differently with CCB applicants, while a net-price simulation suggests that sticker-price comparisons substantially overstate the affordability advantage of CCB programs. Together, these findings provide new evidence on the labor market value and affordability of CCB degrees and inform an ongoing large-scale audit study across additional fields and labor markets.

title: Growth, Firm Scale, and the Energy Intensity of Production
affiliations: Columbia University, Columbia University in the City of New York and Columbia University

detail.title: Growth, Firm Scale, and the Energy Intensity of Production
detail.abstract:
We uncover a new mechanism that links growth and a decline in the energy intensity of production, observed globally since 1990. Using microdata from India and a causal research design, we demonstrate that the expenditure share of energy declines steeply with firm scale, due both to physical scaling laws and technology investment. Given that average firm size increases with growth, this scale dependence implies that production endogenously becomes less energy-intensive along the growth path. We develop a model of this mechanism in general equilibrium, and quantify significant reductions in aggregate energy intensity as low-income countries like India grow. We conclude with a discussion of the future path of emissions in India.

detail.abstract: This study investigates and discusses the controversial question of whether naturebased tourists (NBTs) are more sensitive to socio-cultural and environmental resources, have different attitudes toward local products and more positive economic effects on host communities and destinations than beach tourists (BTs). In order to test these aspects, a simultaneous comparative analysis of these two types of tourist based on an a priori and activity-based segmentation was carried out. Data was collected by questionnaire at two sites in the Maremma (a costal area in southern Tuscany, Italy), each specific to the type of tourist investigated. In line with the findings of other studies, the results confirm that NBTs are older, more educated, more affluent, and more often employed in professional occupations than BTs. They also confirm the hypothesis that NBTs are more sensitive to environmental quality and have a more positive socioeconomic impact. This study likewise highlights the strong role played by psychographic information in explaining tourist behavior. Three innovative findings concerning the relationship between income, education, personal commitment to the environment and tourist type are discussed at the end.

title: Deflation Risks in a Fragmenting Global Monetary World

detail.title: Deflation Risks in a Fragmenting Global Monetary World
detail.abstract: As the dollar-centric monetary system begins to fragment, how much of a risk of deflation each region will experience may differ. The difference in risk for deflation will be driven by diverse levels of debt, the strength of the institutions, and the speed at which individual economies are able to realize productivity gains from the application of artificial intelligence. Thus, while some economies will likely benefit from 'good deflation' generated from the increase in productivity, there are also some economies (i.e. those with high debt levels and reliance on commodities) that will be vulnerable to experiencing debt deflation's spiral because of the fragmentation of global monetary systems. The analysis of how those variables are affecting each other, the paradox of AI driven productivity in adding to the financialization of economies, and what policies and investments should be pursued in this multipolar economy are discussed in this study. To illustrate the analysis, charts and visuals are used throughout the study.

title: A Tale of Two Systems: Competition and Coordination in DEI-and Merit-Based Job Markets
affiliations: , UNSW Australia Business School, School of Marketing, University of Technology Sydney (UTS) and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: A Tale of Two Systems: Competition and Coordination in DEI-and Merit-Based Job Markets
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of a diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policy on recruitment when a merit-based market and a DEI-based market coexist. We build a two-candidate, two-market contest model in which the majority candidate enjoys a structural advantage and the DEI-based market applies an adjustment that amplifies the minority candidate's market performance. Candidates simultaneously allocate effort across the two markets. In equilibrium, an overcompensation effect may arise, where an overly intense DEI adjustment can reduce both candidates' effort in the DEI-based market. Beyond this, a DEI policy can generate a system-wide recession in competitive intensity or serve as a coordination device, segmenting competition as the majority candidate focuses on the merit-based market while the minority candidate concentrates on the DEI-based market. In terms of welfare, although the majority candidate may benefit from a DEI policy, the minority candidate always gains more, so the utility gap narrows. From a market perspective, a DEI policy often raises the DEI-based market's payoff and need not necessarily harm the merit-based market, yielding the potential for a win-win outcome for the two markets.

detail.abstract: Grading open-ended exam responses is a cognitively demanding task and is subject to substantial random variability, or judgment noise, even when performed by the same instructor. While recent studies have explored the use of generative artificial intelligence in assessment, most treat human-assigned grades as ground truth and focus on agreement rather than reliability. This study adopts a different perspective by modeling grading as a stochastic process and examining whether large language models (LLMs) can support instructors in identifying potentially unstable grading decisions. Using real exam data from a university course, we fine-tune LLMs on historical grading data from a single instructor and compare AI-generated grades with two independent grading rounds conducted at different points in time. We find a statistically significant association between AI-human grading discrepancies and intra-rater grading variability, suggesting that AI-generated evaluations capture meaningful signals of grading instability. The results indicate that LLMs can function as evaluation copilots, supporting grading reliability by selectively flagging responses that may benefit from reconsideration, while preserving instructor control over final decisions.

title: Nobody Wants This: Essentially No Experts Advised Retaining Old Discount Rates

detail.title: Nobody Wants This: Essentially No Experts Advised Retaining Old Discount Rates
detail.abstract: Contrary to the suggestion that the 2023 update to OMB's Circular A-4 "ignored [a] consensus" favoring higher discount rates (Blomquist 2024), the positions of the nine peer reviewers on the 2023 update were much more nuanced and diverse. In fact, they included significant support for the 2023 update, including a majority that supported a central value of 2% or lower, and no calls for retaining the 7% capita-based rate. Moreover, public comments, including from noted experts on the discount rate and Nobel laureates, overwhelmingly supported the update. OMB also made several substantive changes to further respond to the feedback from peer reviewers. Given the multitude of expert perspectives on discounting, there is no single consensus view. Yet ironically, to the extent almost all reviews might have agreed on at least one point, it is this: virtually nobody favored the course of action now adopted by the Trump Administration, of simply retaining the twenty-year-old, outdated guidance on discounting without any updates.

title: Generative AI and the Future of Legal Scholarship (June 2026 Edition)
affiliations: Suffolk University Law School

detail.title: Generative AI and the Future of Legal Scholarship (June 2026 Edition)
detail.abstract: For a century and a half, legal scholarship has been organized around a single artifact: the article. The article bundled four functions—discovery, communication, credentialing, and archiving—and every institution of the legal academy, from the student-edited law review to the tenure file to the judicial citation, is built on the artifact's distinctive properties: scarcity, fixity, and attributability. Generative artificial intelligence does not merely assist this system. It dissolves its organizing scarcity. When any competent legal argument can be produced on demand at negligible cost, the authored text loses the properties on which the artifact regime depends. The emerging literature has responded with what this Article calls the authentication paradigm: disclosure rules, certification regimes, and attestations of human authorship. This Article argues that authentication is a category error. It attempts to restore artificial scarcity to texts, when the scarcity that mattered was never textual. In its place, this Article develops a theory of latent scholarship. In the generative age, the de facto repository of legal thought is no longer the corpus of published writings but the model—the latent space from which arguments are drawn—and the scholarly acts that matter are those that form, validate, commit to, and architect regions of that space. The unit of scholarship accordingly shifts from the article to the maintained normative system: an executable, benchmarked, versioned instantiation of a legal theory that can be run against any case, probed adversarially, and revised in public. Influence shifts from the weight of authority to the authority of weights. The Article elaborates the theory's institutional corollaries—law reviews reconstituted as validation institutions, peer review as adversarial evaluation, tenure metrics keyed to measurable uptake, a Daubert framework for machine-mediated normative systems, and corpus stewardship as a public trust—and confronts the strongest objections, including the charge that this is Langdellian scientism reborn, the dangers of model collapse and epistemic monoculture, and the risk that the imperial scholar will simply be succeeded by the imperial model.

title: Frames in Newspaper Coverage of the ICJ Advisory Opinion on Climate Change and their Impact Potential
affiliations: University of Reading - School of Law

detail.title: Frames in Newspaper Coverage of the ICJ Advisory Opinion on Climate Change and their Impact Potential
detail.abstract: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) Advisory Opinion on climate change was widely reported in UK newspapers and internationally. The chapter explores how these reports framed this landmark international judicial decision. The study on which it is based identified four general frames: climate frames, legal frames, political frames, and personalisation frames. Each of these was typically also associated with a number of sub-frames – such as climate justice, accountability, empowerment, and colonial frames as types of political frames. This framing represents how journalists chose to see or construct the decision. Some saw it mostly in legal terms, others through a more political lens. The chapter discusses the range of frames and sub-frames and analyses how and where they appear and in what numbers. It aims to discover what types of frame are dominant and to consider what implications this might have for the impact of climate litigation. How cases or decisions are reported in the media matters for the shaping of public opinion. Might a dominant legal framing make less of an impact than a personalised framing, where the emotions of those with close ties to the proceedings are reported? And might that differ between the general public and more specialised publics like judges, lawyers and policy-makers, who are also likely to have read newspaper reports on the decision? These are key questions which the chapter considers.

detail.abstract: This Article examines Penske Media Corp. v. Google, a potentially landmark antitrust case arising from Google's use of publisher content to power its AI Overviews and train its artificial intelligence models. For decades, publishers permitted Google to index their content in exchange for search referral traffic. Penske alleges that Google has transformed this mutually beneficial arrangement into a coercive one by conditioning inclusion in Google Search on publishers allowing their content to be used for AI purposes, thereby forcing publishers to subsidize products that reduce traffic to their own websites. This Article analyzes Penske's claims through the lenses of reciprocal dealing, monopoly leveraging, and existing antitrust doctrine, while also evaluating Google's defense that AI Overviews constitute lawful product innovation that benefits consumers. The Article further considers the broader consequences of the dispute for journalism, online content creation, and competition in digital markets. Finally, it explores the geopolitical implications of regulating dominant AI firms, including whether concerns about maintaining American leadership in artificial intelligence should influence antitrust enforcement.

title: The Impact of Government Oversight on Lobbying Activities: Evidence from Random GAO Audits
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business, Capital University of Economics and Business, Shanghai International Studies University and University of Sussex

detail.title: The Impact of Government Oversight on Lobbying Activities: Evidence from Random GAO Audits
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of government audits on lobbying practices by exploiting random audits conducted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) on lobbying registrant-client filings. We find that GAO audits not only lead to a significant decline in lobbying activities of the audited lobbying firm - client pair, but they also generate substantial spillover effects for unaudited clients of the audited lobbying firm and unaudited lobbying firms of the audited client. Mechanism tests suggest that these effects operate through increased information saliency: the release of GAO audit reports triggers greater investor attention and information acquisition, broadens dissemination of lobbying information and reduces information exclusivity among investors, and leads to negative stock market reactions among GAO audited public clients. We also find evidence that politicians avoid being associated with entities named in GAO reports, consistent with reputational costs for named entities. Overall, our findings highlight real economic consequences of government oversight in the lobbying industry.

title: The Political Imprint of Revolution: Childhood Cultural Revolution Exposure and Local Fiscal Autonomy in China
affiliations: University of California San Diego

detail.title: The Political Imprint of Revolution: Childhood Cultural Revolution Exposure and Local Fiscal Autonomy in China
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether childhood exposure to political violence shapes later fiscal governance through officials who enter the state. I match Chinese prefecture-level party secretaries and mayors serving from 2004 to 2018 to their birth prefectures and birth cohorts, and measure early-life exposure using Cultural Revolution death rates in their birth prefectures. Party secretaries from more violent birthplaces who were in politically formative cohorts later govern cities with significantly higher fiscal autonomy: a one-standard-deviation increase in birthplace violence predicts a 2.8 percent increase relative to the sample mean. The effect is concentrated among officials aged 10-17 during the 1968 violence peak, is absent for mayors, and is not reproduced by mayor-only exposure in joint-leadership tests. Assignment, promotion, outlier, and K6 mental-health checks do not support strategic selection or clinical distress explanations. Mechanism-consistent evidence points to political socialization filtered by institutional authority: exposed party secretaries build fiscal autonomy mainly through revenue-side capacity expansion and local resource mobilization rather than expenditure compression. CFPS 2014 evidence shows a parallel citizen-level pattern of institutional alienation without open contention. The findings show that historical political violence can shape state behavior through the formative experiences of officials who later govern.

Jerusalem as a Strategic and Symbolic Flashpoint

detail.abstract: This research paper identifies the core nature of the Israel–Iran conflict by analysing its major transformations during the recent escalation cycle of 2024–2026. Not limiting its observation  as a localized geopolitical dispute, the study explores deeper roots of the conflict, particularly the existence of an entrenched and ideologically driven bilateral rivalry. Within this context, Jerusalem functions as one critical arena through which questions of legitimacy, deterrence, and regional influence are contested. By evaluating the gradual deterioration of the prolonged 'shadow war' into direct military confrontation, the report argues that ideological considerations often shape crisis management alongside traditional realpolitik calculations. Finally, it examines the broader regional consequences, including shifting alliance patterns, the status of holy sites under International Humanitarian Law (IHL), and emerging challenges to maritime security.

title: The Effect of Roadside Orientation on Petrol Sales: A Case Study of City-bound vs. Outbound Stations on Major Highways in Kampala, Uganda.

detail.title: The Effect of Roadside Orientation on Petrol Sales: A Case Study of City-bound vs. Outbound Stations on Major Highways in Kampala, Uganda.
detail.abstract:
The performance of petrol stations, like any commercial property, is significantly
influenced by their location [1–3]. The existing literature delineates this into factors such
as proximity to major road networks, urban centres, and traffic intersections, with higher
throughputs consistently associated with increased accessibility [4–6]. Furthermore,
studies have explored location specific attributes, including the number of highway
lanes, the presence of traffic lights signals, and competition density, identifying
statistically significant relationships with sales [1,3].
However, while these macro-level factors have been extensively examined, the intra-
location variation, particularly the directional differences between opposite sides of the
same highway, has received limited scholarly attention. This research seeks to address
this gap by investigating the impact of roadside orientation on petrol sales at stations
situated along major highways in Kampala.
Building upon Alonso’s (1964) Bid-Rent Theory and Christaller’s (1933) Central Place
Theory, this study argues that the intense competition for commercially viable land
necessitates precise site selection to optimise accessibility and customer density [7,8].
In Kampala, the Central Business District (CBD) induces directional commuter flows,
with peak-hour constraints leading to asymmetric demand between city-bound and
outbound roadside orientations. Although land value gradients determine feasible
station’s locations, the directional orientation influences the actual sales volumes once
the location is established, a distinction that this study empirically investigates.

detail.abstract: Canada legalized "medical assistance in dying" (MAID) in 2016; by 2024, one death in twenty was an "assisted death". Over the same period, the priority that the country's main federal funder assigns to research on the diseases at the heart of the paradigmatic MAID case fell markedly. This paper documents that decline and examines its possible link with legalization. Drawing on 21 years of grant data from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), it measures the share of the healthresearch budget devoted to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington's disease (two uniformly fatal untreatable conditions) based on the amount disbursed each year, expressed relative to a budget stripped of emergency COVID-19 credits. Having risen to a plateau of 10.4‰ over 2013-2018, the combined share falls to 8.2‰ in 2022-2025: this 21% decline remains after COVID-19 spending is removed. Overall, the data are consistent with the hypothesis of an effect of legalization on research priority, without the study design (ecological, single-country, single-funder) allowing perfect causation to be established.

detail.title: Monetary policy transmission via banks to firms
detail.abstract: This Occasional Paper reviews evidence from the ChaMP Research Network on the transmission of monetary policy to firms in the euro area. Overall, transmission to firms remains effective, including during the 2022-23 tightening cycle. However, new results show that this transmission is neither uniform nor mechanical. The pass-through from policy rates and other instruments to corporate financing conditions is shaped by multiple layers of heterogeneity that may, in some cases, have aggregate implications. Country-level segmentation, linked to sovereign risk, institutional frameworks and local lending practices, plays an important role in shaping transmission, especially during periods of stress. Beyond cross-country effects, bank balance sheets and business models also influence transmission by affecting the strength of lending responses. In particular, the composition of banks’ liabilities can lead to different speeds of transmission. Firm characteristics further differentiate the impact of monetary policy, with the funding mix playing a critical role. At the contract level, collateralisation and interest rate fixation materially affect both the magnitude and composition of transmission. As some of these heterogeneities may, in certain circumstances, have aggregate implications, this paper explains how a broad and flexible toolkit, centred on the main policy rate and, when needed, complemented by other policy instruments such as asset purchases and targeted liquidity operations, can be deployed in a proportionate manner to ensure effective monetary policy transmission across a structurally diverse monetary union.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates how the quality of public elementary schools is capitalized into residential rents in Osaka City, Japan. Using a boundary fixed-effects (regression discontinuity) design in the tradition of Black (1999), I compare rental listings located on either side of school attendance-zone boundaries, where neighborhood amenities are nearly identical and only the assigned school differs. Exploiting Osaka City's unusual practice of publishing school-level national achievement test scores (2016-2018) and the city's low homeownership rate (40.5%), I find that a one-point increase in a school's average test score raises monthly rents within its attendance zone by approximately 451-540 yen; a one-standard-deviation increase in school quality raises rents by up to about 3%. The estimate is slightly larger than that of Kuroda (2018) for Matsue City and is robust to using school rankings, to controlling for junior-highschool quality, to alternative neighborhood controls, and to a log specification. The results complement Myojo (2024), who studies the abolition of Osaka's school-choice/zoning system at the junior-high and high-school level: capitalization of school quality is clearly present at the elementary level, which Myojo does not cover and where the link between residence and attendance is tighter.

title: Bargaining Order in Organizational Design

detail.title: Bargaining Order in Organizational Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how the sequencing of supplier negotiations affects firm boundaries and global sourcing decisions in sequential production. In existing property-rights models of global value chains, the position of a supplier in the production process plays a central role in determining whether that supplier is integrated or outsourced. We add a distinct margin: the final-good producer chooses the order in which it bargains with suppliers. In the model, suppliers make relationship-specific investments, contracts are incomplete, and the final-good producer bargains bilaterally with suppliers using cash-offer contracts. We compare environments in which the final-good producer can commit to the bargaining order before suppliers invest with environments in which such commitment is not feasible. With commitment, sequencing provides an additional instrument for reallocating investment incentives and can substitute for vertical integration. Without commitment, the chosen order must satisfy an ex post credibility constraint, which restricts feasible organizational designs and can make vertical integration optimal. In an open economy, this credibility constraint creates a strategic motive for sourcing from a higher-cost location: a firm may choose a more costly sourcing location when doing so improves suppliers' investment incentives. The model therefore identifies a contractual channel through which bargaining-order credibility jointly shapes ownership and sourcing decisions in global value chains. It also offers a cautionary note for empirical work: observed ownership and sourcing patterns may depend not only on input importance, wages, and contractibility, but also on whether supplier-negotiation sequences are predetermined, chosen with commitment, or chosen without commitment.

detail.abstract:
This comment letter responds to the Securities and Exchange Commission's proposed Release Nos. 33-11414; 34-105368; 39-2563; IC-36140; File No. S7-2026-15 – Semiannual Reporting, which would permit reporting companies to file semiannual reports on new Form 10-S in lieu of the three interim reports now required on Form 10-Q. Our comments draw on our scholarship relating to the resurgence of retail investors, their participation in corporate governance, and the role of technology in securities markets.

We express concerns that the proposal weakens the disclosure architecture at the foundation of the federal securities laws and falls hardest on self-directed retail investors, who rely on mandated periodic disclosure as the raw material for their own research and cannot purchase the informational advantages available to institutional investors. In an era of renewed retail investor engagement, evidenced by thousands of individual comment letters opposing this proposal, we recommend that the SEC withdraw the proposed rule and preserve the quarterly reporting cadence that constrains agency costs and promotes management accountability. We advise against adopting semiannual reporting.

title: From Alliances to Swarms: Rethinking Competition and Collaboration in the Age of AI
affiliations: INSEAD - Strategy and Cornell University

detail.title: From Alliances to Swarms: Rethinking Competition and Collaboration in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: Established frameworks for inter-organizational strategy-alliance theory, ecosystem analysis, and platform economics-have been developed primarily for a world in which coordination between firms is deliberate, contract-governed, and mediated by human managers. The proliferation of agentic artificial intelligence is rendering these assumptions progressively inadequate. This paper argues that competition and collaboration in AI-enabled environments increasingly occur through what we term swarms: temporary, real-time configurations of agentic agents, data, capabilities, and protocols drawn from multiple firms and ecosystems that assemble to execute a specific interaction, compete and collaborate simultaneously, and dissolve upon its completion. Swarms represent a qualitatively new unit of inter-organizational strategy-distinct from alliances (which are durable relational structures) and from ecosystems (which are enduring participation environments)-and require a correspondingly new analytical framework. We propose a three-layer model in which capability bundle (the capability base defined by M&A and alliances), context (the ecosystem environment within which capabilities can interact), and dynamics (the swarms through which capabilities create and capture value in real time) operate as interdependent competitive layers. We further introduce the Swarm Stack, a six-layer architecture-capability, interface, agent, coordination, competition, and governance-that describes the infrastructure of swarm-based inter-organizational competition. We identify five sources of swarm advantage (selection, prediction, coordination, latency, and trust), examine the distinctive governance challenges that cross-organizational agentic interaction creates, and discuss implications for strategy theory and the reconceptualization of strategic leadership.

title: The 2015/16 El Niño Drought Impacts and Household Coping Strategies: Gender-based Perspective

detail.title: The 2015/16 El Niño Drought Impacts and Household Coping Strategies: Gender-based Perspective

detail.abstract: The 2015/16 El Niño-driven drought is the most severe South Africa has experienced in decades, causing a significant nationwide impact. While drought affects all households, understanding how its impacts manifest across gender is critical, as heterogeneity in household composition could shape the magnitude and distribution of welfare losses. This study examines the effect of the 2015/16 severe drought in South Africa over time and across gender on various household outcomes and how households coped with the drought. To begin, I merged household panel data with gridded drought data from 2010 to 2017 and used the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to explore food security and adaptation expenditure gaps across male-headed and female-headed households (MHHs and FHHs). The results shows that MHHs spend 24\% more on food per capita than FHHs, and that the drought has no impact on food or adaptation expenditure gaps. Next, I examined the contemporaneous and persistent effects of the drought on households and found that average households and MHHs experienced 11.9 and 15.1 percentage point reductions in food security in 2015/16, respectively, compared to FHHs. However, as the drought persisted into 2017, FHHs experienced a greater reduction in food security of 11.8 percentage points. Adaptation expenditure showed a similarly negative impact over time and across gender, but the coefficients were insignificant. MHHs and FHHs coped differently with the drought, with MHHs relying on government transfers while FHHs and overall households relied on wealth. Beyond food security, the drought had adverse impacts on health outcomes, as younger children in MHHs experienced greater effects.

detail.abstract: The theory of weaponized interdependence explains coercion by a state at the hub of an asymmetric economic network. The advanced semiconductor industry has a different structure: its indispensable links are held by several mutually dependent jurisdictions, none controlling the full chain. This article develops a single equilibrium concept, the chokepoint deterrence equilibrium, with three orthogonal causal channels: retaliation, endogenous substitution, and coalition enforcement. The distinctive channel is endogenous substitution. Weaponizing a node revises the target's posterior belief that it will face future denial and raises its return to building a substitute, so the binding deterrent is the holder's own state-contingent value destruction rather than the rival's counter-strike. I specify the belief object and its updating rule, model substitution as the induced investment choice, derive the restraint condition as an incentive constraint, and prove, under stated conditions, that substitution-based deterrence is strictly single-peaked in substitutability and strongest for durable but provocable nodes. An explicit, institutionally mediated firm-state aggregation function locates coalition under-enforcement in a stated political-economy primitive. The framework yields one conditional proposition, a falsification threshold, and a structured comparison of the 2022 semiconductor export controls and China's mineral and rare-earth leverage that discriminates the argument from alliance politics and coercive hierarchy.

title: Comparative Advantage as a Bistable State: Engagement, Technology Leakage, and Hysteresis in International Trade

detail.title: Comparative Advantage as a Bistable State: Engagement, Technology Leakage, and Hysteresis in International Trade

declarations.declarationOfInterest: we do not get funding from any people or organizations for writing this paper

detail.abstract: Why did two decades of engagement with the same rising partner erode one advanced manufacturing economy's technological base and leave another's intact? We model the homepartner technology gap as evolving under engagement-mediated leakage, with the partner's absorptive capacity non-monotone in the gap, a shape we derive by aggregating monotone good-level learning rules. Engagement intensity then generates three regimes separated by a saddle-node (fold) bifurcation, and three results follow. A linear policy frontier: escape depends only on the ratio of net innovation to engagement, making decoupling and coretechnology investment perfect substitutes. Hysteresis: the trap is forward-invariant under any policy keeping engagement above the fold, so marginal de-risking after capture cannot restore advantage. An engagement externality: atomistic firms treat the national gap as a commons, over-engage, and can cross the fold when a patient planner would not, at a welfare cost that diverges in the patient limit. The paper offers a theoretical mechanism together with a pre-specified empirical agenda, not a case-study test: Germany and Japan enter as motivating trajectories, read as, respectively, a decentralized equilibrium past the fold and an economy shocked onto the escape side before capture. The fold rationalizes the negative arm of the China-shock sign conflict, and falsification is staked on a pre-specified horse race that distinguishes the mechanism from the competition-innovation inverted-U.

title: Proportional Representation via Limited Voting: A Laboratory Investigation
affiliations: and University of Cyprus

detail.title: Proportional Representation via Limited Voting: A Laboratory Investigation
detail.abstract: The persistent misrepresentation of minority groups across democratic nations raises significant questions about the fairness of democratic electoral systems. As a remedy, this paper explores the potential of alternative proportional voting systems-in particular, the Limited Voting (LV) system-through both theoretical modelling and laboratory experiments. Theoretically, we develop a model based on Coalition-Proof Nash Equilibria, indicating that LV can provide greater opportunities for minority representation compared to standard at-large-plurality systems. The theoretical predictions are tested in a laboratory experiment that varies both the voting system and the size of the minority group. The experimental results align closely with the theoretical predictions, demonstrating that minority voters can achieve positive levels of representation under LV. Subjects efficiently overcome the coordination challenges inherent in the system, validating LV's practical potential. Our findings shed light on the strategic dynamics of LV and its ability to mitigate the under-representation of minority groups in democratic elections.

detail.abstract:
Small Island Developing States (SIDS) borrow at a persistent and substantial premium over comparably rated emerging-market sovereigns. We argue that this premium is, to a meaningful degree, not only a credit phenomenon but a market-infrastructure one. Most of these states have no liquid secondary bond market, no credit-default-swap (CDS) curve, and therefore no mechanism by which global investors can price, benchmark, or hedge their exposure. Where risk cannot be measured or transferred, it is over-charged. A second component of the premium is a nature-and-climate risk that is a genuine credit fundamental and that the market prices only partially and crudely today. Neither component is well addressed by another one-off concessional loan. The deeper obstacle is a coordination failure: a liquid market for these credits is a public good that no single investor will build alone, which is why, despite trillions of dollars of sovereign risk changing hands elsewhere, almost none of it reaches these states.

The response we propose is a piece of standing market infrastructure rather than a bespoke transaction, built from the ordinary, well-understood machinery of structured credit. The Sovereign Sustainability and Resilience Facility (SSRF) pools the sovereign exposures of a diversified cluster of these states and tranches them. The structured-credit machinery does the primary work of compression, because for sovereigns too small to sustain a single-name CDS the compression cannot ride an existing rail and must be built. Into the resulting spread the facility prices a verified resilience signal, so that improving a sovereign's measured natural-capital and fiscal-resilience conduct lowers its cost of capital rather than merely re-wrapping its illiquidity. A concessional first-loss layer is sized to the stress correlation rather than the comfortable one, and the correlated climate tail is passed to reinsurance capital that prices physical risk for a living. This is the deliberate inverse of the 2008 structure, in which the capital that detonated believed itself preservation-seeking and was destroyed by a mispriced tail.

The paper walks the structured-credit ladder rung by rung, separating the pooling-and-tranching engine, which never failed, from the resecuritisation and opacity that did. It builds a bridge from each rung to a small-island parameter and constructs the model on a ten-sovereign worked example grounded in a sovereign metrics database. It closes by lifting the contribution from a single instrument to a system-level argument: read across the whole asset class, the facility is a capital-orchestration architecture that routes each kind of capital to the role it is built for. The intellectual move is to take the machinery that amplified systemic risk in 2008 and invert its purpose, from leverage in pursuit of arbitrage to leverage in pursuit of resilience and price discovery, bound by transparency, by loss-intent first-loss capital, and by correlation disclosed through every layer.

title: Political Persuasion under Strategic Fact-Checking
affiliations: University of Cyprus,  and University of Cyprus

detail.title: Political Persuasion under Strategic Fact-Checking
detail.abstract: We study political persuasion when communication is disciplined by an endogenous, imperfect fact-checker in an electorate with heterogeneous voters. A strategic Persuader designs a communication policy to influence public beliefs, anticipating a Checker who can audit realized messages. Audits attempt to refute messages by checking for inconsistency and succeed only probabilistically. This imperfection creates a certification channel: when an audit does not refute a message, voters update in the message's favor. Certification reshapes the Checker's incentives. Although auditing can screen out misleading claims, it can also backfire by legitimizing surviving claims and persuading otherwise skeptical voters. We characterize equilibrium auditing and communication, identifying conditions under which the Checker strategically abstains to avoid such certification-induced backfires. Heterogeneous voter skepticism is central to this mechanism, as the Persuader trades off broad persuasion against preserving support among easier-topersuade voters. The Persuader optimally exploits the Checker's reluctance by injecting calibrated noise at the boundary where the Checker is just indifferent to auditing. We extend the model to partial commitment and show that our equilibrium results are robust to sufficiently strong commitment power.

title: Reconstructing the Department of Justice Office for Civil Rights
affiliations: University of South Dakota Law School

detail.title: Reconstructing the Department of Justice Office for Civil Rights
detail.abstract:
The United States has never possessed an effective system for addressing constitutional violations by the police, including privacy intrusions and uses of excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment. The existing remedies, such as the exclusionary rule, criminal prosecution, and suits for monetary damages under Section 1983, have long been recognized as deeply flawed. 

A more effective, complementary approach exists and is already used for addressing civil rights violations in other contexts, such as education, health care, housing, and employment. If an individual believes that a local school has violated her civil rights, for example, she is not required to hire a costly lawyer or find one willing to take her case on contingency. She can simply submit a complaint to the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights (ED OCR) through its web portal. An ED OCR employee will evaluate her claim and, if appropriate, conduct an investigation and negotiate with her local school district to reach a resolution. 

When the United States reconstructs the various institutions of governance degraded by the second Trump administration, Congress should pass a Fair Policing Act that authorizes a reconstructed and expanded Office for Civil Rights in the Department of Justice to investigate and resolve individual complaints of federal rights violations by state and local police, modeled on the complaint procedures that already exist in civil rights offices such as ED OCR.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a public-data actuarial framework for modelling one cyber regulatory liability layer: GDPR Article 83 administrative fine risk. A CMS Enforcement Tracker snapshot contains 3,194 enforcement records and 2,947 core Article 83 positive-fine observations. The core severity distribution is highly concentrated, with total fines of EUR 6.217 billion, median fine EUR 7,000, mean fine EUR 2.110 million, and Gini coefficient 0.9859. The model treats enforcement frequency as a scenario variable and studies conditional fine severity on an explicitly defined A0 non-platform commercial reference sample. Under the 250,000-controller reference denominator, expected Article 83 fine loss ranges from EUR 1,196 to EUR 4,152 per controller-year between the empirical A0 mean and lognormal reference. Across the full denominator-by-severity grid, the range is approximately EUR 280 to EUR 10,381, a 37-fold spread; the contribution is to rank assumptions driving this spread. Tail diagnostics reinforce the same conclusion: the 95% bootstrap interval for the GPD tail-shape parameter spans approximately -0.10 to 0.97, and the q95 tail diagnostic is estimated on only 49 excess observations. Rolling temporal validation rejects stability of the calibrated log-severity distribution in every one-year test split at p < 1e-7. Public data can therefore support an auditable actuarial control framework for Article 83 fine risk, but not a definitive cyber-liability premium.

title: Anticipatory Compliance with the EU AI Act: An Enterprise Architecture Approach for AI-Assisted Maritime Operations

detail.title: Anticipatory Compliance with the EU AI Act: An Enterprise Architecture Approach for AI-Assisted Maritime Operations
detail.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence into safety critical transport systems is no longer a future ambition but an operational reality. Maritime operators preparing to deploy AI assisted navigation systems face an immediate challenge: the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) creates legally binding obligations for high risk AI, yet its provisions are expressed at a high level and offer no concrete blueprint for sectoral implementation. This paper addresses that translation challenge through a single in depth case study of an unmanned ferry operator preparing for EU AI Act compliance. The study deconstructs the operator's preparedness gap into four interconnected challenges (organizational, operational, compliance, and governance) and proposes a structured solution: an Adapted Enterprise Architecture Artifact (AEA) that operationalizes regulatory obligations through enterprise architecture modeling. The AEA integrates the EU AI Act with ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 38507, and ISO/IEC 23894, linking legal standards to specific business processes, accountable human roles, and the data artifacts required to prove conformity. The framework was validated through structured expert walkthroughs across four tracks (legal, operational, organizational, and technical) and refined through an iterative socio technical adaptation cycle. The validated framework provides a traceable governance structure for anticipatory compliance and offers a transferable methodology for other safety critical domains facing similar regulatory transitions.

title: Sons of the Soil: Histories of Tamil Nadu's Land Ownership

detail.title: Sons of the Soil: Histories of Tamil Nadu's Land Ownership

detail.abstract:
This paper traces the historical patterns and evolution of land administration in present-day Tamil Nadu, reading them as both systems of resource management and as cultural geographies shaped by language, power, and identity. The analysis is undertaken through the intersectional lenses of caste hierarchies, cultural symbolism, and spatial inequality. 

It begins with the terminology found in Sangam literature, where the thinai ecological types represent not only agricultural practice but also themes of social organisation. The deliberate use of particular terms produces and reproduces ideas about economies, ownership, and power structures, forming an invisible linguistic foundation for later systems of proprietorship. 

The study examines inam land grants given in relation to service and status, functioning within the dimensions of caste and religion, and the tenure system of the Palayakkarars, which reflected political authority and cultural identity tied to land that transcended its economic functions. Subsequent sections trace agrarian traditions centred on community, their impacts on social structure and environment, and the entrenched hierarchies that persist today. This historical trajectory allows us to contextualise contemporary patterns of land ownership, where legal protections often fail marginalised communities and where dispossession and encroachment remain common. 

Through accounts of peasant uprisings such as the 1785 Paraiyar Insurrection and the 1994 Karanai revolt, the paper highlights how land has served as a focal point of both cultural and political resistance. These narratives reveal not only the material inequalities of ownership but also the culturally enforced systemic rejection of basic entitlements to Dalits, such as the denial of the right to the earth itself.

title: Is Sin a Priced Risk in Indian Equities? Evidence from an Extended Fama-French Five-Factor Model
