detail.title: Is Sin a Priced Risk in Indian Equities? Evidence from an Extended Fama-French Five-Factor Model
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether sin stocks in Indian equity markets earn a premium relative to characteristic matched non-sin peers, testing the social-norms mechanism advanced by Hong and Kacperczyk (2009) in an emerging-market context. We construct eleven matched sin-control pairs from the National Stock Exchange of India and track returns over 72 monthly observations spanning January 2020 through December 2025. Each sin firm is paired with a single non-sin counterpart using sector-disciplined Euclidean distance matching on standardised size, book-to-market, profitability, and sales growth, subject to a strict no-replacement constraint. Risk-adjusted returns are estimated across five factor models, from the CAPM to the Fama-French five-factor model augmented with momentum, under both equal-weighted and purity-weighted portfolio constructions, with Newey-West HAC standard errors throughout. Indian sin stocks earn a monthly alpha of 1.476% under the strictest equal-weighted specification (annualised: 19.22%; HAC t = 2.87; p = 0.006), rising to 1.607% per month under purity-weighting (annualised: 21.08%; t = 3.04; p = 0.003). Both estimates are significant at the 1% level and remain stable across all five factor models, leave-one-out exclusions, subperiod splits, and alternative control assignments. None of the six factor loadings in the headline specification achieves statistical significance. Sin-portfolio Sharpe ratios of 1.29 to 1.31 stand against approximately 0.68 for matched controls, indicating the premium is not attributable to elevated price swings. The findings are consistent with a demand-constraint channel: ESG-driven institutional exclusion depresses sin-stock valuations, generating a persistent return premium for unconstrained investors. To the authors' knowledge, the paper provides the first characteristic-matched, multi-factor evidence of a sin-stock premium in Indian equities; a review of SSRN preprints and India-focused finance journals yielded no prior study combining all three design elements. The paper introduces purity-weighting to account for conglomerate revenue diversification and extends the sin-premium literature into an emerging-market setting that has received limited attention in the existing evidence base.

detail.abstract: As trading apps like Robinhood democratize market access, retail investors are increasingly participating in financial markets alongside their institutional counterparts. This study explores whether these two groups react differently to Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) announcements in the U.S. market. It analyses abnormal market returns to approximate institutional investors' reactions and changes in the number of Robinhood users holding stocks to assess retail behavior across 435 M&A announcements, including 19 acquirers, 65 targets, and 351 internal deals. The findings reveal that institutional investors react swiftly and strategically, showing positive reactions to targets and neutral to negative reactions to acquirers, consistent with prior literature. In contrast, retail investors exhibit a buying pattern on average across all M&A scenarios, a behavior also observed in previous studies of retail reactions to other corporate events. This pattern indicates more reactive investing among retail investors, likely driven by market volatility and institutional activity. Deal size as a proxy for investor attention does not significantly influence institutional behavior. Retail investors are somewhat more affected, but the impact is not consistent enough to show significant differences. The results emphasize the importance of financial literacy and regulatory oversight in a trading environment where retail investors are increasingly participating.

title: Sovereign Debt Management and Sustainability in Emerging Markets A Hybrid Stochastic-Control Framework with Regime Switching, Reserve-Adequacy Coupling, and Tail Dependence A Comparative Study of Egypt, Bahrain, Nigeria, and Pakistan

detail.title: Sovereign Debt Management and Sustainability in Emerging Markets A Hybrid Stochastic-Control Framework with Regime Switching, Reserve-Adequacy Coupling, and Tail Dependence A Comparative Study of Egypt, Bahrain, Nigeria, and Pakistan
detail.abstract: We treat sovereign debt management-the choice of debt composition, the accumulation of foreign reserves, and the fiscal stance-as a single constrained stochastic-control problem rather than as three separate exercises. The operational logic of a medium-term debt strategy (MTDS) and standard debt-sustainability analysis (DSA) is embedded in a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman program in which the macroeconomic environment follows a hidden three-state Markov regime process. Two features are new: the transition intensity into the crisis regime is an explicit function of reserve adequacy, so that the Greenspan-Guidotti rule operates endogenously rather than as an external benchmark; and crosscountry shocks are coupled through a Clayton copula, which generates the asymmetric lower-tail dependence that linear correlation misses and that markets appear to underprice. We calibrate the framework to four contrasting emerging sovereigns-Egypt, Bahrain, Nigeria, and Pakistan-with macroeconomic data current to mid-2026, and solve it by regime filtering, finite-difference policy iteration, and Monte-Carlo simulation. The exercise orders vulnerability in a way that a single solvency ratio cannot, and a rules-based policy combining the optimal composition, reserve accumulation, and a hedging overlay lowers both the breach probability and the conditional tail loss in every case. The macroeconomic inputs are measured and documented; the structural and stochastic parameters are illustrative calibrations, internally consistent with the data and the literature and to be confirmed by full estimation before operational use.

title: Making the Bank Securitisation Capital Rules Work for Europe: What Could be Improved in the June 17 th Proposals?

detail.title: Making the Bank Securitisation Capital Rules Work for Europe: What Could be Improved in the June 17 th Proposals?
detail.abstract:
This report assesses the European Commission’s 17th June 2025 proposals for reforming bank securitisations capital rules. While we welcome the intended goal of unlocking bank issuance and investments in securitisation, and the direction of the proposed rule changes, we believe that some further prudent targeted technical adjustments to the proposals should be made to improve the impact on real economy financing in Europe and contribute to a level playing field across asset classes and EU Member States, while improving risk-sensitivity and preserving financial stability. We suggest that the authorities:

(i) Use as the scale variable in the proposed Securitisation-Internal Ratings-Based Approach (SEC-IRBA) and Securitisation-Standardised Approach (SEC-SA) risk-sensitive Risk Weight Floor (RWF) the Standardised Approach (SA) capital, 𝐾𝑆𝐴, 
(ii) Modify the definition of resilience (a) to allow non-originator banks to invest in resilient positions, (b) to clarify that (re)insurers can provide cover in the resilient position market, (c) to use 𝐾𝐴 (or 𝐾𝐼𝑅𝐵) as scale variable in the SEC-IRBA minimum attachment point, and (d) to remove the attachment point criteria in SEC-ERBA since it is dependent on the external rating, 
(iii) Alter the scalars and absolute value floors in the RWF to make them consistent with the risk dimensions and thereby to enhance banks’ incentives to structure deals satisfying STS and resilient position requirements, and introduce an absolute value cap in the RWF for consistency with non-senior tranches, 
(iv) Similarly, alter the p-factor parameters to make them consistent with the risk dimensions, 
(v) Align the Securitisation-External Ratings Based Approach (SEC-ERBA) with (ii) & (iii).

title: SELRA: A Research Agenda for Reducing Lifecycle Capital-Allocation Losses in Energy-Resource Efficiency Projects — Selection, Economic-Lifecycle Realization, and Capital-Allocation Quality in Industrial Energy Projects

detail.abstract: Industrial projects aimed at improving the economic efficiency of energy-resource use often underperform in ways that familiar evaluation tools do not fully explain. This paper introduces SELRA — the Selection and Economic-Lifecycle Realization Architecture — as the backbone of a research agenda for reducing lifecycle capital-allocation losses in such projects. The central claim is that weak outcomes arise not only from bad equipment, insufficient financing, or incorrect use of standard metrics. They also arise when the economic object is constructed too narrowly at the selection stage and when the selected project is not preserved through structuring, implementation, verification, and post-guarantee life. SELRA distinguishes two analytically separate but economically interdependent layers: selection of the right project and economic-lifecycle realization of the selected project. It ties both to capital-allocation quality at broader scales. Standard tools such as net present value, lifecycle costing, techno-economic analysis, and measurement-and-verification remain necessary, but their practical reliability depends on a prior architecture that defines what is being compared, how alternatives become admissible, and how selected value is carried into realized effect. The framework is presented as the codification and formalization phase of a longer trajectory combining earlier methodological work in economics with sustained applied engagement in industrial lighting, distributed generation, and related energy-resource domains. The paper is not a completed proof or a new valuation formula. Its contribution is architecture, demarcation, and agenda formation: it positions the program against its nearest neighbors in the project-definition and benefits-realization traditions and makes it legible, so that later papers can carry their specific burdens without being forced into a single overloaded manuscript.

title: Oil Shocks, Diversification, and Sectoral Spillovers in Oman:Evidence from Activity and Volatility Connectedness
affiliations: University of Southampton - Centre for Digital Finance, Central Bank of Oman, Central Bank of Oman and Central Bank of Oman

detail.title: Oil Shocks, Diversification, and Sectoral Spillovers in Oman:Evidence from Activity and Volatility Connectedness
detail.abstract: This paper examines how oil-related shocks are transmitted across key sectors of the Omani economy within a dynamic macro-financial connectedness framework. Using a time-varying parameter vector autoregression (TVP-VAR) and wavelet coherenceanalysis, it traces shock propagation across energy, financial, industrial, and tourism channels. The empirical design distinguishes between activity-based and volatility based spillovers, thereby capturing both the real-side and risk-transmission dimensions of oil dependence. The results reveal economically meaningful and time-varying cross sectoral connectedness. In the growth-based system, the Muscat Stock Exchange is the main net transmitter of shocks, indicating that financial markets play the leading role in redistributing oil-related information and macroeconomic expectations across the domestic economy. In the squared-growth system, manufacturing GDP becomes the dominant net transmitter of volatility, while hotel revenues remain a persistent net receiver, underscoring the vulnerability of tourism-related activity to external and domestic disturbances. Dynamic connectedness rises sharply during periods of economic and geopolitical stress, especially around the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent disruption in global energy markets. These findings imply that macro-financial surveillance in Oman should monitor financial-market signals and manufacturing sector volatility jointly as oil-shock transmission evolves under diversification overtime.

title: Dynamic Spillover Connectedness Among Green Finance, Cryptocurrency Markets, and Systemic Risk Indices: A QVAR Network Approach
affiliations: National Yunlin University of Science and Technology, Chung Yuan Christian University and Chung Yuan Christian University

detail.title: Dynamic Spillover Connectedness Among Green Finance, Cryptocurrency Markets, and Systemic Risk Indices: A QVAR Network Approach
detail.abstract: This paper examines the connectedness between green finance instruments and three directly observable risk channels—climate, geopolitical, and market-volatility risk. Green finance is proxied by five exchange-traded funds spanning clean energy, carbon efficiency, ESG equities, and green bonds (ICLN, CRBN, SUSA, ESGU, GRNB), together with three energy-efficient crypto tokens (ADA, XRP, XLM); risk is captured by the Climate Risk Index (CRI), the Geopolitical Risk Index (GPR), and the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX). Using monthly data from April 2017 to September 2025 and a Quantile Vector Autoregression (QVAR) connectedness framework, we estimate dynamic total connectedness, net directional connectedness, and full-sample network structure. Total connectedness is high across all quantiles (roughly 60–78%) and intensifies around the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict. Market volatility is the dominant and most stable net transmitter of shocks, whereas climate and geopolitical risk play passive, receiver-leaning roles that switch in a regime-dependent manner. Green finance instruments, including tokens, are bound more tightly to one another than to any external risk factor, behaving largely as net receivers. The findings are robust to an alternative estimation window and carry direct implications for diversification, hedging, and macroprudential monitoring.

title: Greenwashing: Drivers, Types And Levels

detail.title: Greenwashing: Drivers, Types And Levels
detail.abstract: As environmental awareness intensifies and stakeholder pressure on corporations grows, greenwashing has become one of the most pressing challenges in sustainable finance and corporate governance. This paper provides a comprehensive examination of greenwashing its typologies, levels, and drivers through a systematic review of literature spanning management, finance, sociology, and environmental studies. Anchored in Impression Management Theory (Goffman, 1959) and Signaling Theory (Spence, 1973), the paper argues that greenwashing is a strategic communicative act whereby corporations exploit information asymmetries to project environmental credibility that is decoupled from substantive action. Five types of greenwashing are identified; selective disclosure, attention deflection, decoupling, deceptive labeling, and deceptive manipulation, operating across four organizational levels: corporate, strategic, dark, and product. Drivers are organized into three tiers: external (regulatory gaps, consumer and investor demand), organizational (incentive structures, ethical climate), and individual (cognitive biases and optimistic bias). The findings show that greenwashing persists largely due to regulatory fragmentation, weak ESG enforcement, and the co-optation of certification and voluntary reporting mechanisms. The paper concludes by calling for stricter disclosure mandates, stronger penalties for misleading environmental claims, and independent sustainability oversight at the board level.

title: The Signal beneath the Calm: Benford's Law and the Latent Fragility of Liquidity-Driven Financial Markets

detail.abstract: Benford's Law states that in many natural datasets the leading digit is far more often a 1 than a 9, a regularity used in forensic accounting and financialmarket analysis. This paper applies the Law to a 64-year cross-section of U.S. equity prices and shows that compliance is, to close approximation, a function of how stretched the price distribution is-its cross-sectional amplitude. Using approximately 7.96 million daily closing prices of S&P 500 constituents from 1962 to 2025, the cross-sectional coefficient of variation alone explains 81.6% of the variation in the chi-squared distance from Benford's distribution through an exponential decay. Historically, only crises stretched the distribution far enough for compliance to become strong, and every pre-2018 recession widened the cross-sectional range from below : the floor of prices fell sharply while the ceiling barely moved. Such crisis-driven amplitude was always transient, reverting within months. Since approximately 2018 the picture has reversed. Compliance is now stronger than ever in the sample because the distribution has been stretched 1 from the opposite end: the ceiling has risen sharply while the floor has risen more slowly. This coincides with the largest monetary expansion of the postwar era, and the pass-through is markedly asymmetric: each additional 1% of broad money (M2) lifts the upper end of the cross-section roughly twice as fast as the lower. The resulting configuration is the statistical signature of a latent fragility sustained without the corresponding macroeconomic event.

title: The Impact of a Rising State Pension Age Policy on Women’s Well-Being and Health Using Longitudinal Data from the UK
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE), London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE), Newcastle University, Newcastle University, Newcastle University and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: The Impact of a Rising State Pension Age Policy on Women’s Well-Being and Health Using Longitudinal Data from the UK

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests
declarations.funderStatement: This research is funded through the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Policy Research Unit in Healthy Ageing (funding reference NIHR206119).

detail.abstract:
Background: The UK aimed to prolong the working lives of women by introduced a policy raising women’s state pension age (SPA) from 60 to 66. The impact of involuntary prolonged employment on individual’s health and well-being is debated. We explore how the well-being, mental and physical health of the women impacted by the policy has been affected.

Methods: We used data from the first 12-waves of the longitudinal Understanding Society survey dataset. Using heterogeneous difference-in-difference models with regression adjustment we compared the outcomes of cohort of women affected by the policy born in financial years 1950/51-1955/56 to those unaffected by the policy born in 1949/50.

Findings: Our sample consisted of 16,251 observations across 1,832 women. Women impacted by the policy experienced better well-being and mental functionality, compared to those unaffected by the policy. This impact was significant specifically for the 1952/53 and 1953/54 cohorts and for women in professional and managerial occupations. The policy did not impact physical functionality. A robustness check using an unaffected male sample showed no such impact. 

Interpretation: Women impacted by the SPA increase appeared to have better well-being and mental functionality compared to women not affected by the policy. Trends in impacts appeared similar across sub-groups defined by job type. Limited statistical power for the sub-group analysis meant findings should be interpreted with caution.

detail.abstract:
Background: Despite neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) being the standard treatment for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC), response is profoundly heterogeneous. Pretreatment identification of pathological complete responders (pCR) and primary treatment resistors represents a critical unmet clinical need, yet no validated computational framework has integrated radiomics, topological data analysis (TDA), and deep learning features (DLFs) from multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) for this purpose.

Methods: In this retrospective, five-center study of 1,209 LARC patients, pretreatment mpMRI (T1WI, T2WI, DWI, ADC) was acquired from primary tumor and mesorectal lymph node regions. A tri-paradigm pipeline integrated handcrafted radiomics, TDA via persistent homology, and DLFs from a RadImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121, yielding 24 base classifiers per task. Their risk scores were fused through paradigm-specific, label-specific, and modality-specific branch pathways (generating 13 intermediate branch models), subsequently integrated via RankMeanFusion into final grand fusion models. Two binary tasks were evaluated: Task 1 (TRG 0 vs. TRG 1–3) and Task 2 (TRG 3 vs. TRG 0–2), across training (N=796), internal validation (N=200), and independent external validation (N=213) cohorts.

Findings: The grand fusion model achieved external validation AUROCs of 0.820 (95% CI: 0.752–0.884; sensitivity 0.860) for Task 1 and 0.918 (95% CI: 0.840–0.974; specificity 0.902) for Task 2, with favorable calibration and net clinical benefit on decision curve analysis. SHAP analysis indicated that mesorectal lymph node-derived features and functional MRI sequences (particularly ADC) were among the leading contributors across both tasks.

Interpretation: This unified mpMRI-based framework integrating radiomics, TDA, and DLFs shows promise for pretreatment nCRT response stratification in LARC, potentially supporting organ preservation selection and resistance-guided treatment individualization in prospective clinical workflows.

title: From Minor Ailments to Major Illnesses: A Practical Framework for Valuing Morbidity in Environmental Policy Analysis
affiliations: University of Central Florida and Columbia University

detail.title: From Minor Ailments to Major Illnesses: A Practical Framework for Valuing Morbidity in Environmental Policy Analysis
detail.abstract:
Environmental decisions often impact health, yet morbidity valuation remains challenging, with current approaches like cost-of-illness (COI) measures and Quality-Adjusted Life Years failing to reflect individuals’ willingness to pay to avoid adverse health states. This paper introduces a novel framework for valuing morbidity across health conditions, deriving willingness-to-pay (WTP) estimates using widely available preference weights and a baseline condition with known WTP. Our analysis reveals WTP estimates significantly exceeding commonly used COI measures, indicating undervaluation of health states in policy evaluations. Sensitivity analyses highlight variations consistent with those for the value of statistical life, underscoring the method's robustness. This framework offers a practical tool for integrating morbidity into analyses of environmental policy.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Associations of Combined IPTp and Insecticide-Treated Net Use in Pregnancy with Maternal Anaemia, Low Birth Weight, and Infant Death: A Pooled Survey Analysis Across 22 Sub-Saharan African Countries
affiliations: Tsinghua University, Tsinghua University, Tsinghua University and Tsinghua University - Vanke School of Public Health

detail.title: Associations of Combined IPTp and Insecticide-Treated Net Use in Pregnancy with Maternal Anaemia, Low Birth Weight, and Infant Death: A Pooled Survey Analysis Across 22 Sub-Saharan African Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
Background: Malaria in pregnancy remains a leading cause of preventable maternal and infant morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa. WHO recommends combined intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) and insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), but multi-country evidence on their combined benefit is limited.

Methods: We pooled survey-weighted data from the most recent Demographic and Health Surveys in 22 sub-Saharan African countries (2015-2023), restricting analysis to women aged 15-49 years with a live birth in the preceding 24 months (n=100,061), classified into four mutually exclusive uptake groups and, for dose-response analyses, five groups crossing IPTp intensity with net type. Survey-weighted logistic regression, adjusted for individual, household, and health-system factors and malaria incidence, estimated associations with maternal anaemia, low birth weight, infant death, and uptake determinants.

Findings: Combined protection was achieved by only 24·4% of women. Relative to no intervention, it was associated with 39% lower odds of infant death (adjusted odds ratio 0·61, 95% CI 0·50-0·75), 25% lower odds of low birth weight, and 24% lower odds of anaemia, with a graded dose-response gradient. Antenatal care engagement and household healthcare decision-making were the strongest modifiable determinants; women with zero antenatal visits had near-zero odds of receiving IPTp.

Interpretation: Combined malaria prevention in pregnancy is associated with substantially lower odds of adverse outcomes in a graded, dose-dependent manner, yet fewer than one in four women achieve it. Strengthening antenatal-care-linked IPTp delivery and addressing household barriers to care-seeking could narrow this gap and advance WHO 2030 targets.

title: Beyond Resources: Barriers and Facilitators to Emergency Medicine Development in Latin America and the Caribbean - A Multi-Country Qualitative Study

detail.abstract:
Background: Emergency care is increasingly recognized as a crucial part of health care delivery systems; thus, emergency medicine (EM) is rapidly expanding in Latin America and the Caribbean. Formal evaluation of the implementation of recent EM training programs is lacking to guide the process in other settings.ObjectiveTo describe the barriers and facilitators of developing EM residency training programs in Latin American and Caribbean countries.

Methods: We conducted semi-structured, virtual, individual qualitative interviews with key stakeholders involved in the development of EM training programs in Latin America and the Caribbean. Interviews were conducted in English or Spanish using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to guide interviews and analysis.

Findings: A total of 33 interviews were completed with emergency medicine (EM) physicians from 16 countries across Latin America and the Caribbean. Findings spanned all CFIR domains and included, in the outer setting, the need for structural and political preconditions that support EM development, and, in the inner setting, an institutional culture and resources to oppose inertia. Individual-level drivers included agency, resilience, and a mission-oriented nature amongst trainees and initial faculty. This constellation of preconditions allowed emergency medicine to achieve legitimacy within the health systems of the respective countries.

Interpretation: Emergency medicine development in resource-constrained settings is a process of constructing legitimacy, aligning institutions, and sustaining leadership across fragile systems. Programs that achieve technical capacity without securing political endorsement, institutional support, and faculty succession will remain structurally vulnerable.

title: Hierarchical Analysis of Distal, Occupational, and Proximal Determinants of Multisite Musculoskeletal Pain Among Female Beedi Rollers in India

detail.abstract:
Background: Women comprise more than 90% of India's beedi workforce, yet this predominantly home-based workforce remains largely invisible to occupational health systems. Previous studies have focused on pain at individual anatomical sites, leaving it unclear whether the cumulative musculoskeletal burden among women is driven by prolonged occupational exposure or by individual biological characteristics. We examined the hierarchical determinants of multisite musculoskeletal pain among female beedi rollers.

Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of data from a multicentre cross-sectional study involving 859 female beedi rollers recruited from five major beedi-producing states in India (2023–24). Multisite musculoskeletal pain was defined as the number of painful anatomical regions (0–6). Hierarchical robust Poisson regression sequentially evaluated sociodemographic, occupational, and health-related determinants, reporting adjusted incidence rate ratios (aIRRs) with 95% CIs.

Findings: Nearly one in three women reported pain affecting four or more body regions (mean pain score 2·78 [SD 1·72]). Occupational exposure emerged as the dominant determinant of multisite pain. Compared with women who had rolled beedis for fewer than 10 years, those with more than 20 years of exposure had a 27% higher pain burden (aIRR 1·27, 95% CI 1·07–1·51), while each additional working hour increased pain burden by 7% (1·07, 1·04–1·09). Married (1·69, 1·19–2·41) and widowed (1·77, 1·23–2·54) women also had greater multisite pain. In contrast, age, body mass index, anaemia, waist-to-hip ratio, education, and household wealth were not independently associated.

Interpretation: Among female beedi rollers, multisite musculoskeletal pain reflects cumulative gendered occupational exposure rather than biological vulnerability. Recognising home-based women workers as an occupational health priority is essential for integrating ergonomic interventions, musculoskeletal surveillance, and social protection into primary healthcare.

title: Air Pollution and Concentrated Clinical Severity of Respiratory Illness in Early Childhood: A Nationwide Quasi-Experimental Study in South Korea

detail.abstract:
Background: Fine particulate matter (PM2·5) is a leading environmental threat to child health, yet its effect on the intensity and economic burden of respiratory care in early childhood remains unclear. Most studies aggregate children <5 years or use visit counts alone, masking developmental heterogeneity in severity. We estimated the causal effects of PM2·5 on respiratory healthcare use and expenditure from birth through age 7 in a high-exposure setting.

Methods: We linked population-wide health insurance claims (2015–19) with child health screening records for 3·21 million South Korean children (99 261 945 child-months). Two outcomes were defined per child: monthly respiratory encounters and log respiratory expenditure. Thermal inversions, which trap domestic and transboundary emissions regardless of wind direction, instrumented monthly PM2·5 in two-stage least-squares regressions estimated for each age group, with child, year, and month fixed effects and controls for precipitation, income, occupation, and disability.

Findings: A 1-SD increase in monthly PM2·5 (7·23 μg/m³) raised respiratory encounters across ages 0–6, peaking at age 1 (0·29 additional visits per child-month, ~18·4% above the mean). Expenditure rose sharply only in children under 3 (46·7%, 43·0%, and 35·4% at ages 0, 1, and 2), becoming non-significant from age 4—corresponding to US$215 million in annual excess spending among children <5 years.

detail.title: Does AI Equalize or Amplify? Evidence from Two Field Experiments in AI-powered Learning
detail.abstract: While generative AI is rapidly transforming educational service delivery, most research has focused on taskcompletion settings. Less is known about whether AI can facilitate active skill acquisition, which requires learners to evaluate, absorb, and internalize feedback. This study examines whether AI coaching accelerates students' writing skill acquisition and how learning platforms can design the informational strategies to maximize educational value. We collaborate with a leading digital education platform in Asia to conduct two large-scale randomized field experiments in the context of IELTS writing preparation. In Study 1, involving 13,806 students, we find that access to an AI coaching assistant significantly improves writing performance and increases independent practice intensity. However, these benefits are unevenly distributed; students with higher baseline proficiency gain more from AI, suggesting that AI acts as an amplifier in skill-acquisition contexts. In Study 2, we conduct a 3 × 3 randomized field experiment involving 8,868 students, varying pre-use AI information disclosure and post-use feedback. We find that both AI disclosure and AI feedback improve score gains and stimulate independent practice. Effectiveness disclosure exerts a stronger influence than functionality disclosure, while both mastery feedback and performance feedback significantly improve learning outcomes. Moreover, effectiveness disclosure and mastery feedback interact positively, indicating that platforms can generate stronger engagement gains when they align pre-use expectations about AI effectiveness with post-use feedback about learner progress. Importantly, these interventions enhance performance and drive independent practice without requiring an increase in total AI usage volume. Our findings offer strategic guidance for digital education platforms in designing effective AI implementation strategies. Platforms should implement tailored scaffolding for students with lower baseline proficiency to ensure equitable learning outcomes. Furthermore, maximizing AI's educational impact requires moving beyond algorithmic optimization to focus on managing learner self-motivation and strategically designing the platform's information ecosystem.

title: Beyond Mean Exposure: How Exposure Variance Shapes Air Pollution Mortality Risk
affiliations: Western University, Stanford University, Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Stanford University, Stanford University, Stanford University, Stanford University, Yale University, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Agricultural & Resource Economics, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC) - National Center for Chronic and Noncommunicable Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC) - National Center for Chronic and Noncommunicable Disease Control and Prevention and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), Stanford University - School of Medicine

detail.title: Beyond Mean Exposure: How Exposure Variance Shapes Air Pollution Mortality Risk
detail.abstract:
Ambient air pollution contributes substantially to premature mortality globally, and the effectiveness of policies addressing it depends critically on the shape of the dose-response relationship, which remains poorly understood. Linking hourly air pollution data with daily vital statistics from 251 Chinese cities over four years, we show this relationship depends not only on the mean, but also on the variance of within-period exposure. At a 7-day mean of 150 μg/m3, predicted mortality varies more across observed hourly PM2.5 distributions than across mean exposure differences of 100 μg/m3. The sign of this variance effect also depends on the mean: at low mean concentrations (a convex region), higher variance is associated with modestly higher mortality. At higher concentrations (a concave region), greater variance is associated with lower mortality – implying constant exposure is more harmful than fluctuating exposure for a given mean. These findings reveal important relationships masked using temporally aggregated air pollution data.

detail.abstract: Five years after Bender et al. (2021) reframed large language models as stochastic parrots, the evaluative question has shifted from comprehension to autonomy: as models become agents that act on the world, how do we measure how much they act without human help? The leading answer, the Autonomy Index AIx = 1-interventions/steps (AlShikh et al., 2025), inherits two limitations from a half-century of robotics autonomy metrics. It is unconditional on policy: a strict regime makes the same agent look less autonomous, though the difference lies in the rules. And it is agnostic to infrastructure: every intervention is costed identically, when tooling changes per-intervention cost by an order of magnitude. We propose a conditional-autonomy framework closing both gaps-the policy-conditional coefficient γ Π , the economic form C(γ) with infrastructure factor κ, and Governance Infrastructure Leverage (GIL)-and prove four properties, including an EVOI floor exhibiting a κ-paradox: better infrastructure raises the EVOI-justified intervention rate while lowering total cost. We execute the synthetic experiment (N =120,000): the unconditional rate confounds a strict-tooled deployment with a lax ad-hoc one (0.500 vs. 0.501) while γ Π separates them; GIL recovers the planted κ = 12 exactly; the κ-paradox emerges as predicted. We also condition on time context-after-hours latent-harm exposure runs ∼11× business hours at indistinguishable γ Π-and specify the canonicalization and review-quality requirements that make γ reproducible. Autonomy is not an intrinsic agent property but an emergent property of agent, policy, and infrastructure-a murmuration, not a parrot.

title: Brand-Run or Influencer-Led? Pricing, Commission Design, and Price Transparency in Live Streaming Commerce

detail.title: Brand-Run or Influencer-Led? Pricing, Commission Design, and Price Transparency in Live Streaming Commerce
detail.abstract: Live streaming commerce has become a central retail interface in digital commerce, yet firms still face a fundamental channel-governance question: should they run their own livestreams or collaborate with influencers? We develop an analytical model in which a firm jointly chooses its live streaming mode, channel prices, and, when applicable, the influencer’s commission rate. The model incorporates consumer uncertainty about product fit, the influencer’s follower base, and the influencer’s reputation-based incentive to improve follower welfare through information provision and price-related concessions. We first analyze a same-platform environment in which consumers can directly compare e-commerce and live streaming prices, and then extend the analysis to a cross-platform environment with weaker price transparency. In the sameplatform setting, brand-run live streaming makes price parity optimal, whereas influencer-led live streaming yields three distinct patterns: micro-influencers may collaborate at zero commission; mid-tier influencers are the most prone to illusory discounts; and sufficiently large megainfluencers can induce genuine discounts paired with positive commissions. Relative to the no-livestreaming benchmark, the value of live streaming depends jointly on consumers’ initial information and the operational cost of unfit purchases; in particular, as consumers become better informed in the benchmark channel, the operational cost threshold decreases, making the adoption of live streaming more profitable for the firm. The cross-platform extension shows that weaker price transparency permits additional patterns, including live-streaming prices that exceed e-commerce prices for smaller influencers. Overall, the study endogenizes mode choice, channel pricing, and commission design, and identifies price transparency as a key boundary condition for live-streaming strategy.

affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Accounting Group, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Accountancy and

detail.title: Let's Talk: The Effects of Virtual Financial Advisor Interaction Mode and Gender Expression on Investor Judgments
detail.abstract: A virtual financial advisor (VFA) is an emerging form of robo-advisor that interacts using either an oral or text interaction mode. We conduct three experiments to examine how a VFA’s interaction mode and gender expression affect investors’ judgments, predicting that the oral interaction mode exacerbates investors’ sensitivity to VFA gender. Consistent with investors being more sensitive to a VFA’s gender when it interacts orally, participants in our first experiment favor the female over the male VFA, but only when the VFAs interact orally. Our second and third experiments provide evidence as to why, demonstrating that VFAs’ oral expressions amplify the impact of gender-based responsiveness stereotypes, which favor females. Our study contributes to the literature examining how technology affects investors’ reactions to financial information and educates regulators and brokerage firms about the implications of two central features of robo-advisors.

title: The Price of Correlation: Assortment and Inventory Design for Front-end Warehouses
affiliations: , National University of Singapore and

detail.title: The Price of Correlation: Assortment and Inventory Design for Front-end Warehouses
detail.abstract: This study examines joint assortment and inventory optimization in a two-layer warehouse e-commerce system that balances fast delivery with fulfillment cost efficiency. The system consists of a capacity-constrained front-end warehouse located near customers and a back-end warehouse with ample storage but higher fulfillment costs and longer delivery times. Before demand is realized, the firm decides which products and how much inventory to store in the front-end warehouse. After demand is realized, each order must be fulfilled entirely by either the front-end or the back-end warehouse. We assume that the marginal distributions of order-type demands are known, while their joint dependence structure is unspecified. This leads to a distributionally robust two-stage optimization problem over a Fréchet-class ambiguity set, which is difficult to solve directly because the set contains infinitely many joint distributions. To obtain a tractable model, we develop a pre-allocation approximation that allocates front-end inventory capacity at the order-type level using only marginal demand information. The approximation yields valid lower and upper bounds on the robust fulfillment value, and we identify conditions under which these bounds are tight. These results justify the marginal-distribution-based robust formulation and show that the price-of-correlation ratio is bounded. For a broad class of common-shape marginals with binary order types and linear size-based spillover costs, we show that the approximation admits a closed-form solution to the inventory-allocation subproblem and reduces to a cardinality-constrained assortment problem. We further prove that both the original model and the approximation are NP-hard, even in simplified settings. Numerical experiments show that the proposed approach produces tight bounds, retains most of the benchmark objective value, and delivers substantial computational savings. The results also reveal a clear trade-off between assortment width and inventory depth.

title: Programmable Incentives: Aligning Behavior in the Age of Agentic AI
affiliations: Cornell University and INSEAD - Strategy

detail.title: Programmable Incentives: Aligning Behavior in the Age of Agentic AI
detail.abstract: In the age of agentic AI, competitive advantage depends on two separable but mutually dependent capabilities. The first is intelligence generation: the ability to perceive signals, generate predictions, and execute decisions across the layered architecture of the AI Intelligence Stack (Dutta & Doz, INSEAD Working Paper, 2026/38/STR). The second is behavioral orchestration: the ability to mobilize the actions of all actors-human employees, ecosystem contributors, platform participants, and autonomous AI agents-in ways that convert that intelligence into sustained competitive outcomes. Existing strategy theory has developed increasingly sophisticated accounts of the first capability. This paper addresses the second, which is no less consequential and considerably less theoretically developed. The deployment of agentic artificial intelligence in organizations creates a behavioral alignment problem that existing incentive theory does not adequately address. Classical principal-agent frameworks were designed for dyadic relationships between a principal and a human agent, whose effort is observable only imperfectly and whose incentives must therefore be structured through contracts that balance risk and motivation. In AI-enabled organizations, the alignment challenge is qualitatively different: the relevant actors include not only human employees but also suppliers, ecosystem contributors, platform participants, and AI agents acting autonomously on behalf of principals; the relevant behaviors are observable at a granularity previously impossible; and the relevant timescale is continuous rather than periodic. This paper introduces the concept of programmable incentives: adaptive, software-based mechanisms that dynamically reward, recognize, prioritize, penalize, or grant access based on real-time behavioral signals and contribution assessments. Drawing on principal-agent theory, multi-task incentive design, the economics of intrinsic motivation, collective action theory, mechanism design, and the emerging literature on token economics, we propose a six-layer Programmable Incentives Stack-comprising contribution, measurement, incentive unit, allocation logic, governance, and feedback layers-as an analytical framework for the design and evaluation of programmable incentive systems. We argue that programmable incentives represent a new form of strategic infrastructure: as agentic systems proliferate and value creation becomes increasingly distributed across human, organizational, and machine actors, the ability to shape behavior dynamically and at scale becomes a primary determinant of competitive advantage. The paper situates the framework within a series of companion contributions on AI-era strategy and discusses implications for incentive design theory, ecosystem governance, and the limits of behavioral programmability.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Confidence Composite Index (CCI), a behavioral-institutional framework for measuring system-wide economic trust. The index combines Institutional-Capital Depth (ICDF), Hidden Wealth Integrity fragility (HWI), Liquidity Stress (LSI), and a PCA-based Confidence Multiplier (Phi). Using a 20-country panel covering 2000-2022, this version extends the baseline CCI paper by introducing a Confidence Fragility Index (CFI) and a WarningScore designed to test whether fragility accumulation appears before crisis realization. The empirical results show that the CCI framework is useful descriptively and that the WarningScore contains stronger information for medium-horizon fragility accumulation than the raw CCI alone. In the pilot crisis-window tests, the WarningScore performs better for broad 1-10 year and 3-10 year windows than for narrow one-year crisis prediction, supporting the interpretation that the framework detects structural fragility accumulation rather than precise crisis timing. The findings are preliminary and should be interpreted as a working-paper validation rather than a causal claim.The findings suggest that the framework is particularly useful for detecting the accumulation of systemic fragility several years before crisis realization rather than predicting the precise timing of crises.

title: Digital Transnational Education, Epistemic Sovereignty, and the Governance of Knowledge: A Critical Analytical Framework

detail.title: Digital Transnational Education, Epistemic Sovereignty, and the Governance of Knowledge: A Critical Analytical Framework
detail.abstract: Transnational education (TNE), defined as higher education provision in which learners are located in a country other than that awarding the credential, has undergone a structural transformation from physically bounded delivery modalities toward digitally mediated cross-border systems. This paper examines the structural opportunities, systemic tensions, and governance challenges that characterise contemporary digital TNE. Drawing on a critical conceptual analysis of interdisciplinary literature covering the period from 2007 to 2025, the paper investigates three interrelated problem domains: the conditions under which digital delivery extends access to historically marginalised populations; the regulatory fragmentation and data governance asymmetries that impede institutional accountability; and the epistemological consequences of a global digital education architecture concentrated within Western academic institutions and technology firms. Engaging the theoretical frameworks of Santos (2014), Mignolo (2009, 2011), Ndlovu-Gatsheni (2018), and Spivak (1988), the paper argues that access, taken alone, is an insufficient measure of equity when the underlying knowledge architectures reproduce colonial epistemological hierarchies. The paper contributes an original three-layer co-governance framework that integrates regulatory harmonisation, low-resource infrastructure design, and pluriversal curriculum coproduction as a coherent response to the structural deficiencies of current digital TNE arrangements. The framework is offered as a conceptual instrument for policymakers, institutional leaders, and accreditation bodies engaged in reforming cross-border higher education governance.

title: Optimising for Happiness in EU Technology Policy to Repay Public Subsidies for AI
affiliations: University of Oxford - Oxford Internet Institute, ,  and University of Reading

detail.title: Optimising for Happiness in EU Technology Policy to Repay Public Subsidies for AI

declarations.funderStatement: This work has been supported by the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation in the framework of the Alexander von Humboldt Professorship (Humboldt Professor of Technology and Regulation awarded to Sandra Wachter) endowed by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research via the Hasso-Plattner-Institute.

detail.abstract:
Backlash against the AI industry is growing globally. In recognition of the significant costs and risks borne by society to realise a technology of dubious value, policymakers, civil society, and the public are increasingly calling for action against AI companies. At the same time, AI proponents are loudly declaring that regulatory and ethical burdens are stifling innovation and risk losing the ‘AI arms race’. General-purpose AI systems pose severe and highly uncertain risks for society, and yet are sold predominantly on the basis that they enable economic growth and competitiveness, with little attention given to social or non-financial benefits. Economic growth is no guarantee of economic equality, and yet many of the risks and costs of AI are socialised.

For policymakers tasked with balancing fundamental and individual rights and EU values on the one hand, and innovation and free market competition on the other, striking a balance between these extremes is a seemingly impossible task. In this article we argue that a change of priorities is urgently needed in EU tech policy. We show how current policy predominantly focuses on risk mitigation rather than delivering socially beneficial tech. Making tech less risky does not guarantee it will be socially beneficial. The scales of policy must be tipped in favour of societal interests due to the substantial (in)direct subsidies paid to support the AI industry via tax breaks, public funding, privileged access to public lands, resources, data, and infrastructure, deregulation of data protection, labour, environmental and intellectual property laws. The public is in all but name a shareholder of AI companies, and yet is promised little in return to justify subsidies given on their behalf.

We propose adding a third pillar to re-balance EU AI policymaking: happiness. When policymakers are deciding whether subsidies should be granted or extended for the AI industry, they should require companies to concretely predict measurable benefits for public happiness, and hold them accountable for delivering on their predictions. To unpack this proposal, we examine decades of research in psychology to identify key determinants of happiness, focusing on three widely accepted traits: relatedness, competence, and autonomy.

detail.title: Operational and Competitive Effects of a Major External Supply-Side Shock: The Case of the Boeing 737 MAX Grounding

detail.abstract: We investigate the effects of a significant supply-side disruption in the commercial passenger airline industry-the grounding of the entire Boeing 737 MAX fleet following two fatal crashes involving this aircraft type. Unlike most other supply shocks in the aviation industry, this event impacted airlines differently depending on whether they had this type of aircraft in their fleet. Using data on schedules published before and after the grounding, we employ a difference-indifferences estimation strategy to capture the differentiated impacts of the Boeing 737 MAX grounding on airline operations. We find that Boeing 737 MAX operators quickly adjusted their schedules in response to the grounding, substituting larger aircraft and increasing flight frequency on affected routes. The resulting capacity on routes where the aircraft were scheduled was higher than originally planned before the grounding. We do not detect appreciable competitive responses from non-MAX operators to the extent they were reflected in their schedule adjustments. Overall, the evidence indicates that MAX operators acted quickly to minimize passenger disruption while defending markets where the grounded aircraft were deployed.

title: When Money's Time isn't always Valued: Accounting for behavioral Considerations in Business Tax Reform
affiliations: New York University School of Law

detail.title: When Money's Time isn't always Valued: Accounting for behavioral Considerations in Business Tax Reform
detail.abstract:
One of the fundamental questions in business taxation is whether to allow firms to immediately expense investments or require economic cost recovery, whereby firms deduct the cost over time in line with the asset’s depreciation. In 2025, Congress moved dramatically in the direction of expensing, establishing permanent 100% expensing for most assets for the first time since the inception of the income tax. 

The conventional view is that expensing will generate stronger investment and growth effects holding revenues constant. This view is rooted in traditional models of corporate finance that assume firms look at the net present value of expected tax payments when incorporating taxes into investment decisions. But these models ignore the possibility that firms look at other salient, market-relevant, or self-interested measures of taxes as well. If so, they may respond less to expensing than these models suggest because expensing does not lower firms’ “book” tax rate reported on their public financial statements and, all else equal, requires a higher statutory rate.

This paper explores whether firms undervalue expensing due to a focus on these other tax metrics and, if so, what this implies about business tax reform if the goal is to increase US investment. It develops a framework for what cost recovery rules are optimal, and then uses existing and previously unpublished data to parameterize this framework, holding constant long-run revenues and the relative tax treatment of debt and equity. It tentatively concludes that applying economic cost recovery to public and very large companies would generate more US investment and growth than expensing. Specifically, it estimates that, under reasonable assumptions, one could create the same functional tax incentives for large businesses to invest in the United States by adopting other tax reforms with 40 percent of the cost of expensing on a present value basis, thereby saving almost $1.3 trillion in revenues over 10 years. While, this estimate is sensitive to the underlying empirical parameters and could easily change, it casts considerable doubt on the conventional view that expensing will generate more US investment and growth than its alternatives.

title: New Evidence on the Health-Status Gradient from Imperial China
affiliations: University of Colorado, University of Colorado at Boulder - Department of Economics and Stanford University - Walter H. Shorenstein Asia-Pacific Research Center (APARC)

detail.title: New Evidence on the Health-Status Gradient from Imperial China
detail.abstract: We study the relationship between health and social status in China using genealogical data from the 14th to 19th centuries. The data covers broad segments of the population linking husbands, wives, and sons, allowing us to examine whether status was associated with survival not only for adult men but also across households and generations. In a sample centered on the early 1700s, the typical lifespan of married men is 52, but varies widely. High-status men have a 22 percent higher probability of living past 50 than low-status men, resulting in a lifespan advantage of seven years. High status is also associated with significant survival advantages for wives and children. The lifespan premium of the wife of a high-status man over the wife of a commoner exceeds 10 years, and the chance that the son of a high-status man dies before reaching 10 years is less than half that of a low-status man’s son. Up to the 17th century the lifespan advantage is largely confined to those with top status, while the health-status gradient across all status levels emerges during the 18th century. The findings provide new evidence on health-status inequality in a less-studied setting, and suggest that health-status inequality is usefully analyzed from a family and intergenerational perspective.

title: Who Owns AI?
affiliations: ,  and Independent

detail.title: Who Owns AI?
detail.abstract: Ownership positions established across the frontier AI supply chain over the next five years will determine which countries and companies accrue the economic and geopolitical power that advanced AI creates. This report maps investor positions across all segments of the supply chain — from critical minerals and chip manufacturing through compute infrastructure to model developers — covering venture capital, growth and private equity, corporate strategics, and sovereign wealth funds across the Middle East, East Asia, North America, and Europe, with ownership case studies of OpenAI, Anthropic, and TSMC. We find that influence operates through five mechanisms beyond investment volume; that hybrid compute-plus-equity deals now define the landscape; that value capture concentrates in chip design, advanced-logic manufacturing, and high-bandwidth memory; and that democratic sovereigns are materially under-positioned relative to Gulf and East Asian state capital. We conclude with four principles for democratic capital and jurisdiction-specific recommendations for sovereign and private investors, arguing the window for strategic positioning closes within roughly five years.

detail.title: The Paradox of Invisibility: How Brunello Cucinelli's Humanistic Capitalism Mirrors the Trust Dynamics of Elite Private Wealth Advisory
detail.abstract: This research paper explores the Paradox of Invisibility and Scalability within elite commerce, focusing on how Brunello Cucinelli achieved a record-breaking €1.408 billion in revenue while bypassing traditional conspicuous marketing channels, visible branding, and high-stimulus digital campaigns. By utilizing the framework of evolutionary counter-signaling, the paper analyzes how Cucinelli satisfies the ultra-high-net-worth individual’s (UHNWI) psychological need for discretion, ethical self-actualization, and human intimacy over digital automation. Furthermore, this study establishes a strategic parallel between Cucinelli's humanistic operations and the trust-based, relationship-driven architecture required in Private Wealth Advisory. Ultimately, the case demonstrates that in the era of rapid digital disruption, intentional scarcity and human relationship management remain the ultimate high-margin assets for securing intergenerational client loyalty.

detail.abstract:
Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are expected to play a central role in the digital transformation of transportation systems, yet their successful deployment depends on the interaction between technological learning and firms’ strategic investment decisions. While existing research has extensively examined accident probabilities and safety outcomes, comparatively little attention has been paid to how learning dynamics influence optimal investment and market introduction strategies. This paper develops a two-stage framework that integrates reinforcement learning with dynamic economic optimization to address this gap.

In the first stage, we simulate the learning process of an autonomous vehicle operating in a stylized road environment. Using a TD(0)-Search learning algorithm, the vehicle learns to navigate toward predefined destinations while avoiding accidents and traffic violations. The resulting performance measures—including accident rates, traffic violations, and task completion times—are used to characterize the relationship between training effort and operational performance. The simulation results reveal substantial learning gains over time, although the learning process is marked by considerable fluctuations rather than smooth improvement.

In the second stage, the generated performance data serve as inputs into a dynamic optimization model in which a monopolistic producer determines optimal investments in vehicle training and the timing of market introduction over a finite planning horizon. We first derive an open-loop investment strategy based on average performance outcomes and show that additional investments may become unattractive as the end of the planning horizon approaches. We then develop a state-dependent investment framework based on the Dyna-2 reinforcement learning algorithm, allowing investment decisions to adapt to the vehicle’s current learning state. The resulting closed-loop strategy consistently outperforms the open-loop benchmark and proves particularly effective in responding to heterogeneous and volatile learning trajectories.

By linking technological learning processes with economic decision-making, the paper provides a novel framework for analyzing the strategic deployment of autonomous vehicles and highlights the importance of adaptive investment policies in environments characterized by uncertainty and evolving performance.

title: Rapid Learning and Adaptive Search in Complex Environments: How Underestimating Noise in Performance Feedback Can Leverage and Resolve Errors of Commission
affiliations: Drexel University

detail.title: Rapid Learning and Adaptive Search in Complex Environments: How Underestimating Noise in Performance Feedback Can Leverage and Resolve Errors of Commission
detail.abstract: We investigate how managers' assumptions about noise in performance feedback impact adaptive search in complex environments. Using computer simulation, we demonstrate that rapid learners-managers who underestimate feedback noise and therefore revise their beliefs more aggressively-make more commission errors early on but can quickly self-correct these errors through additional experimentation. Over time, rapid learners reduce commission errors by increasingly detecting feedback with a high signalto-noise ratio, and this prompts resampling and belief refinement, allowing them to outperform even unbiased Bayesian learners in environments that are of greater complexity. In contrast, cautious learners-managers who overestimate feedback noise and therefore take longer to infer confidently the superiority of better alternatives-make fewer commission errors but more omission errors. Cautious learners perform poorly in complex environments but are effective in simpler search spaces, in which sensitivity to subtle performance differences is advantageous. Our findings provide boundary conditions for the learning literature's recommendation of gradual belief updating under uncertainty. Specifically, we show that underestimating feedback noise-and thus learning rapidly-can strike an effective balance: it encourages broad exploration early on, enabling the refinement of beliefs as managers encounter and repeatedly sample exceptionally high-performing solutions.

title: Syria's Path toward International Tax Integration
affiliations: Voyage Consulting

detail.title: Syria's Path toward International Tax Integration
detail.abstract:
This study examines Syria’s pathway toward integration into the modern international tax and financial system through institutional reform, OECD alignment, and long-term participation in advanced international economic governance frameworks. The paper argues that Syria’s most strategically important objective at this stage is not the immediate negotiation of bilateral tax treaties, but the formal initiation of a structured process toward engagement with the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and related international standards frameworks.

The timing of this study is particularly significant following Syria’s invitation to participate in the G7 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors meetings in Paris. This development represents an important political and economic opening for Syria to begin both the political and technical process of requesting structured engagement with OECD countries and institutions. The study presents this moment as a rare strategic opportunity to reposition Syria within the international economic system through a credible reform-oriented framework focused on transparency, governance modernization, financial integrity, and institutional reliability.

The paper explains that modern treaty readiness extends far beyond domestic tax reform. Developed economies increasingly evaluate potential treaty and investment partners based on broader institutional credibility, including regulatory transparency, exchange-of-information capability, anti-abuse enforcement, banking-sector governance, anti-money laundering systems, dispute-resolution mechanisms, and participation in internationally recognized frameworks such as the OECD/G20 BEPS initiative, FATF standards, CRS, and EOIR transparency systems.

The study reviews Syria’s recent reform efforts in fiscal policy, tax modernization, banking-sector rehabilitation, financial transparency, and engagement with international financial institutions. While these developments represent important progress, the paper emphasizes that substantial institutional, technical, and governance gaps remain and that long-term credibility will depend on sustained implementation and operational modernization.

Accordingly, the study strongly advises the Syrian finance ministry in coordination with the Syrian ministry of foreign affairs and related governmental institutions to undertake a comprehensive technical review of the frameworks discussed throughout the paper, particularly those relating to OECD standards, BEPS implementation, transfer pricing, exchange-of-information systems, FATCA cooperation, financial transparency, beneficial ownership, and international tax administration infrastructure. These technical components collectively form the operational foundation required for meaningful participation in modern international tax cooperation frameworks.

Ultimately, the study concludes that Syria’s long-term economic integration and investment competitiveness will depend on its ability to establish durable institutional trust, transparent governance systems, and internationally credible administrative capacity. Within this framework, future tax treaties with developed economies should be viewed not as initial objectives, but as outcomes of sustained institutional reform, international alignment, and successful integration into the global financial and economic system.

title: Why Organizations Resist Artificial Intelligence: Human Factors in AI Adoption

detail.title: Why Organizations Resist Artificial Intelligence: Human Factors in AI Adoption
detail.abstract: Despite advances in artificial intelligence, many organizations struggle to operationalize AI effectively. While technical limitations are often cited as barriers to adoption, this paper argues that organizational resistance to change represents a more significant obstacle. Drawing on literature from AI acceptance, organizational behaviour, and management studies, this paper examines how cultural inertia, mistrust, limited understanding, fear of job displacement, and misaligned incentives hinder AI integration. The findings suggest that successful AI adoption depends not only on technological capability but also on organizations' ability to foster trust, align incentives, and support employees through change.
