detail.abstract:
Enterprise AI transformation research has produced two complementary but separately developed frameworks: architectural models that explain how AI-native digital workplaces should be designed to drive durable adoption, and economic governance models that explain how AI velocity, return, and regulatory responsibility should be jointly managed. Both contribute substantially to the literature, but neither, on its own, gives an organization a way to answer the question every executive sponsor eventually asks: "Where are we right now, and what should we do next?"
This paper introduces the AIconomics Maturity Model, a five-stage diagnostic framework that
synthesizes architectural and economic governance dimensions of enterprise AI transformation
into a single, sector-agnostic progression: Unstructured, Activated, Governed, Calibrated, and
Compounding. Each stage is defined across four dimensions — data foundation, workforce
enablement, governance posture, and dominant organizational archetype — allowing an
organization in any industry to self-assess its current position without reference to industry-
specific benchmarks that may not exist or may not transfer across sectors.
The model is grounded in practitioner observation across enterprise AI programs in financial
services, professional services, and technology sectors, and is explicitly designed for cross-sector
applicability: the stages describe organizational conditions — data governance maturity enablement design, governance discipline — that are structurally identical regardless of the
specific products, regulatory regimes, or customer relationships an industry involves. The paper
introduces a self-assessment instrument practitioners can apply directly, documents the
progression dynamics between stages, including the common failure mode of stage-skipping, and
concludes with five propositions concerning maturity progression, regression risk, and the
conditions under which organizations advance from Governed to Calibrated — the transition this
paper identifies as the most consequential and most frequently mismanaged in enterprise AI
transformation

title: Report of the AI Negotiation Forum 11 January 2026

detail.title: Report of the AI Negotiation Forum 11 January 2026
detail.abstract:
This report presents the findings of the AI Negotiation Forum 2026, a practice-driven initiative examining the integration of artificial intelligence into negotiation, mediation, and diplomacy. Drawing on a global survey of 485 practitioners, focus group discussions, and expert roundtables hosted at Harvard Kennedy School, the study explores how negotiators are using AI, the benefits and risks they perceive, and the capacities and governance frameworks required for responsible adoption.

The findings show that AI is already widely embedded in negotiation practice, primarily for preparation, analysis, drafting, and sense-making. While practitioners report significant gains in efficiency, analytical support, and learning, they also identify substantial risks related to confidentiality, bias, over-reliance, loss of judgment, and institutional accountability. Across all stages of the Forum, participants emphasized that the most significant challenges of AI integration are not technical but cognitive, ethical, and institutional. Human judgment, relational intelligence, and accountability remain central to negotiation and cannot be delegated to AI systems.

The report argues that AI integration should be understood primarily as a workflow and governance challenge rather than a tool-adoption problem. It calls for the development of human-centered AI architectures, enhanced practitioner and institutional capacity, robust governance frameworks, and new approaches to training that preserve judgment while leveraging AI’s analytical capabilities. By grounding analysis in practitioner experience, the report contributes to emerging debates on the responsible use of AI in negotiation, mediation, and diplomacy and offers a roadmap for future research, policy, and professional practice.

title: What Prediction Markets can See

detail.title: What Prediction Markets can See
detail.abstract: Prediction markets are usually evaluated after their contracts exist, by asking how well prices forecast outcomes. We study the prior institutional margin of market formation, asking which uncertainties become tradable contracts at all. Using an audited dataset of 6,047 Africa-topic and Latin Americatopic contracts listed on Polymarket and Kalshi, we construct a coded measure of settlement legibility, the degree to which an uncertainty can be worded, sourced, and credibly resolved by third parties, and validate it on 451 units under a frozen codebook, where independent double scoring reaches ordinal reliabilities of 0.92 and 0.96 on the primary dimensions and blind human benchmarks reach 0.97 and 0.92. Using this measure, we find that formation is selective in ways that public importance does not explain, with African inventory concentrated overwhelmingly in football while salient civic events produce little or no inventory, and Latin American inventory deeper but dominated by Venezuela, where attention to prospective United States military action sustains the largest civic cluster in the data. Legibility orders the inventory steeply, with sports and elections near the top of the scale and conflict at the bottom. In a formation test against an externally assembled frame of 131 civic events, legibility predicts listing in the expected direction but falls short of pre-specified acceptance criteria, while among listed contracts the relation between legibility and trading value is negative, as a model of selective listing implies and as we predicted before estimation. Prediction-market inventories therefore measure what platforms can settle as much as what traders believe, and reading them as maps of public interest conflates the two.

title: Environmental Surveillance and Strategic Action in Turbulent Business Environments: The Roles of Managerial Cognition, Assumption Integrity, and Organizational Power

detail.title: Environmental Surveillance and Strategic Action in Turbulent Business Environments: The Roles of Managerial Cognition, Assumption Integrity, and Organizational Power

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The conceptual article does not involve human participants, animal subjects, identifiable personal data, sources of interest, experiments, or primary data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly operate in turbulent environments marked by technological disruption, market volatility, competitive discontinuity, regulatory change, social pressure, and geopolitical uncertainty. Although environmental scanning and forecasting are widely recognized as important strategic activities, organizations often fail to convert environmental signals into timely strategic action. This conceptual research paper argues that the problem is not merely the availability of data, but the way data are detected, interpreted, legitimized, and authorized inside the firm. Building on environmental surveillance, weak-signal theory, managerial cognition, dominant logic, organizational power, dynamic capabilities, and Ansoffian strategic posture, the paper advances a theoretical model linking weak and strong environmental signals to surveillance systems, incoming data, managerial cognition filters, perceived environmental turbulence, and strategic action. The paper introduces assumption integrity as a central condition for improving the quality of strategic perception. It further argues that power filters may suppress or amplify signals depending on governance structures, political interests, authority patterns, incentives, and leadership behavior. The paper contributes to strategic management by explaining how firms may misread turbulence even when information is available and by offering propositions for future empirical testing. Practical implications are provided for managers seeking to strengthen surveillance openness, mental-model renewal, signal governance, dynamic capability development, and long-term strategic sustainability.

title: Against Corporate Contractualism: A Reappraisal Of Fundamental Neoliberal Ideology Of "Agency Cost" And "Nexus Of Contracts" In Corporate Law And Economics After Five Decades
affiliations: University of Florida Levin College of Law

detail.title: Against Corporate Contractualism: A Reappraisal Of Fundamental Neoliberal Ideology Of "Agency Cost" And "Nexus Of Contracts" In Corporate Law And Economics After Five Decades
detail.abstract: Introduced in 1976, at the neoliberal turn of the American political economy, “agency cost” has been the idée fixe in corporate governance. Having become the foundational economic idea in the field of corporate law and economics, it shifted the paradigm from stakeholder capitalism and managerialism of the post-war consensus to today’s financial capitalism and shareholderism. Despite rapid, widespread acceptance in the legal academy, the ideas of “agency cost” and its antecedent conceptual condition (that the firm is nothing but a “nexus of contracts”) have never had a legitimate legal grounding, explaining why in the past half century lawmakers have never seriously engaged with the economists’ twin metaphors. This Article reappraises the original economic ideas of corporate contractualism. This analysis reveals a deep ignorance or casual disregard of corporate law and the legal and economic foundation of firms. The law must be integrated into any theory of the firm (economic or legal or otherwise) for without the sovereign’s legal endowment per corporate law, the firm could not be and capital creation would be impossible. More pointedly, the corporation’s economic production function and the transformation of mere property to capital are founded on fundamental rules of law, and therefore even economic models of the firm must credulously account for the rule of law. In light of its deep flaws, corporate contractualism is at best a thin analytical framework to understand the actual workings of the corporation at its structural level. But this framework had a specific purpose. It is a reverse engineered product; economists created it to support an ideological normative proposition. The principal–agent model of the manager–shareholder relationship and nexus of contracts conception of the corporation are inextricably constructed as an intellectual architecture in a normative project. Their purpose was intended ab initio to advance a political economic ideology: that set of beliefs being, (1) corporate law and governance lie in the purely private sphere of contract between managers and shareholders, (2) the purpose of that agency relationship is for the latter’s maximal wealth gain, and thus (3) constituent interest and public obligations have no place in corporate purpose. The intellectual project of corporate contractarians had always been to efface the socio-economic institution of the corporation and its publicness, which in the past half century has been embraced as a commitment of academic thinking on corporate law and American brand of financial capitalism. When, however, the corporation is seen as a legal entity born from the rule of law and public endowment, as it surely is, intellectual space in its object function opens up to consider how these distinct legal persons should behave in society, the roles that they can play to promote the public welfare, and the responsibilities that society should rightly expect of them in light of the fact that the indubitable, indispensable antecedent condition of the corporation is a legal–political endowment of the public.

title: Iran's Changing Conflict Posture Under Environmental Turbulence: A Strategic Management Model of Asymmetric Positioning

detail.title: Iran's Changing Conflict Posture Under Environmental Turbulence: A Strategic Management Model of Asymmetric Positioning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No person, any financial interest, or relationship affiliated with this paper.

detail.abstract: This conceptual article examines Iran’s changing conflict posture through a strategic management lens. Rather than interpreting Iran’s regional behavior solely as military confrontation, ideological resistance, or geopolitical defiance, the article frames Iran’s approach as a strategic adaptation to intense environmental turbulence, a conventional military imbalance, economic sanctions, technological disruption, and repeated external pressure. The analysis argues that Iran has developed an asymmetric conflict posture based on distributed deterrence, low-cost technological scaling, regional partner networks, strategic ambiguity, and long-horizon patience. These elements allow Iran to compete indirectly against stronger adversaries by altering the cost structure, time horizon, and operational logic of modern conflict. The article does not endorse the conduct of any state or non-state actor; rather, it examines how asymmetric strategic posture may emerge under conditions of environmental turbulence and conventional imbalance. The article concludes that Iran’s conflict posture illustrates a broader strategic management principle: under high turbulence, weaker actors may survive and exert influence not by directly matching stronger competitors, but by adopting a posture that fits the environment, exploits adversaries' vulnerabilities, and converts structural weakness into asymmetric leverage.

title: Philosopher Inequality for Online Assortment Optimization
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Operations Management Area, Rotman School of Management and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Philosopher Inequality for Online Assortment Optimization

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rotman School of Management Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Online assortment optimization is fundamental to retail and marketplace operations. In this problem, a seller offers subsets of products to customers who arrive sequentially and make stochastic purchase decisions governed by a choice model. In prior work, algorithms for this setting have been evaluated against an offline benchmark that knows future arrivals. However, such guarantees are capped at 1/2, a barrier rooted in well-known prophet inequalities. In this work, we compare against the online optimum, where only stochastic information about future arrivals is known, and study whether stronger guarantees are achievable when the algorithm and benchmark face the same uncertainty. This benchmark is known as the philosopher inequality. We develop a fluid relaxation that captures online feasibility constraints absent from offline formulations, and we design a polynomial-time algorithm that exploits this additional structure. For the basic attraction model (which includes multinomial logit as a special case), we establish a 0.53-approximation ratio in the single-unit inventory setting (i.e., multiple products each with one unit), thereby surpassing the 1/2 barrier. This result extends to multi-unit inventory (i.e., multiple products each with multiple units), where the achievable ratio remains strictly above 1/2. Our philosopher-inequality results can also be extended to incorporate pricing. However, we also prove that for general discrete choice models beyond the basic attraction choice model, no algorithm can beat the approximation ratio of 1/2 with respect to a natural fluid relaxation. Our findings establish the first improvement over the long-standing 1/2 barrier for online assortment problems in stochastic settings, demonstrating the power of the philosopher inequality framework.

title: High sensitivity of the knee joint response in stair ascent to changes in knee kinematics, kinetics and joint center positioning
affiliations: Polytechnique Montreal and Polytechnique Montreal - Department of Mechanical Engineering

detail.title: High sensitivity of the knee joint response in stair ascent to changes in knee kinematics, kinetics and joint center positioning
detail.abstract: Compared to level walking, stair ascent imposes larger mechanical demands on the knee joint involving elevated muscle, ligament, and contact forces. This study investigates knee biomechanics in stair ascent using a lower-extremity coupled musculoskeletal finite element (MS-FE) model. Focus is on the sensitivity of biomechanical response both to reported scatter in knee joint kinematics/kinetics and to the alteration in the knee joint reference point (RP) location. Three highly loaded instances of stance, 25%, 50%, and 75%, were analyzed. Six knee joint kinematics-kinetics variables of flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, and internal-external rotations/moments, were varied at five levels each using a L25 Taguchi design. Regression analyses quantified the contribution of each variable to predicted muscle, ACL, patellar tendon, tibiofemoral (TF), and patellofemoral (PF) contact forces. The effect of shifting the knee RP in anterior-posterior and medial-lateral directions was also examined in our MS-FE model and compared to its scaled OpenSim model. Flexion moment was the dominant contributor to quadriceps, patellar tendon, and PF contact forces, whereas adduction-abduction angle and not moment governed medial-lateral TF load partitioning. ACL force was sensitive to knee rotations and flexion moment suggesting a multiplanar response in stair ascent. Shifting RP location altered passive reaction moments in the MS-FE model with no effects on muscle and internal forces. In contrast, OpenSim results markedly altered with anterior-posterior shifts in RP. These results emphasize the importance of incorporating the reported scatter in measurements as well as the substantial sensitivity of all MS results to the RP positioning in stair ascent biomechanics.

title: Gig Work in India: Between Structural Compulsion and Voluntary Choice
affiliations: and Deen Dayal Upadhyaya College, University of Delhi

detail.title: Gig Work in India: Between Structural Compulsion and Voluntary Choice
detail.abstract: This paper assesses whether the expansion of gig work in India reflects voluntary worker preference or structural compulsion arising from underlying labour market conditions. It explores the possibility that gig labour supply is shaped by factors such as informality, underemployment, and limited formal job creation, rather than being driven solely by a preference for flexible work arrangements. The analysis is guided by a theoretical framework drawing on the Lewis dual-sector model, Rodrik's concept of premature deindustrialisation, and a push-pull approach to labour market entry. Empirically, the paper adopts a quantitative descriptive approach using a time-series analysis for the period 2017-18 to 2020-21. Gig workforce size is treated as the dependent variable, while the unemployment rate and the share of self-employment are used as indicators of labour market conditions. Pearson correlation coefficients are computed to examine the direction of association between these variables. The analysis draws on secondary data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) Annual Reports, along with gig workforce estimates from NITI Aayog (2022) and the Economic Survey 2025-26. In addition, the paper undertakes a qualitative assessment of the classification frameworks of the PLFS and the eShram portal to evaluate whether gig workers can be identified as a distinct category. The results show that gig workforce growth coincides with rising self-employment and falling unemployment. While the limited number of observations precludes causal inference, this pattern is consistent with the possibility that entry into gig work may be shaped more by constrained access to regular salaried employment than by a purely voluntary preference for flexibility. The paper contributes by analysing gig work through the lens of structural compulsion and voluntary choice, and by identifying gaps in official data systems and enumerations that limit the visibility of gig workers.

title: Boundary-Aware Risk-Fidelity Surrogates for Derivative Engines: Realistic Teachers, Hard Payoffs, and Market-Guarded Hybrid Deployment

detail.title: Boundary-Aware Risk-Fidelity Surrogates for Derivative Engines: Realistic Teachers, Hard Payoffs, and Market-Guarded Hybrid Deployment
detail.abstract:
This paper studies boundary-aware supervised surrogates for derivative pricing and risk engines. The final deployment object is interpreted as a repaired, market-guarded hybrid rather than an unconditional neural replacement. The work extends the sensitivity-engine sequence from analytic Greek and boundary decompositions toward an empirical deployment setting with realistic teachers, hard payoff classes, and market-facing option-chain checks.

The empirical design uses two layers. Layer F is a retrospective market-state layer built from MarketData daily candle histories for SPY and QQQ, public Treasury data, volatility-index proxies, and liquidity-related inputs. Layer M adds selected MarketData end-of-day option-chain snapshots for market-facing calibration and validation. The dataset is a selected snapshot archive rather than an exhaustive daily full-history option-surface archive.

The evidence is consistent with a controlled and deliberately modest conclusion. Boundary-aware and decomposition-aware supervision appears most useful in difficult local regions, while the reported deployment gains arise when structural training is combined with uncertainty-aware fallback, financial-consistency repair, and market guards. On the controlled teacher-labeled layer, the repaired hybrid attains the lowest reported global price error within the paper’s test design. On the option-chain validation layer, the coherent marketfacing object is the guarded overlay, which is designed to prevent unstable repaired or overlay values from entering the accepted-contract comparison. The results therefore favor a disciplined deployment architecture rather than a claim of uniform neural-surrogate dominance.

title: Internal Open Innovation Firm Practices & Strategic Value Capture

detail.title: Internal Open Innovation Firm Practices & Strategic Value Capture
detail.abstract:
Authored by Almog Goldstein, Founding Executive Director of the UC Berkeley Open Innovation Labs, this paper examines how the OI Labs helps firms reconfigure internal routines to foster a culture of “strategic openness.” Moving beyond tactical collaboration, the study emphasizes that the success of Open Innovation (OI) is predicated on an internal mindset shift – viewing underutilized R&D not as a “misfit” to be patented and abandoned, but as an asset for Inside-Out value capture.

The summary highlights three critical internal capabilities: 
● Strategic Alignment & Value Capture: Aligning leadership to move beyond “money” as the sole metric, instead focusing on how internal tacit knowledge and cross-functional coordination can be leveraged to meet long-term organizational goals. 
● The WFGM Framework (Want-Find-Get-Manage): A structural tool used to overcome internal inertia. It forces firms to rigorously evaluate internal knowledge before defaulting to R&D, and mandates active partnership governance to prevent “invisible” or stagnant collaborations. 
● Dynamic Capabilities (Sense, Seize, Transform): Based on David Teece’s theory, this practice details how firms like Apple reconfigure internal structures (e.g., creating the App Store) to transform a “seized” opportunity into a sustainable ecosystem.

Ultimately, the case demonstrates that OI success is less about external sourcing and more about the internal absorptive capacity and change management required to navigate a world of knowledge abundance

detail.abstract:
For over half a century, the international monetary and financial system (IMFS) has functioned not as a politically neutral public utility but as a centralized mechanism of geopolitical enforcement dominated by primary Western economic powers. This monograph presents the People's Ledger Network (PLN) — a sovereign-decentralized financial operating system engineered as a direct architectural intervention against both macro-geopolitical coercion and micro-retail rent-seeking.

Architecturally sustained by the Pi Network consensus framework and implementing the Stellar Consensus Protocol (SCP), the PLN decouples cross-border multi-fiat clearance from centralized Western clearers. Across twelve chapters spanning five thematic parts, this work analyzes the structural failures of the legacy IMFS (Part I), details core systems topology and multi-fiat clearing (Part II), presents the PLN's tokenomic and AMM liquidity architecture (Part III), evaluates advanced risk mitigation systems, TWAP oracles, and Byzantine fault tolerance (Part IV), and concludes with concrete policy recommendations and a phased strategic implementation roadmap (Part V).

title: Pricing and Hedging a Jamaican Dollar Quanto Option on the S&P 500 Index
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Pricing and Hedging a Jamaican Dollar Quanto Option on the S&P 500 Index
detail.abstract: This paper presents a practical framework for pricing and hedging Jamaican Dollar (JMD) denominated quanto options, also known as guaranteed exchange rate options, on the S&P 500 Index. Historically, low liquidity in domestic equities has constrained the availability of advanced derivative products for local dealers. By leveraging the deep liquidity of the USDJMD spot market and US-listed options, this study demonstrates how local dealers can synthetically manufacture and dynamically hedge these exotic instruments. The proposed self-financing structure successfully isolates market exposure from exchange rate volatility. We also show that dynamic hedging strategies that incorporate adjusted delta positions and dynamic USD spot trading effectively mitigate the dealer’s residual market and FX risks. Ultimately, this framework provides a scalable foundation for expanding the universe of JMD-investable securities and advancing local capital market capabilities.

title: Canon Omissions: Ten Foundational Papers and the Questions They Deferred

detail.title: Canon Omissions: Ten Foundational Papers and the Questions They Deferred

detail.abstract: The ten most-cited papers in modern AI solved discrete engineering problems with precision and consequence. They also made a shared choice: to abstract away the user. From Turing's imitation game to GPT-3's few-shot generalization, each landmark deferred questions of identity, memory, ownership, and consent — not by accident, but by design. This paper maps those deferrals systematically, argues they are structural rather than incidental, and demonstrates that the resulting capability-accountability gap is now the field's most pressing architectural problem. Emerging work in stateful, privacy-first, and consent-aware AI design addresses what the canon never asked. The omissions were not failures of intelligence. They were failures of scope — and scope can be corrected.

title: Positioning Is Memory Design: A Systemic Architecture for Strategic Positioning in Complex Decision Environments

detail.title: Positioning Is Memory Design: A Systemic Architecture for Strategic Positioning in Complex Decision Environments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Strategic positioning is commonly theorized as a problem of signal emission: actors communicate value and receptor systems evaluate what they receive. This article argues that this framing locates the decisive mechanism too late in the process. In consequential decision environments, the central problem is not only what actors emit but what occurs inside the receptor system after a signal arrives: how value is interpreted, classified, stored in operative memory and retrieved when a decision window opens. Drawing on cybernetic theory (Wiener, Beer), predictive processing (Friston, Clark), organizational sensemaking (Weick), signaling theory (Spence) and bounded rationality (Simon), the article develops a systemic architecture organized around five interdependent variablesinterpretation, legitimacy, eligibility, centrality and activation-operating on a common substrate: operative memory. It also introduces the Prism Effect, a geocognitive mechanism by which an actor's origin conditions interpretation before any deliberate signal is processed, and a dual entropic logic distinguishing positioning within cooperative systems from competition in adversarial environments. Three practitioner-embedded cases across commercial, organizational and closed institutional settings are used for theory elaboration and analytic pattern matching. The article contributes to systems research by reframing strategic positioning as the architecture of retrievability: the disciplined design of conditions under which verified value becomes legible, classifiable, memorable and actionable inside decision systems.

title: OCEAN: A Five-Phase Framework for Meaningful Change

detail.title: OCEAN: A Five-Phase Framework for Meaningful Change
detail.abstract: Managing meaningful change requires more than motivation, insight, or isolated techniques. This paper introduces OCEAN, a five-phase conceptual framework for structuring non-clinical developmental conversations and change-oriented interventions in coaching, leadership, and organizational settings. The five phases are Observe, Create, Expose, Awaken, and Nurture. In Observe, actors develop a systemic, present-oriented understanding of the situation. In Create, they turn that understanding into goals that are meaningful and actionable. In Expose, they identify attempted solutions, resistances, biases, and self-deceptions that maintain ineffective patterns. In Awaken, they activate new behaviors through planning, reframing, paradoxical movement, and emotionally significant experiences. In Nurture, they consolidate progress through repetition, habits, connection, and sustainable contexts. OCEAN integrates insights from systemic and interactional thinking, goal construction, emotional awareness, and habit consolidation into a structured process. I present it as an approach for guiding change in individuals and teams, particularly within coaching and organizational development contexts, and outline directions for future research.

detail.abstract: Some organizations have opened the door to consideration of microcredentials by reducing degree requirements for roles. However, evidence shows that simply changing policies does not necessarily change hiring behaviors. Recent research found that 45% of firms removing degree requirements from job postings showed no significant difference in the share of non-baccalaureate hires, while 20% showed a decrease in hires without degrees. This report shares findings from a national survey of hiring manager. Responses indicate that hiring managers have a high level of awareness of microcredentials. However, they appear to value them more as a sign of a candidate’s ambition, discipline, or learning mindset rather than a measure of specific skill competence. Managers express much lower confidence in their ability to signal specific skills. This perception might be due to the fact that microcredentials currently serve primarily as supplements to degrees. Managers who have, themselves, earned microcredentials are more likely to consider candidates who hold them. To bolster managers’ confidence in microcredentials, it is crucial to align them accurately with job roles, which involves assessing their quality, rigor, content, and relevance. Companies should be encouraged and empowered to process information about microcredentials and develop perspectives on which are the most salient for their specific needs.

detail.title: Monetary policy transmission through the financial system to households
detail.abstract: This Occasional Paper reviews evidence from the ChaMP Research Network on the transmission of monetary policy to households in the euro area – an area of monetary policy that has attracted less attention among researchers. It highlights thecentral role of banks and non-bank intermediaries in shaping how policy affects borrowing, saving and consumption. Despite the overall effectiveness of monetary policy in the euro area, the pass-through of policy rates to household borrowingcosts is incomplete and heterogeneous, reflecting differences in funding structures, market power and institutional settings.A key insight is that transmission depends on household heterogeneity. Differences in balance sheets, credit access and housing market characteristics produce uneven effects across income, age and wealth groups, with important implications foraggregate demand and distributional consequences. Another key finding is that several components of consumption respond more rapidly to changes in interest rates than previously thought, especially in high-debt, variable-rate environments.Overall, the findings point to the need for an integrated, system-wide perspective that accounts for multiple aspects of financial structure and heterogeneity when assessing monetary policy transmission. ChaMP research also highlights the valueof readily available granular data, as many novel findings stem from a major coordinated effort to use new data on households obtained from national credit registers, as well as novel granular data on household expenditure.

detail.title: Monetary policy transmission and non-bank financial intermediation
detail.abstract: The growing importance of non‑bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) also has important implications for the transmission of monetary policy in the euro area. It alters the composition of credit supply and strengthens the role of market‑based finance for the corporate sector. title: The propagation of shocks across the production network and implications for monetary policy
affiliations: European Central Bank, European Central Bank (ECB), CEPR, European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB), , European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research, , Bank of Spain and Austrian National Bank

detail.title: The propagation of shocks across the production network and implications for monetary policy
detail.abstract: The repeated occurrence of supply-chain disruptions since the COVID-19 pandemic reveals the need to complement traditional macroeconomic frameworks with approaches that better capture the complexity of modern economic productionstructures. This paper synthesises the findings of the ChaMP Research Network, highlighting how production network models and heterogeneity across firms, sectors and countries enrich our understanding of monetary policy transmission. Bycapturing input-output relationships between firms and economic sectors, these approaches show how the propagation and persistence of shocks depend on network structure, the position of sectors within the network – where central sectorsexert disproportionate influence – and differences and variations in price and wage flexibility. The inflationary effects of supply shocks tend to be amplified, while the effects of demand shocks, including monetary policy shocks, are dampened. Inaddition, large shocks can give rise to nonlinearities, such as a steepening of the Phillips curve. This aligns with the conclusions of the ECB’s most recent strategy assessment, which emphasise the need to analyse the risks surrounding the inflationoutlook. The findings also point to the emergence of trade-offs between inflation and output gap stabilisation, as production networks and heterogeneity weaken the alignment between price and output dynamics. As a result, stabilising inflation andoutput simultaneously calls for astute fiscal policy. Overall, incorporating production networks provides a more nuanced and policy-relevant framework for designing state-contingent and data-informed monetary policy.

detail.title: Monetary policy transmission and structural changes
detail.abstract: This paper surveys research from the ESCB ChaMP Research Network on how ongoing structural change is affecting monetary policy transmission in the euro area. It shows that transmission is state-dependent and varies systematically with changesin the sectoral composition of the economy, in its international integration, in financial conditions and in inflation regimes. More service-intensive economies exhibit weaker real responses to monetary tightening, while high-inflation environments areassociated with faster and stronger price pass-through, helping explain why the recent disinflation episode entailed relatively low output costs. The paper also shows that variations in leverage, supply shocks and energy-related disturbances alter theinflation-output trade-off and can make appropriate policy responses more contingent on the source and persistence of shocks. Finally, it reviews evidence that monetary policy can affect the supply side through innovation, reallocation and productivity, implying that structural change influences transmission and may itself be influenced by policy.
